title: The Vimalakirti Sutra
summary: The layman Vimalakirti is “ill”. None of the Buddha’s great disciples dare visit him, since he has out-argued each of them; Manjushri goes, and the two talk about non-duality.
compare: 这部经在中文世界几乎只靠鸠摩罗什的译本流传，他的许多句子已经成了熟语：「随其心净，则佛土净」「不断烦恼而入涅槃」「以众生病，是故我病」「一切烦恼为如来种」「芥子纳须弥」。拿梵本对照，这些句子大体忠实，但常被他磨得更短、更像格言，有时意思也随之移动。例如梵文说「心清净到什么程度，佛土就清净到什么程度」，讲的是程度上的对应；「随其心净」读起来却像「只要心净，土就净」。又如 gotra 本是「家族、出身」，中文「种」兼有「种子」的意思，于是「烦恼是如来种」常被读成「烦恼是成佛的种子」。英文照梵文直译，所以英文读者看到的往往比中文读者熟悉的句子更长、更绕，也更贴近原来的论证。

最需要留意的是第八品「不二法门」。梵本里文殊先对前面三十一位菩萨说「你们所说的一切，其实都还是二」，再说「不说」才是不二；鸠摩罗什删去了这句批评，只留下客气的「如我意者」。维摩诘的回应，梵文只有几个词：「离车人维摩诘，沉默了」。没有形容，没有动作。后来禅宗说的「维摩一默」「一默如雷」，是后人的评语。英文和白话都照原文写得一样短，不替经文加戏。还要对照的是第六品的舍利弗：他被天女问住时也沉默了，天女却不认可，说「不要离开文字去说解脱」。同样是沉默，经文刻意分出了两种。

第三个差别是梵文的双关。这部经大量用同一个词根的两层意思来翻转道理：svāgata（欢迎，字面「来得好」）与 anāgata（没有来）；天女的 kalpika（合规矩的）与 kalpayati（妄想分别）；asthāna 的「不可能」与「无处」；tīrthika（外道，字面「造渡口的人」）与 tīrtha（渡口）；gati 的「道路」与「通达」。英文和白话都保不住这些双关，只能把两层意思分开说，再在对照注里指出来。鸠摩罗什的办法常常是把双关改写成一句道理（如「不来相而来」「行于非道，是为通达佛道」），读起来顺，却少了原文那种当场把人问住的机锋。
compareEn: In the Chinese world this sutra has lived almost entirely through Kumarajiva’s translation, and many of his lines have become proverbs: 随其心净，则佛土净 (“as the mind is pure, so the buddha-land is pure”), 不断烦恼而入涅槃 (“entering nirvana without cutting off the afflictions”), 以众生病，是故我病 (“because beings are ill, I am ill”), 一切烦恼为如来种 (“all afflictions are the seed of the Tathagata”). Set against the Sanskrit, these lines are broadly faithful, but he often polishes them into shorter, more aphoristic sayings, and sometimes the meaning shifts with them. The Sanskrit says “to whatever degree the mind is pure, to that degree the buddha-field is pure,” a correspondence of degree; 随其心净 (suí qí xīn jìng) reads more like “just purify the mind and the land is pure.” Likewise gotra means “family, lineage,” but the Chinese 种 (zhǒng) also means “seed,” so “afflictions are the Tathagata’s 种” is usually read as “afflictions are the seed of buddhahood.” The English follows the Sanskrit, so English readers often meet a longer, more winding sentence than the one Chinese readers know, but one closer to the original argument.

The place that most needs attention is chapter 8, on non-duality. In the Sanskrit, Manjushri first tells the thirty-one bodhisattvas before him that “everything you have explained is still two,” and only then says that not speaking is non-duality; Kumarajiva drops this criticism and keeps only a polite 如我意者 (“as I see it”). Vimalakirti’s answer, in the Sanskrit, is a few words: “Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi became silent.” No description, no gesture. The later Chan phrases 维摩一默 (“Vimalakirti’s one silence”) and 一默如雷 (“a silence like thunder”) are later readers’ comments. The English and the plain Chinese keep it just as short and add no drama. Compare Shariputra in chapter 6: when the goddess stumps him he too falls silent, but she does not accept it, telling him not to teach liberation by doing away with words. Both are silences; the sutra deliberately distinguishes them.

The third difference is Sanskrit wordplay. The sutra constantly turns its arguments on two senses of one root: svāgata (“welcome,” literally “well come”) and anāgata (“not come”); the goddess’s kalpika (“proper, allowable”) and kalpayati (“to imagine, to construct”); asthāna as both “impossible” and “no-place”; tīrthika (“teacher of another school,” literally “ford-maker”) and tīrtha (“ford”); gati as both “road” and “arrival.” Neither English nor plain Chinese can keep these puns; both have to give the two senses separately and point them out in the notes. Kumarajiva’s usual solution is to rewrite the pun as a statement of doctrine, such as 不来相而来 (“coming without the mark of coming”) or 行于非道，是为通达佛道 (“walking the non-way is mastering the Buddha’s way”): smooth to read, but without the original’s quick, cornering wit.

verses.en: The Teaching of Vimalakirti (his name means “Spotless Fame”)

cmp.note: 梵文书名是「维摩诘的教说」：nirdeśa 是「指出、讲说」。鸠摩罗什译《维摩诘所说经》，意思一样；玄奘另译作《说无垢称经》，把人名意译成「无垢称」。英文书名用通行的 The Vimalakirti Sutra，这一行照梵文直译。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit title means “The Teaching of Vimalakirti”: nirdeśa is “pointing out, explaining.” Kumarajiva’s title 维摩诘所说经 (Wéimójié suǒ shuō jīng, “the sutra spoken by Vimalakirti”) says the same; Xuanzang’s later version translates the name itself, 无垢称 (Wúgòuchēng, “Spotless Fame”). The book title on this site uses the familiar “The Vimalakirti Sutra”; this line follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas!

This is what I heard. Once the Blessed One was staying at Vaishali (the great city of the Licchavi clan), in the Amrapali grove (a park given to the Buddha by the courtesan Amrapali), together with a great community of monks, eight thousand monks in all,

cmp.note: 「我这样听到」。英文 This is what I heard、白话「我是这样听说的」都照字面；鸠摩罗什译「如是我闻」，语序照搬梵文，成了中文佛经的固定开头。
cmp.en: “Thus by me heard.” The English “This is what I heard” and the plain Chinese are literal; Kumarajiva’s 如是我闻 (rúshì wǒ wén, “thus I heard”) keeps the Sanskrit word order and became the fixed opening of Chinese sutras.

verses.en: all of them arhats. Their outflows were spent and they were free of afflictions; they had mastered themselves; their minds were well freed and their wisdom well freed. They were thoroughbreds, great elephants. They had done what was to be done and finished what was to be finished; they had laid down the burden and reached their own goal. The fetters that bind one to becoming were completely worn away; their minds were well freed through right understanding; and they had reached the highest perfection in mastery of the mind.

cmp.note: nāga 可以是「龙（蛇神）」，也可以是「大象」，用来比喻最杰出的人。白话译「大龙象」两者都保留；英文取「大象」，和前面的 thoroughbreds（良种马）配成一对动物比喻。
cmp.en: Nāga can mean a serpent-deity (“dragon”) or an elephant, and is used for an outstanding person. The plain Chinese 大龙象 (dà lóngxiàng, “great dragon-elephant”) keeps both; the English takes “elephant,” pairing it with “thoroughbreds” as two animal images.

verses.en: With them were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, well known for their higher knowledges. All of them had been brought to completion through training in the great higher knowledges. They were upheld by the power of the buddhas. They guarded the city of the true Dharma and held on to the true Dharma. They roared the great lion’s roar, and their voices sounded through the ten directions. Without being asked, they were good friends to all beings. They kept the line of the Three Jewels from being cut. They had struck down Mara, their enemy, and no opponent’s argument could overpower them. They had mindfulness, samadhi and dharani (the power to hold teachings in memory). They were free of all hindrances and entanglements, and they stood in unobstructed liberation. Their eloquence could not be cut off. They had been brought to completion through giving, self-control, discipline, restraint, morality, patience, effort, meditation, wisdom and skill in means. They had the acceptance that things are unborn and that nothing is to be grasped. They turned the wheel of the Dharma that never turns back. They were sealed with the seal of marklessness. They were skilled in knowing the faculties of every being. They moved through every assembly with a confidence nothing could overpower. They had gathered great stores of merit and knowledge. Their bodies were adorned with the marks and minor signs of a great person; they bore the finest of forms, yet wore no ornaments. Their fame and renown rose higher than the peak of Mount Sumeru. With intent as firm as diamond they had gained unbreakable faith in the Buddha’s teaching. They rained down the nectar of the Dharma-jewel scattered everywhere. Their voices were pure, with every tone and sound of every being’s speech. They had entered the deep Dharma of dependent arising and cut off the habit-traces of views about ends and no-ends. They roared like fearless lions. They had passed beyond everything comparable and incomparable. They were great caravan leaders who had gathered the Dharma-jewel and wisdom. They were skilled in all things, the straightforward, the subtle, the gentle, the hard to see and the hard to understand. Their knowledge had entered the comings and goings of beings, their inclinations and their thoughts. They had been consecrated with the consecration of the Buddha’s knowledge, equal to the unequaled. Their intent had reached the ten powers, the kinds of confidence, and the qualities unique to a buddha. They had crossed the moat of every bad destiny, every miserable state and every downfall, yet they deliberately showed themselves being born in the realms of existence. They were great physician-kings who knew how to train every being and applied the medicine of the Dharma as each one needed. They possessed endless mines of good qualities and were adorned with the good qualities and splendors of endless buddha-fields. To hear them or see them was never in vain, and no step they took was wasted. The flood of their good qualities was without limit, even if one praised them for hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of immeasurable eons.

cmp.note: 「不等人请就主动做善友」。鸠摩罗什译成「众人不请，友而安之」，中国佛教后来常说的「不请之友」就出自这里。英文 without being asked, they were good friends 照字面。
cmp.en: “Good friends without being asked.” Kumarajiva’s 众人不请，友而安之 (“unasked by anyone, they befriend and comfort them”) is the source of the later Chinese Buddhist phrase 不请之友 (bù qǐng zhī yǒu, “the uninvited friend”). The English is literal.

verses.en: They included the bodhisattva, the great being Samadarshin, and Samavishamadarshin, Samadhivikurvanaraja, Dharmeshvara, Dharmaketu, Prabhaketu, Prabhavyuha, Mahavyuha, Ratnakuta, Pratibhanakuta, Ratnamudrahasta, Nityotkshiptahasta, Nityotpalakritahasta, Nityotkanthita, Nityaprahasitapramuditendriya, Pramodyaraja, Devaraja, Pranidhiprayataprapta, Pratisamvitpranadaprapta, Gaganaganja, Ratnolkadharin, Ratnavira, Ratnashri, Ratnanandin, Indrajalin, Jaliniprabha, Anarambanadhyayin, Prajnakuta, Ratnajaha, Marapramardin, Vidyuddeva, Vikurvanaraja, Lakshanakuta, Lakshanakutasamatikranta, Simhaghoshabhigarjitasvara, Shailashikharasamghattanaraja, Gandhahastin, Gajagandhahastin, Satatodyukta, Anikshiptadhura, Sumati, Sujata, Padmashrigarbha, Padmavyuha, Avalokiteshvara (the bodhisattva known for compassion), Mahasthamaprapta, Brahmajalin, Ratnayashti, Marajita, Kshetralamkrita, Maniratnacchatra, Suvarnachuda, Manichuda, Maitreya (the bodhisattva who will be the next buddha), and Manjushri (“Gentle Glory,” the bodhisattva of wisdom), the bodhisattva, the great being, who had become a young prince. With these at their head there were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas.

cmp.note: 「已成为童子的」，常解作「法王子」，即将继承佛位的王子。英文译 who had become a young prince（照《阿弥陀经》英译的写法）；白话「童子相」偏向外貌年轻。
cmp.en: “Who has become a youth,” often understood as “prince of the Dharma,” the heir who will inherit the buddha’s place. The English “who had become a young prince” follows the site’s English Amitabha Sutra; the plain Chinese 童子相 (tóngzǐ xiàng, “in the form of a youth”) leans toward looking young.

verses.en: There were also ten thousand Brahmas, led by Brahma Jatin (“the Ascetic with Matted Hair”), who had come from many worlds of four great continents to see the Blessed One, to bow to him, to attend on him and to hear the Dharma; they gathered there in that same assembly. Twelve thousand Shakras (Shakra is lord of the gods) came from other worlds of four great continents and gathered in that same assembly. Likewise other very mighty Shakras, Brahmas, world-guardians, gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras and mahoragas gathered in that same assembly and sat down. And the four assemblies came too: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.

There the Blessed One, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, was teaching the Dharma. Seated on a lion throne called Womb of Glory, he outshone the whole assembly, the way Sumeru, king of mountains, rises from the middle of the ocean; he shone, he blazed, he glowed.

Then the bodhisattva Ratnakara (“Mine of Jewels”), a young man of the Licchavi clan, together with about five hundred Licchavi young men, took parasols made of the seven precious things, left the great city of Vaishali, and went to the Amrapali grove, to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he bowed his head to the Blessed One’s feet, walked around him seven times keeping him on his right, and covered the Blessed One with the parasols they had brought. Having covered him, he stood to one side.

The moment those jewel parasols were offered, by the Buddha’s power they became one great jewel parasol. And under that great jewel parasol this whole great galaxy of a billion worlds was seen to be covered. However long and wide this great galaxy of a billion worlds is, that much was seen within that great jewel parasol. All the Sumerus, great kings of mountains, in this great galaxy of a billion worlds, the Himalaya, Muchilinda, Great Muchilinda, Gandhamadana and the Jewel Mountains, the Chakravada and the Great Chakravada ranges, all of them were seen in that one great jewel parasol. All the great oceans, lakes and ponds, rivers, streams and brooks flowing in this great galaxy of a billion worlds, they too were all seen in that one great jewel parasol.

And the palaces of the sun and moon in this great galaxy of a billion worlds, the stars, the dwellings of the gods, the nagas, the yakshas, the gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras and mahoragas, the dwellings of the Four Great Kings, the villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms and capitals, all of them were seen in that one great jewel parasol. And the Dharma teaching of the buddhas, the blessed ones, going on in the worlds of the ten directions, was heard coming out of that one great jewel parasol.

Then the whole assembly, struck with wonder at seeing such a great miracle from the Blessed One, was delighted, uplifted and thrilled, full of joy and gladness. They bowed to the Tathagata and stood gazing at him without blinking.

Then Ratnakara, the young Licchavi, having seen such a great miracle from the Blessed One, put his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, raised his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and praised him in verses:

“Your eyes are wide as the petals of the fine, pure, lovely lotus; your intent is pure; you have reached the summit, the perfection of calm. You have heaped up pure deeds; your good qualities are vast beyond measure. I bow to you, who lead the way of the ascetic’s peace. (1)”

“Look at the power of the leader, the bull among men: the finest Sugata-fields are seen shining forth. And the noble, excellent Dharma talk that leads to the deathless, all of it is heard here, out of the sky. (2)”

“By the Dharma you won this kingdom, the finest kingdom of Dharma; you give the Dharma as wealth to the world, you who conquered the foe. Skilled in telling things apart, seeing the ultimate truth, lord of the Dharma, King of the Dharma, I bow my head to you. (3)”

“You speak words that say neither ‘it is’ nor ‘it is not’: all things come into being dependent on causes. Here there is no self, no doer and no one who feels; yet no deed, good or bad, is ever lost. (4)”

cmp.w: na ca nāma asti na ca nāsti
cmp.note: 这首偈是全经最早出现的「不二」：既不说有，也不说无。鸠摩罗什译「说法不有亦不无，以因缘故诸法生；无我无造无受者，善恶之业亦不亡」，是中文佛教最常被引用的偈子之一，意思和梵文一致。
cmp.en: This verse is the sutra’s first glimpse of non-duality: neither “it is” nor “it is not.” Kumarajiva’s 说法不有亦不无，以因缘故诸法生 (“you teach that things neither are nor are not; through causes and conditions all things arise”) is one of the most quoted verses in Chinese Buddhism, and agrees with the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “Lord of sages, you have conquered Mara and his army; you have reached the auspicious, deathless, peaceful, supreme awakening, in which nothing is felt and mind and thought do not move, and into which no crowd of other teachers can plunge. (5)”

“You set turning the wheel of three turnings and many forms, which brings peace and is pure by nature. Gods and humans saw it with their own eyes, wondrous King of the Dharma; at that time the Three Jewels were shown. (6)”

“Those you have rightly trained with the jewel of the Dharma no longer build up imaginings and are always at peace. Supreme physician, who puts an end to death, birth and old age, ocean of good qualities beyond measure, I bow my head to you. (7)”

“Honored with honors, you do not tremble, like Mount Sumeru; toward the immoral and the moral alike your great kindness goes. Your mind is clear as the sky, you dwell in sameness: who would not worship such a jewel among beings? (8)”
“Great sage, the people gathered here look up at your face with minds full of faith, and each of them sees the Victor right in front of them: that is a mark unique to the Victor, a buddha. (9)”

cmp.note: 「胜者」，打败了烦恼的人，是佛的称号（耆那教也用这个词）。英文 the Victor、白话「胜者」都照字面；鸠摩罗什在这几首偈里改用「世尊」「佛」，看不出这个比喻。
cmp.en: “Victor,” the one who has conquered the afflictions, a title of the Buddha (the Jains use the same word). The English “the Victor” and the plain Chinese 胜者 (shèngzhě, “victor”) are literal; in these verses Kumarajiva uses 世尊 (“World-Honored One”) or 佛 (“Buddha”) instead, so the image disappears.

verses.en: “Blessed One, you utter a single speech, and the assembly hears it in many languages, and each person understands the meaning in their own way: that is a mark unique to the Victor, a buddha. (10)”

cmp.note: 「佛以一音演说法，众生随类各得解」是鸠摩罗什对这首偈的著名译法，后来成了成语式的说法。梵文的意思相同。
cmp.en: Kumarajiva’s rendering of this verse, 佛以一音演说法，众生随类各得解 (“the Buddha teaches with a single voice, and beings each understand according to their kind”), became a proverb-like saying in Chinese. The Sanskrit means the same.

verses.en: “With a single word spoken, you frighten some and make others turn away from the world; and you, the leader, settle the doubts of those who doubt: that is a mark unique to the Victor, a buddha. (11)”

“I bow to you, who have the ten powers, whose courage is real; I bow to you, who have reached fearlessness and are confident; who have arrived at certainty in the qualities unique to a buddha; I bow to you, the guide of the whole world. (12)”

“I bow to the one who cuts the bonds of the fetters; I bow to you, who have gone to the far shore and stand on dry land; I bow to the one who carries weary people across; I bow to you, who lean on nothing in the round of samsara. (13)”

“Together with beings, you have gone into all their destinies, yet in every destiny your mind is free. Like a lotus born in water, you are not stained by it: lotus of sages, emptiness is what you practice. (14)”

cmp.note: 上半句原文不太好读：可解作「与众生同处、进入一切去处」。白话译「深知众生往来的去处」，英文取「与众生一起进入他们的去处」。两种理解都可通，这里拿不准。
cmp.en: The first half-line is hard to read; it may mean “being together with beings, having gone into their destinies.” The plain Chinese reads it as 深知众生往来的去处 (“knowing well where beings come and go”); the English takes “together with beings, you have gone into their destinies.” Both are possible; this is uncertain.

verses.en: “You have seen through every sign entirely; there is no wishing in you for anything anywhere. Inconceivable is the great power of a buddha: I bow to you, who are like space and lean on nothing. (15)”

When Ratnakara, the young Licchavi, had praised the Blessed One with these verses, he said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, these five hundred or so young Licchavis have all set out for unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And they ask about purifying a buddha-field: what is the bodhisattvas’ purification of a buddha-field? Blessed One, please, may the Tathagata teach these bodhisattvas about purifying a buddha-field.”

cmp.note: 「佛的田地」：一尊佛教化众生的范围。英文 buddha-field 照字面，保留「田」的画面（可以耕种、可以清理）；中文「佛土、佛国」变成了「国土」，更像一个地方。本章的核心问题就是「怎样清净佛的田」。
cmp.en: “A buddha’s field”: the range in which a buddha guides beings. The English “buddha-field” is literal and keeps the picture of a field that can be cultivated and cleared; the Chinese 佛土 (fótǔ, “buddha-land”) or 佛国 (“buddha-country”) turns it into a territory, more like a place. This chapter’s central question is how such a field is purified.

verses.en: When he had said this, the Blessed One gave his approval to Ratnakara, the young Licchavi: “Excellent, excellent, young man! It is excellent that you ask the Tathagata about purifying a buddha-field. So listen, young man, and pay close and careful attention. I will tell you about the bodhisattvas’ purification of a buddha-field.”
“Very well, Blessed One,” said Ratnakara, the young Licchavi, and the five hundred or so young Licchavis, and they listened to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said to them:

“Son of good family, the field of beings is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. Why? As far as a bodhisattva helps beings grow, that much of a buddha-field he takes up. Whatever kind of training beings need, that kind of buddha-field he takes up. Through whatever kind of entry into a buddha-field beings enter the knowledge of a buddha, that kind of buddha-field he takes up. Through whatever kind of entry into a buddha-field the faculties of noble ones arise in beings, that kind of buddha-field he takes up. Why? Because, son of good family, the bodhisattvas’ buddha-field comes into being for the good of beings. Ratnakara, it is like someone who wants to build in empty space: he can build whatever he likes, but space itself cannot be built or decorated. In the same way, Ratnakara, knowing that all things are like space,

cmp.note: 「众生的田」。这一句是全章的要点：佛土不是另外造出来的地方，而是众生本身。鸠摩罗什译「众生之类是菩萨佛土」，意思相同。
cmp.en: “The field of beings.” This line is the key of the chapter: a buddha-field is not some separate place to be built, it is the beings themselves. Kumarajiva’s 众生之类是菩萨佛土 (“the kinds of beings are the bodhisattva’s buddha-land”) says the same.

verses.en: a bodhisattva builds whatever kind of buddha-field he wishes to build in order to bring beings to maturity; yet the space-like nature of a buddha-field cannot be built or decorated.
“Moreover, Ratnakara:
a field of sincere intent is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who are not crooked and not deceitful are born in his buddha-field.

cmp.note: 「心意、存心」。白话译「意乐（真诚的心意）」；鸠摩罗什译「直心是菩萨净土」，「直心」后来成了禅宗常用词（「直心是道场」）。英文 sincere intent 取的是和下文「不虚伪」相配的意思。
cmp.en: “Intent, disposition.” The plain Chinese renders it 意乐 (yìlè, “intention”) with a gloss “sincere intent”; Kumarajiva writes 直心是菩萨净土 (“a straight mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land”), and 直心 (zhíxīn, “straight mind”) later became a favorite Chan term. The English “sincere intent” matches the “not crooked, not deceitful” that follows.

verses.en: Son of good family, a field of deep resolve is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who have gathered every store of the wholesome are born in his buddha-field.
A field of practice is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who stand in all wholesome things are born there, in his buddha-field.
The bodhisattva’s noble raising of the mind set on awakening is his buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who have set out in the Great Vehicle are born there, in his buddha-field.
A field of giving is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who give up everything are born there, in his buddha-field.

A field of morality is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings whose every aim is fulfilled and who guard the ten paths of wholesome action are born there, in his buddha-field.

Son of good family, a field of patience is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings adorned with the thirty-two marks, who have reached the perfection of patience, self-control and calm, are born in his buddha-field.
A field of effort is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who have set their effort to seeking every good thing are born in his buddha-field.
A field of meditation is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who are mindful, clearly aware and collected are born in his buddha-field.
A field of wisdom is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who are certain of the right way are born in his buddha-field.
The four immeasurables are the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who dwell in kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity are born in his buddha-field.
Son of good family, the four ways of gathering people are the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings held together by every kind of liberation are born in his buddha-field.
Skill in means is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings skilled in weighing every means are born in his buddha-field.

The thirty-seven things that belong to awakening are the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, beings who know the methods of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the strengths, the factors of awakening and the path are born in his buddha-field.
A mind of dedication is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, his buddha-field is seen adorned with every good quality.

Son of good family, teaching how to put an end to the eight unfree states (the eight conditions in which one cannot practice) is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, his buddha-field comes to be cut off from every bad destiny and free of the eight unfree states.
Keeping to the training rules oneself and not accusing others of their offenses is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, not even the word ‘offense’ comes up in his buddha-field.

Son of good family, purity in the ten paths of wholesome action is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field. When he reaches awakening, the beings born in his buddha-field have a secure lifespan and great wealth; they live the holy life; their speech is adorned with truthfulness and their words are sweet; their circles do not break apart and they are skilled at reconciling those who have fallen out; they are free of envy, their minds are without ill will, and they have right view.

So, son of good family, however much practice a bodhisattva has, that much intent he has. However much intent, that much deep resolve. However much deep resolve, that much reflection. However much reflection, that much carrying out. However much carrying out, that much dedication. However much dedication, that much skill in means. However much skill in means, that much purification of the field. As the purity of the field is, so is the purity of beings. As the purity of beings is, so is the purity of knowledge. As the purity of knowledge is, so is the purity of teaching. As the purity of teaching is, so is the purity of practicing knowledge. As the purity of practicing knowledge is, so is the purity of one’s own mind.

Therefore, son of good family, a bodhisattva who wants to purify a buddha-field should work at purifying his own mind. Why? As the purity of a bodhisattva’s mind is, so the purity of his buddha-field comes to be.”

cmp.note: 鸠摩罗什译「随其心净，则佛土净」，是这部经在中文世界最有名的一句，后来净土宗、禅宗都常引。梵文是「心清净到什么程度，佛土就清净到什么程度」，说的是程度上的对应；鸠摩罗什的句子读起来更像「只要心净，土就净」。
cmp.en: Kumarajiva’s 随其心净，则佛土净 (suí qí xīn jìng, zé fótǔ jìng, “as the mind is pure, so the buddha-land is pure”) is the most famous line of this sutra in the Chinese world, quoted by both Pure Land and Chan. The Sanskrit says “to whatever degree the mind is pure, to that degree the field is pure,” a matter of correspondence in degree; Kumarajiva’s line reads more like “just purify the mind and the land is pure.”

verses.en: Then, through the Buddha’s power, this thought came to the venerable Shariputra (the Buddha’s great disciple, foremost in wisdom): “If a bodhisattva’s buddha-field is as pure as his mind is pure, then surely the mind of the Blessed One Shakyamuni was not pure while he was carrying out the bodhisattva’s practice, since this buddha-field looks so impure.”

The Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thought in the venerable Shariputra’s mind, said to the venerable Shariputra: “What do you think, Shariputra? When someone blind from birth does not see the sun and moon, is it that the sun and moon are impure?”
He said: “No indeed, Blessed One. That is the fault of the one born blind, not of the sun and moon.”

He said: “In the same way, Shariputra, when some beings do not see the splendid array of good qualities of the Tathagata’s buddha-field, that is the fault of their ignorance; it is not the Tathagata’s fault. Shariputra, the Tathagata’s buddha-field is pure; it is you who do not see it.”

Then Brahma Jatin said to the elder Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, don’t say that this buddha-field of the Tathagata is impure. Reverend Shariputra, the Blessed One’s buddha-field is pure. Shariputra, just like the splendid palaces of the gods who wield power over others’ creations: that is how we see the splendid array of good qualities in the buddha-field of the Blessed One Shakyamuni.”
Then the elder Shariputra said to Brahma Jatin: “But Brahma, we see this great earth full of highs and lows, thorns, cliffs, peaks, pits, dung and filth.”

Brahma Jatin said: “Surely, Reverend Shariputra, it is because your mind has highs and lows and your intent does not rest on the pure knowledge of a buddha that you see the buddha-field like this. Reverend Shariputra, those bodhisattvas whose minds are the same toward all beings, and whose intent rests on the pure knowledge of a buddha, see this buddha-field as pure.”

cmp.note: 梵文用同一个词形容大地和心：「高低不平」。舍利弗说地高低不平，梵天回答：是你的心高低不平。英文 highs and lows、白话「高低不平」都保住了这个双关；鸠摩罗什译「仁者心有高下」，也保留了。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit uses the same word for the ground and for the mind: “full of highs and lows.” Shariputra says the earth is uneven, and Brahma answers that it is his mind that is uneven. The English “highs and lows” and the plain Chinese keep this echo, as does Kumarajiva’s 仁者心有高下 (“your mind, sir, has high and low”).

verses.en: Then the Blessed One touched this great galaxy of a billion worlds with his big toe. At that very moment this great galaxy of a billion worlds became heaped with many hundreds of thousands of jewels and inlaid with many hundreds of thousands of jewels. This world was seen to be just like the world of the Tathagata Ratnavyuha, the world arrayed with jewels of endless good qualities. And that whole assembly, struck with wonder, found itself seated on jeweled lotuses.
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Shariputra: “Shariputra, do you see these splendid arrays of good qualities of the buddha-field?”
He said: “I see them, Blessed One. Splendors never seen or heard of before have appeared.”

He said: “Shariputra, my buddha-field is always like this. But in order to bring inferior beings to maturity, the Tathagata shows a buddha-field spoiled by many faults like this. Shariputra, it is like the young gods eating from a single bowl: the divine nectar-food appears to each according to the difference in the merit he has gathered. In the same way, Shariputra, beings born in a single buddha-field see the splendid arrays of good qualities of the buddhas’ fields according to the purity of their minds.”

While this splendid array of the buddha-field’s good qualities was being shown, eighty-four thousand living beings raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And the five hundred young Licchavis who had come with Ratnakara, the young Licchavi, gained the acceptance that conforms to the truth.

Then the Blessed One withdrew that supernormal power again, and this buddha-field went back to looking as it had before. Then, among the gods and humans of the disciples’ vehicle, thirty-two thousand living beings understood, “Ah, all conditioned things are impermanent,” and the Dharma-eye, dustless and stainless, became pure in them regarding things. Eight thousand monks, no longer grasping, had their minds freed from the outflows. And eighty-four thousand living beings with faith in the vast qualities of a buddha understood that all things have the mark of being fabricated appearances, and raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

cmp.note: viṭhapana 是「虚构、变出来的东西」，pratyupasthāna 是「当下呈现」。白话译「虚构安立、当下显现的相」，英文压成 fabricated appearances。这个词组少见，确切意思不完全有把握。
cmp.en: Viṭhapana means “a fabrication, something conjured up,” and pratyupasthāna “present appearance.” The plain Chinese gives 虚构安立、当下显现的相 (“marks of being fabricated and presently appearing”); the English compresses it to “fabricated appearances.” The phrase is rare, and its exact sense is not fully certain.

verses.en: This was chapter one, “The Setting: Purifying the Buddha-Field.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · Skill in Means Beyond Thought

verses.en: Now at that time, in the great city of Vaishali, there lived a Licchavi named Vimalakirti (“Spotless Fame”).

cmp.note: 离车（Licchavi）是毗舍离一带的贵族部族，那里当时实行部族共和。维摩诘在梵本里几乎每次出场都被称作「离车人维摩诘」，强调他是在家的贵族；鸠摩罗什多半只写「维摩诘」或「长者」。英文照梵本保留 the Licchavi。
cmp.en: The Licchavis were a noble clan around Vaishali, which was then governed as a clan republic. In the Sanskrit, Vimalakirti is called “Vimalakirti the Licchavi” almost every time he appears, stressing that he is a lay nobleman; Kumarajiva usually writes just 维摩诘 (Wéimójié) or 长者 (zhǎngzhě, “elder, man of standing”). The English follows the Sanskrit and keeps “the Licchavi.”

verses.en: He had served the victors of the past and planted roots of goodness; he had attended on many buddhas. He had gained acceptance and gained eloquence; he played with the great higher knowledges; he had won the dharanis and reached confidence; he had struck down Mara, his enemy. He had gone deep into the profound way of the Dharma; he was born of the perfection of wisdom; he had mastered skill in means; he was full of eloquence; he was skilled in the intentions and conduct of beings; he was accomplished in knowing which faculties are higher and which lower; he taught the Dharma as suited each person. He had made up his mind and worked hard in this Great Vehicle; he acted only after careful examination; he kept the bearing of a buddha; he had entered a mind as vast as the ocean; all the buddhas praised, extolled and commended him; all the Shakras, Brahmas and world-guardians bowed to him. To bring beings to maturity, through skill in means, he lived in the great city of Vaishali.

He had inexhaustible wealth, to take care of poor and helpless beings. His morality was pure, to take care of the immoral. He had patience and self-control, to take care of beings who were spiteful, vicious, malicious and angry. His effort burned bright, to take care of lazy beings. He was steady in meditation, mindfulness and samadhi, to take care of beings with scattered minds. He had reached certainty in wisdom, to take care of beings with poor wisdom.

cmp.note: 「拉拢、摄取、照顾」。中文「摄受」是专门的佛教词，现代读者不易懂；英文译 take care of，比较口语。原文的意思是用对方需要的东西把人拉到身边，不只是照顾。
cmp.en: “To draw in, gather, look after.” The Chinese 摄受 (shèshòu, “gather and receive”) is a technical Buddhist term hard for modern readers; the English “take care of” is more everyday. The Sanskrit means drawing people close by offering what they need, not merely looking after them.

verses.en: He wore the white clothes of a layman, yet he had the bearing of an ascetic. He lived as a householder, yet he was untouched by the realm of desire, the realm of form and the formless realm. He showed himself with a wife, sons and household, yet he always lived the holy life. He was surrounded by followers, yet he always lived in solitude. He was seen wearing ornaments, yet he was always marked by the marks of a great person. He was seen living on food and drink, yet he always fed on meditation. He was seen in every gambling hall, and he brought to maturity beings whose minds were hooked on gambling, yet he always lived with care. He looked into every other teaching, yet his faith in the Buddha could not be broken. He knew the methods of every worldly and other-worldly science, yet he always took his delight in the pleasure garden of the Dharma. He was seen at every gathering, and everywhere he was honored as the foremost.

cmp.note: 「穿白衣的」：古印度在家人穿白衣，出家人穿染色的袈裟。中文「白衣」后来就成了在家居士的代称。英文加了 of a layman 来说明，否则读者不知道白衣代表什么。
cmp.en: “Wearing white clothes”: in ancient India laypeople wore white, while monastics wore dyed robes. In Chinese 白衣 (báiyī, “white-clothed”) later became a standard word for a lay Buddhist. The English adds “of a layman” to explain it, since otherwise the reader would not know what white clothes stand for.

verses.en: He spoke the Dharma, and to go along with the world he was a companion to the old, the middle-aged and the young.
He was busy in every kind of business, yet he did not hanker after profit or possessions.
He was seen at every crossroads and street corner, to train every being.
He took part in the king’s affairs, to protect beings.
He was seen at every hearing and discussion of the Dharma, to turn people away from the lesser vehicle and urge them toward the Great Vehicle.
He went into every writing school, to bring children to maturity.
He went into every brothel, to show the harm of sensual desire.
He went into every tavern, to set up mindfulness and clear awareness.
Among merchant bankers he was honored as a merchant banker, to proclaim the best of teachings.
Among householders he was honored as a householder, to cut through every grasping and clinging.
Among kshatriyas (the warrior and ruling class) he was honored as a kshatriya, to establish the strength of patience and gentleness.
Among brahmins (the priestly class) he was honored as a brahmin, to strike down pride, conceit and arrogance.
Among ministers he was honored as a minister, to bring all the king’s affairs into line with the Dharma.
Among princes he was honored as a prince, to turn them away from craving royal pleasures and power.
In the women’s quarters of the palace he was honored as the chamberlain, to bring the women and girls to maturity.
He went along with ordinary people, to help them aim for merit beyond the ordinary.
Among Shakras he was honored as a Shakra, to show that power is impermanent.
Among Brahmas he was honored as a Brahma, to show a higher knowledge.
Among world-guardians he was honored as a world-guardian, to protect all beings.
That is how Vimalakirti the Licchavi, possessed of measureless skill in means and knowledge, lived in the great city of Vaishali.

Through skill in means he made himself appear ill. Because he was ill, kings, royal ministers, officials, princes and courtiers of the great city of Vaishali, brahmins, householders, merchant bankers, townspeople and country people, and many thousands of other living beings came to ask after him.

cmp.note: 「把自己显示成生病的样子」。梵文明说病是「示现」出来的，是方便；英文 made himself appear ill、白话「示现自己生了病」都照译。鸠摩罗什译「以其方便，现身有疾」，意思一样。这也是全经的引子。
cmp.en: “He showed himself as ill.” The Sanskrit says plainly that the illness is a display, a skillful means; the English “made himself appear ill” and the plain Chinese follow it, as does Kumarajiva’s 以其方便，现身有疾 (“by his skillful means he showed his body as sick”). This sets the whole sutra in motion.

verses.en: When they had come, Vimalakirti the Licchavi taught them the Dharma, taking this very body made of the four great elements as his subject: “Friends, this body is impermanent like this. It is unstable like this, untrustworthy like this, feeble like this, without substance like this. It is decrepit like this, fleeting like this, painful like this, full of ailments like this, bound to change like this. Friends, this body is a vessel for many diseases like this. A wise person should not rely on it.

cmp.note: 「诸位朋友」，是客气、亲切的称呼。白话译「诸位」，英文 Friends 比较贴近原来的口气；鸠摩罗什译「诸仁者」。
cmp.en: “Friends, sirs,” a polite and warm form of address. The plain Chinese says 诸位 (zhūwèi, “everyone”), and the English “Friends” is closer to the original tone; Kumarajiva writes 诸仁者 (zhū rénzhě, “you kind ones”).

verses.en: Friends, this body is like a lump of foam: it cannot stand being squeezed.
This body is like a bubble: it does not last long.
This body is like a mirage: it is born of afflictions and thirst.
This body is like the trunk of a banana tree: it has no core.

cmp.note: 芭蕉（香蕉树）的「树干」其实是一层层叶鞘卷成的，剥到最后中间没有木质的芯。英文 banana tree 对现代读者更好懂，中文古译「芭蕉」指的也是同类植物。
cmp.en: The “trunk” of a banana plant is really layer upon layer of rolled leaf-sheaths; peel them all away and there is no wooden core in the middle. The English “banana tree” is easy for modern readers to picture; the Chinese 芭蕉 (bājiāo, “plantain”) is the same kind of plant.

verses.en: Alas, this body is like a machine, tied together with bones and sinews.
This body is like a magic show: it is born of mistaken views.
This body is like a dream: what it shows is false.
This body is like a reflection: it appears as a reflection of past deeds.
This body is like an echo: it depends on conditions.
This body is like a cloud: its mark is turmoil and dispersing.

cmp.note: 这个复合词原文可能有误（citta「心」放在这里不太通）。白话译「翻腾纷乱、终将消散」，英文同样取「纷乱与消散」。拿不准。
cmp.en: This compound may be corrupt (citta, “mind,” does not fit well here). The plain Chinese takes it as “churning, confused and bound to disperse,” and the English likewise as “turmoil and dispersing.” Uncertain.

verses.en: This body is like lightning: it breaks up in an instant and does not stay.
This body has no owner: it is born of many conditions.
This body does nothing by itself, like the earth.
This body has no self, like water.
This body has no living soul, like fire.
This body has no person in it, like the wind.
This body has no nature of its own, like space.
This body has not really come into being: it is a lodging for the great elements.
This body is empty: it is without self and without anything belonging to a self.
This body is inert, like grass, wood, walls, clods of earth and reflections.
This body cannot move by itself: it runs because it is driven by a machinery of winds.
This body is hollow: a heap of filth and rot.
This body is worthless: it is bound to need rubbing and kneading, and to scatter and be destroyed.
This body is beset by four hundred and four diseases.
This body is like an old well: it is always overcome by age.
Alas, this body lasts only to its limit: it ends in death.
This body is like an executioner, like a poisonous snake, like an empty village: it is made up of the heaps, the elements and the sense fields.

cmp.note: 这是佛经里的一个旧比喻：刽子手指五蕴，毒蛇指四大，空村指六处（内六根，里面没有人住）。英文、白话都只照字面列出三样，没有解释背后的典故。
cmp.en: This is an old image from the early sutras: the executioners stand for the five heaps, the poisonous snakes for the four elements, and the empty village for the six sense bases (inside, no one lives there). The English and the plain Chinese simply list the three things without explaining the allusion.

verses.en: So you should feel weariness and dispassion toward a body like this, and longing for the body of a Tathagata.

For, friends, the body of a Tathagata is the Dharma-body. It is born of giving, born of morality, born of samadhi, born of wisdom, born of liberation, born of the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is born of kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity. It is born of giving, self-control and restraint; born of patience and gentleness; born of firm effort and roots of goodness; born of the meditations, liberations, samadhis and attainments; born of learning, wisdom and skill in means. It is born of the thirty-seven things that belong to awakening; born of calm and insight; born of the ten powers; born of the four kinds of confidence. It is born of the eighteen qualities unique to a buddha; born of all the perfections. It is born of the higher knowledges and the clear knowings; born to abandon every unwholesome thing; born of taking up every wholesome thing; born of truth; born of what is real; born of care. Friends, the body of a Tathagata is born of measureless good deeds. That is what you should long for.

cmp.note: 「法身」：字面是「由法构成的身体」。这里梵文明说法身是由布施、持戒等修行「生出来的」，是一身功德的总和；后来中国佛教常把法身理解成形而上的「真如本体」，和这里的用法不完全一样。
cmp.en: Dharmakāya, “the Dharma-body,” literally “a body made of Dharma.” Here the Sanskrit says plainly that it is “born of” giving, morality and the other practices: it is the sum of a buddha’s good qualities. Later Chinese Buddhism often took 法身 (fǎshēn) as a metaphysical “true reality” itself, which is not quite how the word is used here.

verses.en: And to rid all beings of every disease of the afflictions, you should raise your minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.”

In this way Vimalakirti the Licchavi taught the Dharma in one way and another to those who had gathered to ask after his illness, so that many hundreds of thousands of beings raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.
This was chapter two, called “Skill in Means Beyond Thought.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · The Disciples and Bodhisattvas Excuse Themselves

verses.en: Then this thought came to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Here I am, ill and in pain, lying in bed, and the Tathagata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, does not think of me, and out of compassion does not send anyone to ask after my illness.”
But the Blessed One did have Vimalakirti the Licchavi in mind. So the Blessed One said to the venerable Shariputra: “Shariputra, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

When this was said, the venerable Shariputra said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once I was sitting in retreat at the foot of a tree. Vimalakirti the Licchavi came to the foot of that tree and said to me: ‘Reverend Shariputra, retreat is not to be done the way you are doing it. Sit in retreat in such a way that neither body nor mind is seen anywhere in the three realms. Sit in retreat in such a way that you do not rise from cessation, and yet you are seen in every posture. Sit in retreat in such a way that you do not give up the mark of attainment, and yet you are seen with the marks of an ordinary person.

cmp.note: 「退隐独处、收摄静坐」。白话译「静坐」，鸠摩罗什译「宴坐」。英文 retreat 保留了「从人群中退出来」的意思，这正是维摩诘要反驳的：真正的静坐不需要躲起来。
cmp.en: “Withdrawing into solitude, collected sitting.” The plain Chinese says 静坐 (jìngzuò, “sitting quietly”) and Kumarajiva 宴坐 (yànzuò, “sitting at ease”). The English “retreat” keeps the sense of withdrawing from people, which is exactly what Vimalakirti challenges: true sitting does not need to hide away.

verses.en: Sit in retreat in such a way that your mind neither settles inside nor wanders outside. Sit in retreat in such a way that you do not budge from any of the views, and yet you are seen in the thirty-seven things that belong to awakening. Sit in retreat in such a way that you do not abandon the afflictions that belong to samsara, and yet you enter nirvana. Reverend Shariputra, those who sit in retreat in this way, it is their retreat that the Blessed One approves.’

cmp.w: kleśān na prajahāsi nirvāṇasamavasaraṇaś ca bhavasi
cmp.note: 鸠摩罗什译「不断烦恼而入涅槃」，是这部经在中文里最常被引用的句子之一。梵文意思相同，英文照译。
cmp.en: Kumarajiva’s 不断烦恼而入涅槃 (bú duàn fánnǎo ér rù nièpán, “entering nirvana without cutting off the afflictions”) is one of this sutra’s most quoted lines in Chinese. The Sanskrit says the same, and the English follows it.

verses.en: When I heard this, Blessed One, I simply fell silent; I could not give him any answer. So I don’t dare go and ask after that son of good family’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Mahamaudgalyayana (the disciple foremost in supernormal powers): “Maudgalyayana, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Maudgalyayana too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once I was teaching the Dharma to some householders at the entrance to a street in the great city of Vaishali. Vimalakirti the Licchavi came up to me there and said:
‘Reverend Maudgalyayana, the Dharma should not be taught to white-clothed householders the way you are teaching it. Reverend Maudgalyayana, the Dharma should be taught just as that Dharma is.

For, Reverend Maudgalyayana, the Dharma has no beings in it: it is free of the dust of ‘beings.’ It has no self: it is free of the dust of passion. It has no living soul: it is free of birth and death. It has no person: past and future are cut off from it. It is peaceful: its mark is calm. It is free of passion: it has nothing to hold on to. It has no letters: all speech is cut off. It cannot be uttered: it is free of every wave. It goes everywhere, like space. It has no color, sign or shape: it is free of all activity. It has no ‘mine’: it is free of making things ‘mine.’ It is not made known: it is free of mind, thought and consciousness. It has no equal, because it has no opposite. It is unlike a cause, and no conditions can be laid on it. It flows into the realm of the Dharma, at one with all things. It follows suchness by way of not following. It stands on the limit of reality, because it never moves at all. It does not move, because it does not lean on the six kinds of sense object. It does not go or come anywhere, because it does not stay put. It is at one with emptiness, shown forth by signlessness, marked by wishlessness. It is free of adding and taking away. It is not lifted up and not thrown down. It is free of arising and perishing. It has no home; it goes beyond the range of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind. It is not high and not low. It stands firm, it has reached the imperturbable. It is free of all activity.

Reverend Mahamaudgalyayana, what kind of teaching can there be of a Dharma like this? Reverend Mahamaudgalyayana, ‘teaching the Dharma’ is itself a projection. Those who listen also listen through projection. Reverend Maudgalyayana, where nothing is projected, nothing is taught, nothing is heard, nothing is understood. It is like a magically made man teaching the Dharma to magically made men.

cmp.note: 「加上去、强加、虚构」。白话译「增益（给本来没有的东西加上名相）」，英文 projection 取「投射」的意思。中文「增益」是专门术语，日常意思却是「增加好处」，容易误读。
cmp.en: “Adding on, superimposing, fabricating.” The plain Chinese uses 增益 (zēngyì, “superimposition”) with an explanation; the English “projection” takes the sense of casting something onto things. The Chinese term 增益 in everyday use means “increase, benefit,” so it is easy to misread.

verses.en: With your mind settled like this, you should teach the Dharma. You should be skilled in the faculties of beings, with wisdom that sees clearly, with great compassion leading the way; you should praise the Great Vehicle, be grateful to the Buddha, have pure intent and know the ways of expressing the Dharma. And you should teach the Dharma so that the line of the Three Jewels is not cut off.’

Blessed One, he taught the Dharma in such a way that eight hundred householders in that gathering raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And I had nothing to say. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Mahakashyapa (the disciple foremost in austerity): “Mahakashyapa, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Mahakashyapa too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, I was going for alms in a poor street. Vimalakirti the Licchavi came up to me there and said:

‘Reverend Mahakashyapa’s kindness and compassion are partial, since you pass over the great families and go to the poor ones. Reverend Mahakashyapa, you should stand in the sameness of all things. You should seek alms always keeping all beings in mind. You should seek food for the sake of no longer needing food. You should go for alms to remove the clinging to other people’s lumps of food. You should enter a village holding it as an empty village. You should enter a city to bring men and women to maturity. You should visit families as one born into the family of the buddhas.

cmp.note: 「局部的、有限的」。大迦叶专去穷人家乞食，本意是让穷人有机会种福；维摩诘说这种慈悲「有偏」。英文 partial 一词两义（局部的／偏心的），刚好合用。
cmp.en: “Local, limited.” Mahakashyapa went for alms only among the poor, meaning to give them a chance to make merit; Vimalakirti calls such compassion “partial.” The English word “partial” has both senses (limited and biased), which suits it well.

verses.en: You should accept alms by way of not accepting them. You should see forms the way someone blind from birth does; hear sounds as if they were echoes; smell smells as if they were wind; taste tastes without telling them apart; touch things touched with a knowing that does not touch; and know things as one knows a magically made man. What has no nature of its own and no other nature was never set alight; and what was never set alight is not put out.

If the elder Mahakashyapa could pass beyond the eight wrong ways and enter the eight liberations; if through the sameness of the wrong he could enter the sameness of the right; if with a single portion of alms he could provide for all beings, and after offering it to all the buddhas and all the noble ones eat it himself; if he could eat it in such a way that he is neither afflicted nor free of afflictions, neither in concentration nor out of it, dwelling neither in samsara nor in nirvana; then for those who give alms to the Reverend, the fruit would be neither small nor great, would lead neither to loss nor to gain, and would lead to the destiny of a buddha, not to the destiny of a disciple. That is how the elder Mahakashyapa would eat the country’s alms without it going to waste.’

Blessed One, when I heard this teaching I was amazed, and I bowed to all bodhisattvas: if even a layman has such eloquence, who would not raise his mind toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Since then I have never urged any being toward the disciples’ vehicle or the solitary buddhas’ vehicle, only toward the Great Vehicle. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that son of good family’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhuti (the disciple foremost in understanding emptiness): “Subhuti, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Subhuti too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once I was going for alms in the great city of Vaishali, and I entered the house of Vimalakirti the Licchavi for alms. Vimalakirti the Licchavi took my bowl, filled it with fine food, and said to me:

‘Reverend Subhuti, if through the sameness of food you have followed through to the sameness of all things, and through the sameness of all things to the sameness of the qualities of a buddha, then take this alms food. Reverend Subhuti, if you have not abandoned passion, hatred and delusion, and yet do not live with them; if, without disturbing the view of an existing self, you have followed the one-way path; if you have neither uprooted ignorance and the thirst for existence nor produced knowledge and liberation; if through the sameness of the worst crimes you have the liberation of samadhi; if you are neither freed nor bound; if you have not seen the four noble truths, and yet are not someone who has not seen the truth; if you have neither attained the fruit nor joined the ordinary people; if you are neither noble nor not noble; if you do not possess all things and yet have realized all things;

if you have not seen the Teacher, not heard the Dharma, not attended on the Sangha; if those six teachers, Purana Kashyapa, Maskarin Goshaliputra, Samjayin Vairattiputra, Kakuda Katyayana, Ajita Keshakambala and Nirgrantha Jnatiputra, are the Reverend’s teachers, and you went forth relying on them, and wherever those six teachers go, the noble Subhuti goes too;

cmp.note: 这六位是佛陀同时代的六位外道导师，佛经里常常点名批评。维摩诘故意说「他们就是你的老师，他们去哪你就去哪」，是用最刺耳的话逼须菩提放下「正与邪」的二分。英文、白话都照字面，没有缓和语气。
cmp.en: These six were teachers of other schools in the Buddha’s day, often named and criticized in the sutras. Vimalakirti deliberately says “they are your teachers, and wherever they go you go,” using the harshest words possible to force Subhuti to drop the split between right and wrong. The English and the plain Chinese are literal and do not soften it.

verses.en: if you have gone into all the views, yet reached neither the extremes nor the middle; if you have landed in the eight unfree states, yet have not reached a free moment; if you are the same as the afflictions, yet have not realized purification; if the peace from conflict of all beings is also the Reverend’s peace from conflict; if offerings are not made pure by you; if you bring down those who give the Reverend alms; if you have joined hands with all the Maras; if all the afflictions are your companions, and the Reverend has the same nature as the afflictions; if you have the mind of a killer toward all beings; if you slander all the buddhas, revile all the qualities of a buddha, do not take refuge in the Sangha, and will never enter final nirvana; then take this alms food.’

cmp.note: 「无诤、没有冲突」。须菩提在佛弟子中以「无诤第一」著称，所以维摩诘特意说「一切众生的无诤，也就是你的无诤」，是针对他本人的。英文 peace from conflict 照字面，读者需要知道这个背景。
cmp.en: “Freedom from conflict.” Subhuti was known as the disciple foremost in dwelling free of conflict, so Vimalakirti deliberately says “the freedom from conflict of all beings is also yours,” aimed at Subhuti himself. The English “peace from conflict” is literal; the reader needs this background to see the barb.

cmp.w: aṣṭākṣaṇasamavasaraṇaś cāsi na cāsi lakṣaṇam anuprāptaḥ
cmp.note: 后半句原文读作「没有得到相」，意思不通；白话据上下文译作「得不到闲暇」（kṣaṇa，与 akṣaṇa「无暇」相对）。英文同样按「闲暇」理解。原文可能有误。
cmp.en: The second half reads “you have not reached the mark (lakṣaṇa),” which makes little sense; the plain Chinese follows the context and reads it as “a free moment” (kṣaṇa, the opposite of akṣaṇa, “unfree state”). The English takes it the same way. The text may be corrupt.

verses.en: Blessed One, when I heard this teaching, everything around me went dark, and I thought: ‘What shall I say to him? How should I act?’ So I was going to put down the bowl and leave the house.

Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to me: ‘Reverend Subhuti, don’t be frightened by words. Take this bowl. What do you think, Reverend Subhuti? If someone conjured up by the Tathagata were spoken to like this, would he be frightened?’
I said: ‘No indeed, son of good family.’

He said to me: ‘Reverend Subhuti, there is no need to be frightened of any thing, since all things have the nature of a conjured illusion. Why? All words have that nature too, so the wise do not get stuck on words and are not frightened by them. Why? Because all those words are no-words, except for liberation; and all things have the mark of liberation.’

While he was giving this teaching, two hundred young gods gained the Dharma-eye, dustless and stainless, pure regarding things, and five hundred young gods gained the acceptance that conforms to the truth. And I had nothing to say; I could not give him any answer. So I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Purna Maitrayaniputra (the disciple foremost in teaching the Dharma): “Purna, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Purna too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once, in a spot in a certain forest, I was teaching the Dharma to some monks who were beginners.
Vimalakirti the Licchavi came up to me there and said:

‘Reverend Purna, first go into concentration, look into these monks’ minds, and then teach them the Dharma. Don’t put rotten food into a great jeweled vessel. First find out what these monks are aiming for. Don’t treat a beryl gem as the same as glass beads. Reverend Purna, don’t, without looking, force narrow faculties onto beings. Don’t wound those who have no wound. Don’t lead those who want to travel the great road into a narrow alley. Don’t pour the great ocean into a cow’s hoofprint. Don’t try to make sunlight out of fireflies. Don’t set those ready to roar the lion’s roar to howling like jackals. Reverend Purna, all these monks have set out in the Great Vehicle, and their minds set on awakening are not lost. Reverend Purna, don’t show them the disciples’ vehicle. The disciples’ vehicle is a sorry thing.
When it comes to knowing how the faculties of beings differ, the disciples seem to me like people blind from birth.’

Then, at that moment, Vimalakirti the Licchavi entered a samadhi of such a kind that those monks remembered many kinds of former lives. They had planted roots of goodness under five hundred buddhas for the sake of perfect awakening, and their minds set on awakening came back before them. They bowed their heads to that good man’s feet and sat down right there with their palms joined. He taught them the Dharma in such a way that they could never again turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening.
So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Katyayana (the disciple foremost in explaining the teaching): “Katyayana, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Katyayana too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that the Blessed One had given the monks a brief instruction, and afterward I was teaching them the Dharma to settle the meaning of the words of that discourse, namely: the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of no-self, and the meaning of peace.
Vimalakirti the Licchavi came up to me there and said:

‘Reverend Katyayana, don’t teach the nature of things as something active, bound up with arising and perishing. Reverend Mahakatyayana, what in the final sense was never born and will never be born, has not arisen and has not ceased and will not cease: that is the meaning of impermanence. That the five heaps, following emptiness, neither arise nor cease: that is the meaning of suffering. That self and no-self are not two: that is the meaning of no-self. What has no nature of its own and no other nature was never set alight; what was never set alight is not put out; and that utter calm is the meaning of peace.’

cmp.note: 维摩诘在这里把四个词都翻转过来讲：「无常」的意思竟是「从来不生不灭」。这不是说万物是永恒的，而是说「生、灭」本身都不可得。英文、白话都照梵文直译，读者第一次读会觉得自相矛盾，这是原文有意的。
cmp.en: Vimalakirti turns all four words inside out: “impermanence” means “never born, never ceasing.” This does not say things are eternal; it says that arising and perishing themselves cannot be found. The English and the plain Chinese translate the Sanskrit directly; a first-time reader will find it self-contradictory, and the original intends that.

verses.en: While he was giving this teaching, the minds of those monks were freed from the outflows, no longer grasping. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Aniruddha (the disciple foremost in the divine eye): “Aniruddha, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”
Aniruddha too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why?

I remember, Blessed One, I was walking up and down on a walking path. A Brahma named Shubhavyuha (“Lovely Array”), with ten thousand Brahmas, lit up that place, came to me, bowed his head to my feet, stood to one side and said to me: ‘How far does the venerable Aniruddha see with the divine eye?’
I said to him: ‘Friend, I see this great galaxy of a billion worlds, the buddha-field of the Blessed One Shakyamuni, the way one sees an amalaka fruit placed in the palm of one’s hand.’

While we were talking, Vimalakirti the Licchavi came to that place, bowed his head to my feet and said: ‘Reverend Aniruddha, does the divine eye have the mark of being put together, or the mark of not being put together? If it has the mark of being put together, it is the same as the five higher knowledges of outsiders. If it has the mark of not being put together, what is not put together is unconditioned, and it cannot see. So how does the elder see?’
I fell silent.
And that Brahma, hearing this teaching from that good man, was amazed. He bowed to him and said: ‘Who in the world has the divine eye?’
He said: ‘In the world it is the buddhas, the blessed ones, who have the divine eye: without leaving the state of concentration they see all buddha-fields, and they do not see by way of two.’

When that Brahma heard this teaching, he and his following of ten thousand raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening with deep resolve. He bowed to me, saluted that good man, and vanished right there. And I had nothing to say. So I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Upali (the disciple foremost in the monastic discipline): “Upali, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Upali too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, two monks had committed an offense. They were ashamed before the Blessed One and did not go to him. They came to me and said: ‘Reverend Upali, we two have committed an offense, and we are too ashamed to go to the Blessed One. Venerable Upali, please, dispel our remorse and lift us out of the offense.’

So, Blessed One, I was instructing those two monks with a talk on the Dharma. Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi arrived there and said to me: ‘Reverend Upali, don’t make things worse for these two monks. Clear away their offense; don’t stir them up. Reverend Upali, an offense is not found standing inside, nor passing outside, nor in between the two. Why? Because the Blessed One has said: beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind, and purified by the purification of the mind. And, Reverend Upali, the mind is not found standing inside, nor outside, nor in between the two. As the mind is, so is the offense; as the offense is, so are all things: they do not stray from suchness.

cmp.note: 「心染则众生染，心净则众生净」。这句话在早期佛经里本来就有，维摩诘引用它，但接着说「心不在内、不在外、不在中间」，把这句话从「要努力净心」推到「心本身找不到」。
cmp.en: “Beings are defiled when the mind is defiled, purified when the mind is purified.” This saying already exists in the early sutras; Vimalakirti quotes it, then adds that the mind is “not inside, not outside, not in between,” pushing it from “work to purify the mind” to “the mind itself cannot be found.”

verses.en: Reverend Upali, the nature of mind by which the Reverend’s mind was freed: was that nature of mind ever defiled?’
I said: ‘No indeed.’
He said: ‘Reverend Upali, the minds of all beings have that same nature.

Reverend Upali, imagining is affliction; not imagining and not distinguishing is the nature. Distortion is defilement; being undistorted is the nature. Projecting a self is defilement; selflessness is the nature. Reverend Upali, all things arise, break up and do not stay, like a magic show, a cloud, a flash of lightning. All things depend on nothing and do not last even a moment. All things are like a dream or a mirage: what they show is false. All things are like the reflection of the moon in water: they arise from the mind’s imagining. Those who know this are called keepers of the discipline; those who are trained this way are well trained.’

cmp.note: 「持律者」，懂戒律、守戒律的人。优波离是佛弟子中「持律第一」，维摩诘偏偏对他说：懂得诸法如幻，才叫持律。英文 keepers of the discipline 照字面；律（vinaya）字面是「调伏、训练」，所以下句「这样受调伏的才是调伏好了」是同一个词根的双关。
cmp.en: “Keeper of the discipline,” one who knows and upholds the monastic rules. Upali was the disciple foremost in the discipline, and Vimalakirti tells him that only one who knows things are like illusions keeps the discipline. The English “keepers of the discipline” is literal; vinaya literally means “training, taming,” so the next phrase, “those who are trained this way are well trained,” is a pun on the same root.

verses.en: Then those two monks said: ‘This lay follower is the one with wisdom who keeps the discipline, not the Reverend Upali whom the Blessed One declared foremost among the keepers of the discipline!’

I said to them: ‘Monks, don’t think of him as a mere householder. Why? Apart from the Tathagata, there is no disciple or bodhisattva who could cut off his eloquence. That is how bright the light of his wisdom is.’

Then those two monks, their remorse dispelled, raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening right there with deep resolve. They bowed to that good man and said: ‘May all beings gain eloquence like this!’ So I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Rahula (the son the Buddha had before he left home): “Rahula, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Rahula too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once a lot of young Licchavis came to me and said: ‘Rahula, you are the Blessed One’s son; you gave up the kingdom of a wheel-turning king and went forth. What are the virtues and benefits of going forth?’
While I was explaining to them, as is proper, the virtues and benefits of going forth, Vimalakirti the Licchavi came to me. He bowed to me and said:

‘Reverend Rahula, the virtues and benefits of going forth should not be explained the way you are explaining them. Why? Because going forth has no virtues and no benefits. Reverend Rahula, where conditioned things are at work, there are virtues and benefits. But going forth is unconditioned, and in the unconditioned there are no virtues and no benefits.

cmp.note: 字面是「往前走出去」，指离开家庭去做游方修行者。中文「出家」是意译，非常贴切；英文 going forth 照字面，英文读者不一定知道它指出家为僧。
cmp.en: Literally “going forth,” leaving home to become a wandering renunciant. The Chinese 出家 (chūjiā, “leaving the household”) is an apt rendering of the sense; the English “going forth” is literal, and English readers may not realize it means becoming a monk.

verses.en: Reverend Rahula, going forth is formless, free of form. It is the road to nirvana. The wise praise it; the noble ones embrace it. It is the defeat of all the Maras. It carries one across the five destinies. It purifies the five eyes. It wins the five strengths. It establishes the five faculties. It does no harm to others. It is not mixed with evil things. It crushes the other teachers. It goes beyond conventional designations. It is a bridge over the mud. It has no ‘mine’ and is free of making things ‘mine.’ It owns nothing. It grasps nothing. It is untroubled and has left trouble behind. It sees one’s own mind and guards the minds of others. It is in tune with calm. It is blameless in every way. That is what is called going forth. Those who go forth like this have truly gone forth.
Young men, go forth in this well-taught Dharma and discipline. For the appearance of a buddha is rare, the right moment is rare, and gaining a human birth is rare.’
The young men said: ‘Householder, we have heard that the Tathagata does not let anyone go forth without the permission of their mother and father.’
He said to them: ‘Young men, raise your minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening and carry it through in practice. That will be your going forth and your full ordination.’
Then thirty-two young Licchavis raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ananda (the Buddha’s attendant, foremost in learning): “Ananda, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Ananda said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once the Blessed One’s body had some ailment, and milk was needed for it. So I took my bowl and stood at the door of the house of a very wealthy brahmin.
Vimalakirti the Licchavi arrived there, bowed to me and said:
‘Reverend Ananda, why are you standing near the door of this house with your bowl so early in the morning?’
I said to him: ‘Householder, the Blessed One’s body has some ailment, and milk is needed for it. That is what I am looking for.’

He said to me: ‘Enough, Reverend Ananda, don’t say that. Reverend Ananda, the Tathagata’s body is as solid as diamond; it has abandoned every unwholesome habit-trace and possesses every wholesome quality of great power. Where would illness come from for him? Where would harm come from?

Reverend Ananda, go quietly. Don’t slander the Blessed One. Don’t say this to anyone else. Don’t let the mighty young gods and the bodhisattvas gathered here from other buddha-fields hear it. Reverend Ananda, even a wheel-turning king, who has only a few fleeting roots of goodness, does not get sick. How could the Blessed One, who has measureless goodness, get sick? That is impossible. Go, go, Reverend Ananda. Don’t put us to shame. Don’t let the other teachers, the wandering ascetics, the Jain monks and the Ajivikas hear of it, or they will think: “What kind of teacher do these people have? He can’t even save himself when he is sick; how could he save sick beings?” So, Reverend Ananda, go quickly and quietly.
Don’t let anyone hear.

Moreover, Reverend Ananda, the Tathagatas have a body of Dharma, not a body fed on food. The Tathagatas have a body beyond the world, gone past all worldly things. The Tathagata’s body has no ailment; it has turned away from every outflow. The Tathagata’s body is unconditioned; it is free of all reckoning. For the Reverend to suppose it could be ill is unfitting and out of place.’

cmp.note: āmiṣa 是「肉、食物」，āmiṣakāya 就是「靠食物养的肉身」。英文 a body fed on food、白话「血肉滋养的身体」都照字面；鸠摩罗什译「思欲身」，意思转向了「欲望的身体」。
cmp.en: Āmiṣa means “flesh, food,” so āmiṣakāya is “a body of flesh nourished by food.” The English “a body fed on food” and the plain Chinese are literal; Kumarajiva’s 思欲身 (sīyù shēn, “body of longing and desire”) shifts the sense toward a body of desires.

verses.en: Blessed One, I felt deeply ashamed, and thought: ‘Can it be that I, so close to the Blessed One, heard wrongly or understood wrongly?’ Then I heard a voice from the sky:

‘Ananda, it is just as the householder says. And yet the Blessed One has appeared in a time of the five corruptions, and so beings have to be trained through this humble, rough, poor way of living. So go, Ananda, take the milk, and don’t be ashamed.’

cmp.note: 「五种浑浊」：时代、见解、烦恼、众生、寿命的浑浊。中文「五浊」是固定译名；英文 five corruptions 是意译，kaṣāya 原义是「涩、混浊的颜色」。
cmp.en: “The five turbidities”: the corruption of the age, of views, of afflictions, of beings and of lifespan. The Chinese 五浊 (wǔ zhuó, “five turbidities”) is the fixed rendering; the English “five corruptions” translates the sense, since kaṣāya originally means “astringent, a muddy color.”

verses.en: Blessed One, such were Vimalakirti the Licchavi’s questions, answers and teachings. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that son of good family’s illness.”
In this way the five hundred or so disciples told the Blessed One they did not dare go, and they told the Blessed One all the conversations they had had with Vimalakirti the Licchavi.
Then the Blessed One said to the bodhisattva Maitreya (who will be the next buddha after Shakyamuni): “Maitreya, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Maitreya too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once I was giving a talk on the Dharma to the young god Samtushita and the young gods of the Tushita heaven, about the stage of no turning back of the bodhisattvas, the great beings. Vimalakirti the Licchavi came to that place and said to me:

‘Maitreya, the Blessed One has predicted that you are only one birth away from unsurpassed, perfect awakening. So in which birth were you predicted, Maitreya? Past, future or present? A past birth has ended; a future birth has not yet arrived; and a present birth does not stay. As the Blessed One has said: “Monk, at every moment you are born, grow old, die, pass away and are reborn.” Entering certainty comes from the unborn; but the unborn is not predicted, and the unborn does not awaken.

cmp.note: 「被预言、被授记」：佛预先宣告某人将来会成佛。中文「授记」是专门术语；英文 predicted 比较口语，但少了「正式宣告」的郑重。
cmp.en: “Predicted, declared”: a buddha’s formal announcement that someone will become a buddha in the future. The Chinese 授记 (shòujì, “conferring the prediction”) is a technical term; the English “predicted” is more everyday but loses the solemnity of a formal declaration.

verses.en: So how were you predicted, Maitreya: by the arising of suchness, or by the ceasing of suchness? But suchness does not arise, does not cease, and will not cease. The suchness of all beings and the suchness of all things is the very suchness of Maitreya too. So if you have been predicted, all beings have been predicted too. Why? Because suchness does not appear as two, or as many. So when Maitreya wakes up to awakening, all beings too will wake up to that same awakening at that time. Why? Because awakening is the awakening of all beings. And when Maitreya enters final nirvana, all beings too will enter final nirvana then. Why? Because the Tathagatas do not enter final nirvana while all beings have not.
They see those beings as already at final rest, as having nirvana for their nature. So, Maitreya, don’t lead these young gods on; don’t mislead them.
No one stands firm in awakening, and no one turns back from it. Rather, Maitreya, make these young gods give up their view that imagines awakening as something.

For awakening is not reached by the body, nor by the mind. Awakening is the calming of all signs. Awakening is not projecting anything onto any object. Awakening is the stilling of all mental attention. Awakening is the cutting off of all views. Awakening is being free of all imaginings. Awakening is release from all agitation, conceit and wavering. Awakening is not resting on any vow. Awakening is entering non-attachment, free of all grasping. Awakening stands in the place of the realm of the Dharma. Awakening follows suchness. Awakening is established at the limit of reality. Awakening is non-dual, free of mind and its objects.

cmp.note: 「觉悟」，动词 budh 是「醒来」。英文 awakening 保留了「醒」的画面；中文「菩提」是音译，「觉悟」是意译，后者的「觉」也有醒的意思。下面一长串都在说觉悟「不是」什么，几乎没有一句说它「是」什么。
cmp.en: “Awakening,” from the verb budh, “to wake up.” The English “awakening” keeps the picture of waking; the Chinese has both the transliteration 菩提 (pútí) and the rendering 觉悟 (juéwù, “awakening, realizing”), whose 觉 also means “to wake.” The long list that follows says almost entirely what awakening is not.

verses.en: Awakening is even, as space is even. Awakening is unconditioned, free of arising, perishing, staying and changing. Awakening is the full knowledge of the thoughts, conduct and intentions of all beings. Awakening has no door for the sense fields. Awakening is unmixed, free of all afflictions linked by habit-traces. Awakening is not in any place or any region; it is free of place and no-place. Awakening is established in suchness and cannot be seen from anywhere. Awakening is a mere name, and that name does nothing. Awakening is selfless, free of taking up and throwing out. Awakening is untroubled, pure by nature. Awakening is bright, pure in its own being. Awakening cannot be grasped, free of every support. Awakening has no differences, because it understands the sameness of all things. Awakening is beyond compare, free of every simile. Awakening is subtle, because it is hard to understand. Awakening goes everywhere, because its nature is space. It cannot be reached by body, speech or mind.’
