Blessed One, while he was giving this teaching, two hundred young gods in that assembly gained the acceptance that things are unborn. And I had nothing to say. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to Prabhavyuha (“Array of Light”), the young Licchavi: “Good sir, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Prabhavyuha too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once I was leaving the great city of Vaishali just as Vimalakirti the Licchavi was coming in. I greeted him and said: ‘Householder, where are you coming from?’
He said to me: ‘I am coming from the seat of awakening.’

cmp.note: 「觉悟之座」，原指佛陀在菩提树下成道的那块地方。中文译「道场」，后来泛指寺院、修行的场所；鸠摩罗什的「直心是道场」就是从这一段来的。英文 seat of awakening 保留了原意，下文维摩诘把它推广到一切心与行。
cmp.en: “The seat (or terrace) of awakening,” originally the spot under the bodhi tree where the Buddha awoke. The Chinese renders it 道场 (dàochǎng, “place of the Way”), which later came to mean any temple or place of practice; Kumarajiva’s 直心是道场 (“a straight mind is the place of awakening”) comes from this passage. The English “seat of awakening” keeps the original sense, which Vimalakirti then extends to every mind and act.

verses.en: I said to him: ‘What is this name, “seat of awakening,” a name for?’
He said to me:

‘Son of good family, the seat of awakening is the seat of sincere intent, because it is not artificial. It is the seat of practice, because it carries through what it starts. It is the seat of deep resolve, because it reaches distinction. It is the seat of the mind set on awakening, because it does not forget.

It is the seat of giving, because it expects no reward. It is the seat of morality, because it fulfills its vows. It is the seat of patience, because its mind has no aversion to any being. It is the seat of effort, because it does not turn back. It is the seat of meditation, because the mind is workable. It is the seat of wisdom, because it sees directly.

It is the seat of kindness, because its mind is the same toward all beings. It is the seat of compassion, because it bears weariness. It is the seat of sympathetic joy, because it delights in the pleasure garden of the Dharma. It is the seat of equanimity, because it has abandoned liking and disliking.

It is the seat of the higher knowledges, because it has the six higher knowledges. It is the seat of liberation, because it does not imagine. It is the seat of skill in means, because it brings beings to maturity. It is the seat of the ways of gathering people, because it gathers in all beings. It is the seat of learning, because practice is its core. It is the seat of reflection, because it examines things properly. It is the seat of the things that belong to awakening, because it lets go of both the conditioned and the unconditioned. It is the seat of truth, because it deceives no one in the world. It is the seat of dependent arising, because it is the ending of the outflows from ignorance all the way to the ending of the outflows from old age and death. It is the seat of calming all afflictions, because it awakens to things as they really are.

It is the seat of all beings, because beings have no nature of their own. It is the seat of all things, because it awakens to emptiness. It is the seat of striking down all Maras, because it does not waver. It is the seat of the three realms, because it has left off setting out anywhere. It is the seat of the courage to roar the lion’s roar, because it is fearless and unafraid. It is the seat of the powers, the kinds of confidence, the unique qualities and all the qualities of a buddha, because it is beyond reproach in every way. It is the seat of the three knowledges, because no afflictions are left. It is the seat of understanding all things completely in a single moment of mind, because it brings all-knowing knowledge to completion.

So, son of good family, whenever bodhisattvas lift their feet and set them down in matters connected with the perfections, with bringing beings to maturity, with taking up the true Dharma and with roots of goodness, all of them are coming from the seat of awakening; they come from the qualities of a buddha, and they stand in the qualities of a buddha.’

Blessed One, while he was giving this teaching, five hundred or so gods and humans raised their minds toward awakening. And I had nothing to say. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to the bodhisattva Jagatindhara (“Upholder of the World”): “Jagatindhara, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Jagatindhara too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, that once I was staying in my own dwelling. Then Mara the Evil One (the lord of death and desire, who obstructs practice), surrounded by twelve thousand heavenly maidens and disguised as Shakra, came to me to the sound of instruments and song. He bowed his head to my feet and, with his retinue, stood respectfully to one side. I took him for Shakra, lord of the gods.

I said to him: ‘Welcome, Kaushika (Shakra’s clan name). You should be careful amid all the pleasures of the senses. You should often reflect on impermanence, and take what has real substance out of your body, your life and your wealth.’
He said to me: ‘Good sir, accept these twelve thousand heavenly maidens from me; let them be your servants.’
I said to him: ‘Kaushika, don’t offer the Shakyan ascetics things that are not allowed for them. These women are not proper for us.’

While we were talking, Vimalakirti the Licchavi came up and said to me: ‘Son of good family, don’t take him for Shakra. This is Mara the Evil One, who has come meaning to trouble you. This is not Shakra.’
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to Mara the Evil One: ‘Evil One, hand these heavenly maidens over to us. They are proper for us, not for the Shakyan ascetics.’

Then Mara the Evil One was afraid, frightened and agitated: ‘I must not be made a fool of by Vimalakirti the Licchavi!’ He wanted to vanish, but even using all his magic powers he could not vanish. Then he heard a voice from the sky: ‘Evil One, hand these heavenly maidens over to this good man, and then you will be able to go back to your own palace.’ So Mara, afraid and frightened, unwillingly handed the heavenly maidens over to him.

Vimalakirti accepted the heavenly maidens and said to them: ‘Mara the Evil One has handed you over to me. Now raise your minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.’ He gave them a talk suited to them, one that ripens them for awakening, and so led them to raise their minds toward awakening.
He said to them: ‘Now that you have raised the mind set on awakening, from now on you should take your delight in the pleasure garden of the Dharma, not in the pleasures of the senses.’
They said: ‘And what is the delight in the pleasure garden of the Dharma?’

He said: ‘Delight in unbreakable faith in the Buddha; delight in longing to hear the Dharma; delight in serving the Sangha; delight in honoring and serving teachers; delight in escaping the three realms; delight in not leaning on sense objects; delight in regarding the heaps as killers and as impermanent; delight in weighing the elements as poisonous snakes; delight in seeing the sense fields as an empty village, in solitude; delight in guarding the mind set on awakening; delight in being of use to beings; delight in sharing when giving; delight in not slackening in morality; delight in forbearance and self-control in patience; delight in gathering the wholesome through effort; delight in training in the meditations; delight in the light of wisdom that is free of afflictions; delight in the vastness of awakening; delight in subduing Mara; delight in destroying the afflictions; delight in purifying a buddha-field; delight in gathering every root of goodness to perfect the marks and minor signs; delight in hearing the deep Dharma without fear; delight in mastering the three doors of liberation; delight in nirvana as one’s aim; delight in adorning the seat of awakening, and no delight in reaching it before its time; delight in keeping company with people of like mind; delight in feeling no hatred or hostility toward those of unlike mind; delight in keeping company with good friends; delight in leaving bad friends; delight in the joy and gladness of the Dharma; delight in gathering people through skill in means; delight in practicing, with care, the things that belong to awakening.
That is how a bodhisattva takes his delight in the pleasure garden of the Dharma.’
Then Mara the Evil One said to the heavenly maidens: ‘Come. Now we will go back to our own palace.’
They said: ‘You have handed us over to this householder. Now we must take our delight in the pleasure garden of the Dharma, not in the pleasures of the senses.’
Then Mara the Evil One said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: ‘Householder, let these heavenly maidens go. Bodhisattvas, great beings, are people who give away everything they own.’
Vimalakirti said: ‘Let them be released. Go, Evil One. May the righteous wishes of all beings be fulfilled.’
Then the heavenly maidens bowed to Vimalakirti and said: ‘Householder, how should we live in Mara’s palace?’

He said: ‘Sisters, there is a Dharma-door called the Inexhaustible Lamp. Practice it. What is it? Sisters, it is like this: from a single oil lamp, hundreds of thousands of lamps are lit, and that lamp does not lose anything. In the same way, sisters, a single bodhisattva establishes many hundreds of thousands of beings in awakening, and that bodhisattva’s mindfulness does not decrease or fade away; on the contrary, it grows. In the same way, the more he tells and teaches all good things to others, the more he grows in all good things. That is the Dharma-door called the Inexhaustible Lamp. Living there in Mara’s palace, you should make countless young gods and heavenly maidens delight in the mind set on awakening. In this way you will show your gratitude to the Tathagata,

cmp.note: 「无尽灯」：一盏灯点燃千百盏灯，自己不减。这个比喻后来在中文里变成了「传灯」「无尽灯」的说法，用来比喻佛法代代相传。英文 Inexhaustible Lamp 照字面。
cmp.en: “The Inexhaustible Lamp”: one lamp lights hundreds of thousands without losing anything itself. In Chinese this image became the phrases 传灯 (chuándēng, “passing on the lamp”) and 无尽灯 (wújìn dēng, “inexhaustible lamp”) for the Dharma handed down through generations. The English is literal.

verses.en: and you will be a source of life for all beings.’

Then the heavenly maidens bowed their heads to the feet of Vimalakirti the Licchavi and left with Mara. Blessed One, such are the extraordinary transformations of Vimalakirti the Licchavi, which I did not recognize. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
Then the Blessed One said to Sudatta, the son of a merchant banker: “Son of good family, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Sudatta too said: “Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness. Why? I remember, Blessed One, I was holding a great sacrifice in my father’s house, giving gifts to all the poor and suffering, to all ascetics and brahmins, to the wretched, to vagrants and beggars. I held the great sacrifice for seven days.

On the seventh day, Vimalakirti the Licchavi came into the hall of the great sacrifice and said to me: ‘Merchant’s son, a sacrifice should not be held the way you are holding it. You should hold a sacrifice of the Dharma. What use to you is a sacrifice of material things?’

cmp.note: 「祭祀」：婆罗门教的献祭大典，常伴随大规模布施。中文「祭祀」保留了宗教色彩；鸠摩罗什译「大施会」，把它说成布施大会，淡化了献祭的背景。英文 sacrifice 照字面。维摩诘把「财物的祭祀」换成「法的祭祀」，是借用婆罗门的词讲佛法。
cmp.en: “Sacrifice”: the great Brahmanical offering rite, often accompanied by large-scale giving. The plain Chinese 祭祀 (jìsì, “sacrificial rite”) keeps the religious color; Kumarajiva’s 大施会 (dà shī huì, “great almsgiving assembly”) turns it into a charity event and plays down the sacrificial background. The English “sacrifice” is literal. Vimalakirti swaps a “sacrifice of material things” for a “sacrifice of the Dharma,” borrowing a brahmin word to teach Buddhism.

verses.en: I said to him: ‘Then how should a sacrifice of the Dharma be held?’
He said to me:

‘A sacrifice of the Dharma is one by which all beings are brought to maturity all at once, without first or last. What is it? It is great kindness brought forth in the form of awakening; great compassion brought forth by taking up the true Dharma; great sympathetic joy brought forth with the gladness of all beings as its object; great equanimity brought forth by taking up knowledge;

the perfection of giving, brought forth by calm and self-control; the perfection of morality, brought forth by bringing immoral beings to maturity; the perfection of patience, brought forth by the truth of no-self; the perfection of effort, brought forth by the factors of awakening; the perfection of meditation, brought forth by solitude of body and mind; the perfection of wisdom, brought forth by all-knowing knowledge;

the cultivation of emptiness, brought forth by bringing all beings to maturity; the cultivation of signlessness, brought forth by attending to conditioned things; the cultivation of wishlessness, brought forth by being born deliberately;

strength and courage, brought forth by taking up the true Dharma; the life-force, brought forth by the ways of gathering people; freedom from pride, brought forth by becoming the servant and pupil of all beings; gaining body, life and wealth, brought forth by taking what has substance out of what has none; mindfulness, brought forth by the six recollections; deep resolve, brought forth by things that bring joy; purity of livelihood, brought forth by right practice; attending on the noble ones, brought forth by serving them with faith and gladness; reflection of mind, brought forth by feeling no hostility toward those who are not noble; deep resolve, brought forth by going forth; skill in learning, brought forth by practice; living in the forest, brought forth by penetrating the Dharma of non-conflict; retreat, brought forth by attaining the knowledge of a buddha; the stage of yoga practice, brought forth by the practice of freeing all beings from their afflictions;

bringing beings to maturity, brought forth by the stores for the marks and minor signs; the store of merit, brought forth by adorning a buddha-field; the store of knowledge, brought forth by teaching the Dharma to suit the thoughts, conduct and intentions of all beings; the store of wisdom, brought forth by knowing the single way in which all things are neither taken up nor thrown out; the store of all roots of goodness, brought forth by abandoning all afflictions, all obstructions and all unwholesome things;
and the arising of all the things that belong to awakening, brought forth by waking up to all-knowing knowledge and all wholesome things.

Son of good family, that is the sacrifice of the Dharma. Bodhisattvas who stand in this sacrifice of the Dharma are the true sacrificers, those who have offered the sacrifice well, and they are worthy of offerings from the world with its gods.’ Blessed One, while that householder was teaching like this, two hundred brahmins in that gathering of brahmins raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Amazed and filled with faith, I bowed at that good man’s feet, took from my neck a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand, and offered it to him. He would not accept the pearl necklace. I said to him: ‘Please accept it, and give it to whomever you have faith in.’

So he took the pearl necklace and divided it in two. One half he gave to the poorest man in the city, whom everyone despised, who was there in the sacrificial hall. The other half he offered to the Tathagata Dushprasaha (“Hard to Overcome”). And the whole assembly saw the world called Marichi (“Ray of Light”) and the Tathagata Dushprasaha, and saw that pearl necklace become a pearl pavilion above the crown of Dushprasaha’s head, colorful and lovely to look at, four-sided, with four pillars, evenly proportioned and well laid out.

Having shown this miracle, he spoke these words: ‘When a giver, a patron, regards the poorest man in the city as just as worthy of offerings as he regards the Tathagata, without any difference, the same; when he gives with a mind of great compassion, expecting no reward: that is the fulfillment of the sacrifice of the Dharma.’

cmp.note: 「值得供养的想法」：佛教认为供养越神圣的对象福报越大，所以如来是最好的「福田」。维摩诘把最穷的人和如来放在同一个位置，正是在推翻这种计算。鸠摩罗什译「等于如来福田之相，无所分别」，意思一致。
cmp.en: “The notion that someone is worthy of offerings”: Buddhists held that the holier the recipient, the greater the merit, which made the Tathagata the best “field of merit.” By putting the poorest beggar in the same place as the Tathagata, Vimalakirti overturns that calculation. Kumarajiva’s 等于如来福田之相，无所分别 (“equal to the mark of the Tathagata as field of merit, without distinction”) says the same.

verses.en: Then the poorest man in the city, seeing this miracle and hearing this teaching, raised his mind toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. So, Blessed One, I don’t dare go and ask after that good man’s illness.”
In this way all those bodhisattvas, great beings, each told their own story and the conversations they had had with that good man, and none of them dared to go.
This was chapter three, called “Asking the Disciples and Bodhisattvas to Go.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · Asking After the Sick Man

verses.en: Then the Blessed One said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, go and ask after the illness of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.”

Manjushri too said: “Blessed One, that Vimalakirti the Licchavi is hard to approach. He has gone deep into the profound way and into eloquence. He is skilled at putting things into words, whether taken apart or put together. His eloquence never gets stuck. His understanding is beyond compare among all beings. He has completed all the work of a bodhisattva. He has gone deep into all the secret places of all the bodhisattvas and all the buddhas. He plays with the great higher knowledges that are skilled at overturning every stronghold of Mara. He has reached the highest perfection in the sphere of the realm of the Dharma, which is non-dual and undivided. He teaches a Dharma of endless kinds of splendor within the single splendor of the realm of the Dharma. He is skilled in the knowledge that brings the faculties of all beings to fulfillment. He has mastered skill in means. He has settled every question. He cannot be satisfied with a little preparation. And yet I will go, upheld by the Buddha, and there I will talk with him as far as my ability and strength allow.”

cmp.note: 「难以接近、难以应对」。鸠摩罗什译「彼上人者，难为酬对」，强调对答困难；英文 hard to approach 照字面，带一点「不好惹」的意思。
cmp.en: “Hard to approach, hard to face.” Kumarajiva’s 彼上人者，难为酬对 (“that superior man is hard to answer”) stresses how difficult he is to debate; the English “hard to approach” is literal and carries a hint of “not someone to take on lightly.”

verses.en: Then this thought came to the bodhisattvas, the disciples, the Shakras, Brahmas and world-guardians and the young gods in that assembly: “Surely, where Manjushri, the young prince, and that good man are going to talk with each other, there will be a great conversation, a great hearing of the Dharma.” So eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred or so disciples, many Shakras, Brahmas and world-guardians, and many hundreds of thousands of young gods followed Manjushri to hear the Dharma. Then Manjushri, the young prince, surrounded by those bodhisattvas, great beings, by those disciples, and by those Shakras, Brahmas, world-guardians and young gods, entered the great city of Vaishali.

Then this thought came to Vimalakirti: “Here comes Manjushri, the young prince, with a great following. Why don’t I make my house empty by my power?” So by his power he made the house empty, with no doorkeeper. No beds, chairs or seats were to be seen there, except for the one bed on which he himself lay sick. Then Manjushri and his following went to Vimalakirti’s house. When he arrived, he went in. He saw the house empty, with no doorkeeper, and he saw no beds or chairs there except the one bed where Vimalakirti was lying. Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi saw Manjushri, the young prince.
Seeing him, he said: “Welcome, Manjushri! And not welcome, Manjushri: you have not come at all. Here is a sight of one who has not come, never seen or heard before.”

cmp.note: svāgata 字面是「来得好」（su「好」+ āgata「来」），是「欢迎」的意思。维摩诘接着说 asvāgata「不是来得好」，再接 anāgata「没有来过的」，是在拿「来」字做文章。英文 welcome 拆不开，只能用 not welcome … not come at all 勉强保留。鸠摩罗什改写成「善来文殊师利！不来相而来，不见相而见」，把双关说成了道理。
cmp.en: Svāgata literally means “well come” (su, “well” + āgata, “come”), that is, “welcome.” Vimalakirti then says asvāgata, “not well come,” and anāgata, “one who has not come,” playing on the word “come.” The English “welcome” cannot be split this way, so “not welcome … not come at all” keeps the play only roughly. Kumarajiva rewrites it as 善来文殊师利！不来相而来，不见相而见 (“Welcome, Manjushri! Coming without the mark of coming, seeing without the mark of seeing”), turning the pun into a statement of doctrine.

verses.en: Manjushri said: “It is just as you say, householder. One who has come will not come again, and one who has gone will not go again. Why? Because no coming is found for one who has come, and no going for one who has gone; and one who has been seen is not to be seen again.

But are you bearing up, good sir? Are you getting by? Are your elements thrown out of balance by wind? Is the illness going away, and not getting worse? The Blessed One asks whether you have little pain and little trouble, little sickness; whether you get up easily; whether you have vigor, strength and ease, are free of fault, and live in comfort.
Householder, where did this illness of yours arise from? How long have you had it? And when will it settle down?”

Vimalakirti said: “Manjushri, for as long as there have been ignorance and the thirst for existence, for that long I have had this illness. When all beings are free of illness, then my illness will subside. Why? Because, Manjushri, a bodhisattva’s samsara rests on beings, and illness depends on samsara. When all beings are free of illness, then the bodhisattva will be well.

Manjushri, it is like this: suppose a merchant banker’s only son were ill. His mother and father would be ill too, and they would suffer for as long as their only son was not free of his illness. In the same way, Manjushri, a bodhisattva loves all beings as an only son. He is ill because beings are ill, and well when beings are well. And when you ask, Manjushri, where the illness arose from: the bodhisattvas’ illness arises from great compassion.”

cmp.note: 鸠摩罗什译「以众生病，是故我病」「菩萨病者，以大悲起」，是全经最常被引用的句子。梵文意思一样。英文照直译，没有加修饰。
cmp.en: Kumarajiva’s 以众生病，是故我病 (“because beings are ill, I am ill”) and 菩萨病者，以大悲起 (“a bodhisattva’s illness arises from great compassion”) are the most quoted lines in the whole sutra. The Sanskrit means the same, and the English translates it plainly without embellishment.

verses.en: Manjushri said: “Householder, your house is empty, and you have no attendant at all.”
He said: “Manjushri, all the buddha-fields are empty too.”
He said: “What makes them empty?”
He said: “Emptiness makes them empty.”
He said: “What is empty about emptiness?”
He said: “Emptinesses are empty of imagining.”
He said: “Then can emptiness be imagined?”
He said: “Even that which would imagine it is empty. And emptiness does not imagine emptiness.”
He said: “Householder, where should emptiness be looked for?”
He said: “Manjushri, emptiness should be looked for in the sixty-two views.”

cmp.note: 「六十二见」：早期佛经列出的六十二种关于自我与世界的错误见解。白话加了「邪见」，英文只写 views；梵文 dṛṣṭigata 本身就带贬义（「落入见解」），英文读者需要知道这一点。
cmp.en: “The sixty-two views”: the list, in the early sutras, of sixty-two mistaken views about the self and the world. The plain Chinese adds 邪见 (xiéjiàn, “wrong views”), while the English says just “views”; the Sanskrit dṛṣṭigata (“gone into views”) is already pejorative, which the English reader should know.

verses.en: He said: “And where should the sixty-two views be looked for?”
He said: “They should be looked for in the Tathagata’s liberation.”
He said: “And where should the Tathagata’s liberation be looked for?”

He said: “It should be looked for in the thoughts and conduct of all beings. And when you ask, Manjushri, who my attendants are: all the Maras and all the teachers of other doctrines are my attendants. Why? Because the Maras speak in praise of samsara, and samsara is a bodhisattva’s attendant; and the teachers of other doctrines speak in praise of views, and a bodhisattva is not moved by any view. That is why all the Maras and all the teachers of other doctrines are my attendants.”
Manjushri said: “Householder, what is this illness of yours like?”
He said: “It cannot be seen and cannot be pointed out.”
He said: “Is this illness joined to the body, or joined to the mind?”
He said: “It is not joined to the body, because the body is detached; and it is not joined to the mind, because the mind’s nature is illusion.”
He said: “Householder, there are these four elements. Which four? The earth element, the water element, the fire element and the wind element. Which of these elements is troubling you?”
He said: “Manjushri, whatever element the illness of all beings comes from, that is the one I am ill from.”
“But tell me, Manjushri: how should a bodhisattva comfort a bodhisattva who is ill?”

Manjushri said: “By speaking of the body’s impermanence, but not of weariness and turning away from it. By speaking of the body’s suffering, but not of delighting in nirvana. By speaking of the body’s lack of self, and of bringing beings to maturity. By speaking of the body’s calm, but not of final extinction. By speaking of confessing all misdeeds, but not of their passing over into the past. By feeling compassion for the illness of other beings through his own illness. By recalling the suffering of beginningless past time. By recalling the work done for the good of beings. By bringing roots of goodness to the fore. By speaking of original purity. By speaking of not craving. By always making an effort. And by saying: ‘You will become a king of physicians who cures every illness.’ That is how a bodhisattva should comfort a bodhisattva who is ill.”
Manjushri said: “Son of good family, how should a bodhisattva who is ill reflect on his own mind?”

Vimalakirti said: “Manjushri, a bodhisattva who is ill should reflect on his own mind like this: ‘This illness has arisen from past actions rooted in unreal distortions; it has arisen from afflictions that imagine what is unreal. In the ultimate sense, no thing can be found here that has this illness. Why? This bundle is made of the four great elements, and these elements have no owner and no one who makes them arise. This bundle has no self. What is called illness cannot be found in the ultimate sense, apart from clinging to a self. So let us not live clinging to a self, but know the root of the illness fully.’ Therefore he should set aside the notion of a self and raise the notion of things: ‘This body is a collection of things. When things arise, it is just things arising; when things cease, it is just things ceasing.
And these things do not think about one another or know one another. When they arise, they do not think, “We are arising”; when they cease, they do not think, “We are ceasing.”’

Then, to deal with the notion of things, he should raise this thought: ‘This notion of things, too, is a distortion, and distortion is a great illness. I must be free of illness, and I must work to get rid of illness.’ And what is getting rid of illness? It is getting rid of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ And what is getting rid of ‘I’ and ‘mine’? It is leaving behind two. And what is leaving behind two? It is not operating inside or outside. And what is not operating inside or outside? It is not moving and not wavering, through sameness. And what is sameness? The sameness of the self is the sameness of nirvana. Why? Because both of these, the self and nirvana, are empty. What makes them empty? They are empty because they are mere names spoken. Neither of these, the self or nirvana, is actually established.
One who sees sameness like this does not treat illness as one thing and emptiness as another: the illness itself is emptiness.

Feeling should be felt as not felt, but he should not therefore realize the cessation of feeling. As long as the qualities of a buddha are not complete, he should not give up either kind of feeling. And he must not fail to feel great compassion for beings born in the bad destinies. ‘We will act so as to take away the illness that these beings have from thinking about things wrongly.’

cmp.note: ayoniśo 是「不如理、不正确地」，指众生因为想错了而生病。白话译成「用这种如理的观察」，方向弄反了。英文照梵文译：去除众生因「想错」而得的病。
cmp.en: Ayoniśo means “improperly, wrongly”: beings are ill because they think about things the wrong way. The plain Chinese renders it 用这种如理的观察 (“through this proper reflection”), which reverses the sense. The English follows the Sanskrit: taking away the illness beings have from thinking wrongly.

verses.en: We will not add any thing to them or take any thing away from them. We will teach them the Dharma so that they understand the cause from which illness arises. And what is that cause? It is the cause of grasping at objects. As long as one grasps at objects, there is a cause of illness. And what does one grasp at? One grasps at the three realms. And how is grasping at objects understood? By not finding the object. What one does not find, one does not grasp. And what does one not find? One does not find either of two views: the view of self and the view of other. That is called not finding.’ That is how, Manjushri, a bodhisattva who is ill should reflect on his own mind, so as to get rid of old age, illness, death and rebirth.

Manjushri, if the bodhisattvas’ awakening were not like this, wouldn’t their effort be pointless? Just as people are called heroes because they strike down enemies, bodhisattvas are called bodhisattvas because they calm the suffering of old age, illness and death.

A bodhisattva who is ill should consider: ‘Just as my illness is unreal and does not exist, so the illness of all beings is unreal and does not exist.’ When he considers things like this, his great compassion for beings does not fall into views about rewards; his great compassion for beings arises only from the effort to get rid of afflictions that are mere passing visitors. Why? Because when great compassion has fallen into views about rewards, a bodhisattva grows weary of being reborn again and again. But when great compassion is free of entanglement in views about rewards, a bodhisattva does not grow weary of being reborn. He is reborn, but not reborn entangled in views. Being reborn with an untangled mind, he is reborn already free; he is born already free.

cmp.note: anuśaṃsā 是「利益、好处、回报」。梵文说：悲心如果落入「想得好处」的见解，菩萨就会累。鸠摩罗什译成「爱见大悲」，把它说成「带着爱执的悲心」，后来成了中文佛教的常用词，意思和梵文略有不同。
cmp.en: Anuśaṃsā means “benefit, advantage, reward.” The Sanskrit says that if compassion falls into views about rewards, the bodhisattva grows weary. Kumarajiva renders it 爱见大悲 (àijiàn dàbēi, “great compassion of affectionate views”), compassion tinged with attachment; the phrase became common in Chinese Buddhism, but its sense differs slightly from the Sanskrit.

cmp.note: 「外来的、客人般的烦恼」：烦恼不是心本来有的，只是暂时来访的客人。中文后来叫「客尘烦恼」。英文 mere passing visitors 保留了「客人」的比喻。
cmp.en: “Adventitious afflictions,” afflictions that are like guests: not part of the mind itself, only temporary visitors. Chinese later called them 客尘烦恼 (kèchén fánnǎo, “guest-dust afflictions”). The English “mere passing visitors” keeps the guest image.

verses.en: Being reborn already free, born already free, he is able and fit to teach the Dharma to beings who are bound, so as to free them from their bonds. As the Blessed One has said: ‘That someone who is himself bound should free another from his bonds is impossible. That someone who is himself free should free another from his bonds is possible.’ So a bodhisattva should be free, not bound.

And what is bondage, and what is freedom? Taking up destinies of existence without skill in means is a bodhisattva’s bondage; going into destinies of existence with skill in means is freedom. Savoring the meditations and samadhis without skill in means is a bodhisattva’s bondage; savoring the meditations and samadhis with skill in means is freedom. Wisdom not held by skill in means is bondage; wisdom held by skill in means is freedom. Skill in means not held by wisdom is bondage; skill in means held by wisdom is freedom.

What is wisdom not held by skill in means, which is bondage? It is reflecting on emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness, but not reflecting on the marks and minor signs, on adorning a buddha-field and on bringing beings to maturity. That is wisdom not held by skill in means, which is bondage. What is wisdom held by skill in means, which is freedom? It is a mind that reflects on the marks and minor signs, on adorning a buddha-field and on bringing beings to maturity, together with mastery of emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness. That is wisdom held by skill in means, which is freedom. What is skill in means not held by wisdom, which is bondage? It is undertaking every root of goodness while standing in all the views, the outbursts and latent tendencies of the afflictions, liking and aversion, and not dedicating them to awakening. That is skill in means not held by wisdom, which is bondage.

What is skill in means held by wisdom, which is freedom? It is undertaking every root of goodness, having abandoned all the views, the outbursts and latent tendencies of the afflictions, liking and aversion; dedicating it to awakening; and not clinging to it. That is a bodhisattva’s skill in means held by wisdom, which is freedom.

cmp.note: 这几段是全经的理论核心：智慧（看透一切是空）和方便（仍然投入度众生的事）必须互相「摄持」，缺一个就成了束缚。鸠摩罗什译「无方便慧缚，有方便慧解；无慧方便缚，有慧方便解」，四句对仗，非常好记。英文照梵文逐句译，读起来比较长。
cmp.en: These passages are the theoretical core of the sutra: wisdom (seeing that all is empty) and skill in means (still throwing oneself into helping beings) must each “hold” the other, and either one alone is bondage. Kumarajiva compresses it into four balanced lines, 无方便慧缚，有方便慧解；无慧方便缚，有慧方便解 (“wisdom without means binds, wisdom with means frees; means without wisdom binds, means with wisdom frees”), which are easy to memorize. The English follows the Sanskrit clause by clause and is longer.

verses.en: Manjushri, a bodhisattva who is ill should reflect on these things like this. Seeing body, mind and illness as impermanent, painful, empty and without self: that is his wisdom. Not growing weary of looking after the body’s illness, not cutting off samsara, devoting himself to the good of beings: that is his skill in means. Again, seeing body, illness and mind as following one after another, neither new nor old: that is his wisdom. Not bringing body, illness and mind to final calm and cessation: that is his skill in means.

That is how, Manjushri, a bodhisattva who is ill should reflect on his mind. Yet he should not stay in reflecting or in not reflecting. Why? If he stayed in not reflecting, that would be the way of fools; if he stayed in reflecting, that would be the way of the disciples. So a bodhisattva should not stay in reflection. Not staying anywhere here: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere.

cmp.note: 「行境、活动的范围」，字面是「牛吃草的地方、牧场」。英文 sphere 是比较中性的译法；鸠摩罗什译「菩萨行」，把它说成「菩萨的行为」，重点从「范围」移到「行动」。
cmp.en: “Sphere of activity,” literally “a pasture, where cattle graze.” The English “sphere” is a neutral rendering; Kumarajiva’s 菩萨行 (púsà xíng, “bodhisattva conduct”) shifts the focus from the range to the action.

verses.en: What is neither the sphere of ordinary people nor the sphere of the noble ones: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in samsara, yet not move in the afflictions: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To contemplate nirvana, yet not enter final nirvana: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To show the four Maras, yet go beyond the domain of all Maras: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To seek all-knowing knowledge, yet not attain knowledge before its time: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To know the four truths, yet not penetrate the truth before its time: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To examine oneself inwardly, yet deliberately take up rebirth in existence: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere.

To contemplate the unborn, yet not enter certainty: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in dependent arising, yet be free of all views: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To mix with all beings, yet not move in the afflictions and latent tendencies: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in solitude, yet not rely on the ending of body and mind: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the three realms, yet not break up the realm of the Dharma: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in emptiness, yet seek good qualities of every kind: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in signlessness, yet keep thinking about freeing beings: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere.

cmp.note: 「进入决定」：在部派佛教里，指一旦见道就「定」了，必然走向阿罗汉的涅槃。对菩萨来说，这意味着落入声闻的终点。白话加了一段说明；英文只写 enter certainty，读者需要这层背景。
cmp.en: “Entering certainty”: in the early schools, once one sees the path one is “fixed,” bound to reach the arhat’s nirvana. For a bodhisattva that would mean ending up at the disciples’ goal. The plain Chinese adds an explanation; the English says only “enter certainty,” and the reader needs this background.

verses.en: To move in wishlessness, yet deliberately show oneself in the destinies of existence: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in not-putting-together, yet never stop putting together every root of goodness: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the six perfections, yet reach the far shore of the thoughts and conduct of all beings: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the six recollections, yet not move in the ending of all outflows: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To stand in the true Dharma, yet not grasp at wrong paths: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the six higher knowledges, yet not move in the ending of the outflows: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the four immeasurables, yet not reach out for rebirth in the Brahma worlds: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere.

To move in the meditations, samadhis and attainments, yet not be reborn by the force of samadhi and attainment: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the foundations of mindfulness, yet not overdo body, feeling, mind and mental objects: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the right efforts, yet not take wholesome and unwholesome as two: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To develop the bases of power, yet wield the bases of power without effort: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To move in the five faculties, yet know which faculties of all beings are higher and which lower: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To stand in the five strengths, yet show the ten powers of a Tathagata: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere.

To perfect the seven factors of awakening, yet be skilled in knowing the distinctions of understanding: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To stand on the path, yet not grasp at wrong paths: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To seek the stores of calm and insight, yet not fall into final peace: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To examine all things as having the mark of non-arising, yet perfect the body of a buddha adorned with form, marks and minor signs: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To show the behavior of disciples and solitary buddhas, yet not give up the qualities of a buddha: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere.

To follow all things, which have reached a nature that is utterly pure, yet show every kind of conduct to suit what beings are inclined to: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To see all buddha-fields as having the nature of space, utterly without forming and dissolving, yet show the splendid arrays of good qualities of buddha-fields in many different kinds of splendor: that is a bodhisattva’s sphere. To show the turning of the wheel of the Dharma and the great final nirvana, yet not give up the bodhisattva’s practice: that too is a bodhisattva’s sphere.”
While this teaching was being given, eight thousand of the young gods who had come with Manjushri, the young prince, raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.
This was chapter four, “Asking After the Sick Man.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5 · Showing the Liberation Beyond Thought

verses.en: Then this thought came to the venerable Shariputra: “Where will these bodhisattvas and these great disciples sit? There are no seats in this house.”

Vimalakirti the Licchavi, knowing the thought in the venerable Shariputra’s mind, said to the venerable Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, have you come for the sake of the Dharma, or for the sake of a seat?”
He said: “We have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat.”

He said: “Well then, Reverend Shariputra, someone who seeks the Dharma does not seek even his own body, let alone a seat. Reverend Shariputra, someone who seeks the Dharma does not seek physical form, feeling, perception, mental formations or consciousness; he does not seek the heaps, the elements or the sense fields. Someone who seeks the Dharma does not seek the realm of desire, the realm of form or the formless realm; he does not seek to cling to the Buddha, nor to cling to the Dharma or the Sangha.

cmp.note: 「为法而来的、求法的人」。维摩诘抓住舍利弗心里想「坐哪儿」这件小事，借「求法还是求座」引出整段讲法。arthika 在梵文里既是「想要」也是「为了……的目的」，英文 seek 兼顾了两层；白话「求法」也一样。
cmp.en: “One who has come for the Dharma, one who seeks the Dharma.” Vimalakirti seizes on Shariputra’s small worry about where to sit and turns “Dharma or a seat?” into a whole teaching. Arthika means both “wanting” and “for the purpose of”; the English “seek” covers both, as does the plain Chinese 求法 (qiú fǎ, “seek the Dharma”).

verses.en: Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, someone who seeks the Dharma does not seek to understand suffering, nor to abandon its origin, nor to realize its cessation, nor to develop the path. Why? Because the Dharma is free of elaboration and has no letters. Whoever elaborates there, ‘I will understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, develop the path,’ is not seeking the Dharma; he is seeking elaboration. Reverend Shariputra, the Dharma is calm. Those who move in arising and passing away are not seeking the Dharma, nor seeking solitude; they are seeking arising and passing away. The Dharma is stainless, free of dust. Those who hold on to anything at all, even nirvana, are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking dust. The Dharma is not an object.

cmp.note: prapañca 是「展开、铺陈」，指心对事物不断加上概念、说法。中文译「戏论」，现代读者会误以为是「开玩笑的话」；英文 elaboration 照字面，指的是这种越想越多的概念增生。
cmp.en: Prapañca means “spreading out, proliferation”: the mind piling concept upon concept onto things. The Chinese 戏论 (xìlùn, literally “playful talk”) can mislead a modern reader into thinking of jokes; the English “elaboration” is literal and refers to this endless multiplying of concepts.

verses.en: Those who count it as an object are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking objects. The Dharma is neither taken up nor thrown out. Those who grab the Dharma or let it go are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking grabbing and letting go.

The Dharma has no home. Those who delight in a home are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking a home. The Dharma is signless. Those whose consciousness follows after signs are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking signs. The Dharma is not something to live with. Those who live together with the Dharma are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking company. The Dharma is not seen, heard, sensed or known. Those who move in what is seen, heard, sensed and known are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking what is seen, heard, sensed and known.

Reverend Shariputra, the Dharma is unconditioned, free of the conditioned. Those whose sphere is the conditioned are not seeking the Dharma; they are seeking to grasp the conditioned. So, Reverend Shariputra, if you want to be someone who seeks the Dharma, you should seek nothing at all.” While this teaching was being given, the Dharma-eye became pure in five hundred young gods regarding things.

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, you travel through countless hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields in the ten directions. In which buddha-field have you seen the finest lion thrones, endowed with every good quality?” When this was said, Manjushri, the young prince, said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Son of good family, to the east, past buddha-fields as many as the sands of thirty-six Ganges rivers, there is a world called Merudhvaja (“Banner of Meru”). There a Tathagata named Merupradiparaja (“King of the Lamp of Meru”), an arhat, a perfectly awakened one, lives, dwells and carries on. That Tathagata’s body is eight million four hundred thousand leagues tall, and that Blessed One’s lion throne is six million eight hundred thousand leagues tall.

cmp.note: 「由旬」：古印度的长度单位，原意是牛车套一次轭走的路程，大约十几公里，说法不一。白话保留「由旬」并加注，英文意译为 leagues（英制古长度单位，约五公里），只取「一大段路」的意思，并不精确对应。
cmp.en: Yojana: an ancient Indian unit of length, originally the distance an ox-cart travels in one yoking, roughly a dozen kilometers or so, with estimates varying. The plain Chinese keeps the transliteration 由旬 (yóuxún) with a note; the English renders it “leagues” (an old English measure of about five kilometers), taking only the sense of “a long stretch of road,” not an exact match.

verses.en: The bodhisattvas there are four million leagues tall, and the bodhisattvas’ lion thrones are three million four hundred thousand leagues tall. In the world Merudhvaja, in the buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathagata Merupradiparaja, are the finest lion thrones, endowed with every good quality.”

Then, at that moment, Vimalakirti the Licchavi focused his mind and performed such a feat of supernormal power that the Blessed One, the Tathagata Merupradiparaja, sent three million two hundred thousand lion thrones from the world Merudhvaja, so tall, so broad and so lovely that those bodhisattvas, those great disciples, and those Shakras, Brahmas, world-guardians and young gods had never seen the like. They came through the sky and came to rest in the house of Vimalakirti the Licchavi. And the house was seen to be wide enough that the three million two hundred thousand splendid lion thrones were in it without crowding. And the great city of Vaishali was not blocked out, nor was Jambudvipa (the continent we live on), nor the world of four continents.
Everything looked just the same as before.
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, sit on a lion throne, together with these bodhisattvas. And by your power take on bodies that suit the lion thrones.”

Then the bodhisattvas who had gained the higher knowledges took on bodies four million two hundred thousand leagues tall and sat on those lion thrones. But the bodhisattvas who were beginners could not sit on those lion thrones.
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to the venerable Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, sit on a lion throne.”
He said: “Good sir, I can’t sit on them. These lion thrones are too high and too big.”
He said: “Then, Reverend Shariputra, bow to that very Blessed One, the Tathagata Merupradiparaja. Then you will be able to sit.”
So those great disciples bowed to the Blessed One, the Tathagata Merupradiparaja, and after that they sat down on those lion thrones.

Then the venerable Shariputra said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Son of good family, it is amazing that so many thousands of lion thrones, so high, so big and so splendid, have been brought into such a small house, and yet the great city of Vaishali is not blocked out, nor Jambudvipa, nor the villages, towns, market towns, countryside, kingdoms and capitals, nor the world of four great continents in any way; nor are the dwellings of the gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras and mahoragas blocked out. Everything looks just the same as before.”

Vimalakirti said: “Reverend Shariputra, the Tathagatas and bodhisattvas have a liberation called Beyond Thought. A bodhisattva who stands in this liberation beyond thought can put Sumeru, king of mountains, so high, so huge, so lofty and so broad, inside the husk of a mustard seed, without making the mustard seed bigger and without making Sumeru smaller, and he can show this happening. And the gods of the Four Great Kings and of the Thirty-Three do not know where they have been put. Only other beings who are to be trained through supernormal power know and see Sumeru, king of mountains, gone into the husk of a mustard seed. Reverend Shariputra, this is entering the domain of the bodhisattvas’ liberation beyond thought.

cmp.note: 「不可思议解脱」：acintya 字面是「不能被想的」，超出思维范围的。中文「不可思议」后来成了日常词，意思变成「令人惊奇」；英文 beyond thought 保留了「想不到、想不进去」的原意。「芥子纳须弥」这个中文成语就出自这一段。
cmp.en: “The liberation beyond thought”: acintya literally means “that cannot be thought,” beyond the reach of thinking. The Chinese 不可思议 (bù kě sīyì, “inconceivable”) later became an everyday word for “amazing”; the English “beyond thought” keeps the original sense of something thought cannot get into. The Chinese idiom 芥子纳须弥 (jièzǐ nà Xūmí, “a mustard seed holds Mount Sumeru”) comes from this passage.

verses.en: Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, a bodhisattva who stands in the liberation beyond thought can put all the water in the four great oceans into a single pore of his skin, without harming the fish, turtles, crocodiles, frogs or other water creatures, and without the nagas, yakshas, gandharvas and asuras thinking, ‘Where have we been put?’ The feat can be seen, and yet no being is hurt or troubled.

He can pick up this great galaxy of a billion worlds like a potter’s wheel, spin it on his right hand, and throw it beyond worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges, without beings knowing, ‘Where have we been taken? Where have we come from?’ And he can bring it back again and set it in its place, without their noticing any going or coming. And the feat can be seen.

Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, there are beings who are trained through a measureless samsara, and there are beings who are trained through a short samsara. A bodhisattva who stands in the liberation beyond thought, to suit what will train them, shows to beings who are trained through a measureless samsara seven days passing as an eon; and to beings who are trained through a short samsara he shows an eon passing as seven days. Then beings trained through a measureless samsara perceive seven days as an eon gone by, and beings trained through a short samsara perceive an eon as seven days gone by.

So a bodhisattva who stands in the liberation beyond thought shows the splendid arrays of good qualities of all buddha-fields in a single buddha-field. He can set all beings on the palm of his right hand and travel with a power as swift as thought, showing them all buddha-fields, without ever moving from his one field. He can show in a single pore all the offerings made to the buddhas, the blessed ones, in the ten directions. He can show in a single pore all the suns, moons and stars in the ten directions. He can take into his mouth all the circles of wind that blow in the ten directions, without his body being scattered and without the grass and trees in that buddha-field bending.

When the buddha-fields in the ten directions are burning in the fire at the end of an eon, he can put that whole mass of fire into his own mouth, and still the fire does what it has to do. He can lift a buddha-field from below, past buddha-fields as many as kotis of Ganges sands, and set it above, past buddha-fields as many as kotis of Ganges sands, as easily as a strong man lifts a jujube leaf on the tip of a needle.
In this way a bodhisattva who stands in the liberation beyond thought can, by his power, take on the forms of all beings, such as wheel-turning kings.

And all the sounds and spoken expressions in the ten directions, of beings low, middling and high, he can turn by his power into the voice and speech of a buddha, and from that speech and voice make come forth the words ‘impermanent, painful, empty, without self.’ And all the ways in which the buddhas, the blessed ones, teach the Dharma in the ten directions, he can make come forth from those sounds and voices.

Reverend Shariputra, this is just a tiny sample of the teaching on entering the domain of bodhisattvas who stand in the liberation beyond thought. Reverend Shariputra, I could explain the domains of bodhisattvas who stand in the liberation beyond thought for an eon, or the rest of an eon, or even longer.”

Then the elder Mahakashyapa, hearing about this liberation beyond thought of the bodhisattvas, was amazed and said to the elder Shariputra: “Venerable Shariputra, it is as if someone were to show all kinds of forms in front of a man blind from birth, and the man blind from birth could not see a single one. In the same way, venerable Shariputra, when this liberation beyond thought is being taught here, all the disciples and solitary buddhas are like men blind from birth, without eyes, and cannot directly see a single one of these things beyond thought. What wise person, hearing of this liberation beyond thought, would not raise his mind toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening? But what more can we do now, with our faculties utterly ruined, like seeds burned and rotted, no longer fit vessels for this Great Vehicle?

cmp.note: 「像烧焦、腐坏的种子」：大迦叶说声闻弟子已经不可能再发菩提心，就像种子烧坏了不会再发芽。鸠摩罗什译「如败种」，后来中文有「焦芽败种」的说法，专指声闻。英文照字面。
cmp.en: “Like seeds burned and rotted”: Mahakashyapa says the disciples can no longer raise the mind of awakening, just as burned seeds will never sprout. Kumarajiva writes 如败种 (rú bài zhǒng, “like spoiled seeds”), and Chinese later spoke of 焦芽败种 (jiāo yá bài zhǒng, “scorched sprouts and spoiled seeds”) to mean the disciples. The English is literal.

verses.en: All the disciples and solitary buddhas who hear this teaching should cry out until the great galaxy of a billion worlds hears them; and all the bodhisattvas who hear of this liberation beyond thought should rejoice and take it on their heads, and generate the power of conviction. What can all the Maras do to someone who has conviction in this liberation beyond thought?” While the elder Mahakashyapa was saying this, thirty-two thousand young gods raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to the elder Mahakashyapa: “Reverend Mahakashyapa, as many Maras as are playing the part of Mara in the countless worlds of the ten directions, most of them are bodhisattvas standing in the liberation beyond thought, playing the part of Mara through skill in means in order to bring beings to maturity.

Reverend Mahakashyapa, in the countless worlds of the ten directions, bodhisattvas are approached by beggars who ask for hands or feet, ears or nose, blood, sinews, bones or marrow, eyes, heads or limbs; for kingdoms, countries or provinces; for wives, sons or daughters; for male or female servants; for horses, elephants, chariots or vehicles; for gold, gems, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral and all kinds of jewels; for food, drink or delicacies; who even badger them for their clothes. Most of those beggars are bodhisattvas standing in the liberation beyond thought, who through skill in means show this firm resolve. Why? Because, Reverend Mahakashyapa, those bodhisattvas show this through fierce austerity. An ordinary person who has not been given leave has no power to put pressure on a bodhisattva.

Reverend Mahakashyapa, just as a firefly has no power to outshine the light of the sun’s disk, in the same way, Reverend Mahakashyapa, an ordinary person who has not been given leave by a bodhisattva has no power to approach him or beg from him. Reverend Mahakashyapa, just as a donkey cannot bear the blow of a great elephant, in the same way, Reverend Mahakashyapa, one who is not a bodhisattva cannot bear a bodhisattva’s pressure; only a bodhisattva can bear a bodhisattva’s pressure. Reverend Mahakashyapa, this is entering the power of skill in means and knowledge of the bodhisattvas who stand in the liberation beyond thought.”
This was chapter five, “Showing the Liberation Beyond Thought.”
Then Manjushri, the young prince, said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Good sir, how should a bodhisattva look at all beings?”

He said: “Manjushri, the way a wise man looks at the moon in the water: that is how a bodhisattva should look at all beings. Manjushri, the way one looks at one’s face in the disk of a mirror: that is how a bodhisattva should look at all beings. Manjushri, like the water in a mirage: that is how a bodhisattva should look at all beings. Manjushri, the way a magician looks at a man made by his magic: that is how a bodhisattva should look at all beings. Manjushri, like the sound of an echo: that is how a bodhisattva should look at all beings. Manjushri, like a bank of clouds in the sky: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like the first moment of a lump of foam: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings.

Manjushri, like the arising and bursting of bubbles on water: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like finding a core in a banana tree: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a flash of lightning staying put: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a fifth element: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a seventh sense field: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like form appearing in the formless realms: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a sprout growing from scorched seeds: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings.

cmp.note: 这一长串比喻，后半都是「根本不存在的东西」：只有四大，没有第五大；只有六处，没有第七处。白话译「第七种感官」，英文 seventh sense field，意思都是「不可能有的东西」。读者要知道这一点，才明白这些比喻在说什么。
cmp.en: Most of the comparisons in this long list are “things that do not exist at all”: there are only four elements, so there is no fifth; there are only six sense fields, so there is no seventh. The plain Chinese 第七种感官 (“a seventh sense”) and the English “seventh sense field” both mean “something impossible.” The reader needs to know this to see what the comparisons are saying.

verses.en: Manjushri, like a cloak made of frog’s hair: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a dead man’s delight in the play of love: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like the view of an existing self in a stream-enterer (one who has reached the first stage of holiness): that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a third existence for a once-returner: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a non-returner entering a womb: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like passion, hatred and delusion in an arhat: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings.

Manjushri, like thoughts of stinginess, immorality, ill will and cruelty in a bodhisattva who has gained acceptance: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like habit-traces of the afflictions in a Tathagata: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a man blind from birth seeing forms: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like breathing in someone who has entered the attainment of cessation: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a bird’s tracks in the sky: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a eunuch’s organ appearing: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings.

Manjushri, like a barren woman having a son: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like afflictions arising in someone conjured up by a Tathagata: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like the sight of a dream seen by someone who has woken up: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like afflictions in someone who does not imagine: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like a fire arising without fuel: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. Manjushri, like rebirth for someone who has passed into final nirvana: that is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings. That, Manjushri, is how a bodhisattva should regard all beings.”
He said: “Son of good family, if a bodhisattva should regard all beings like this, then how does he have great kindness toward all beings?”

He said: “Manjushri, when a bodhisattva considers like this: ‘I should teach these beings the Dharma so that they understand things in this way,’ then a true kindness that protects beings arises in him toward all beings, because it has no object. It is a kindness of calm, because it does not arise. A kindness without fever, because it has no afflictions. A kindness true to things, because the three times are the same. A kindness without conflict, because nothing breaks out. A non-dual kindness, because inside and outside do not mix. An unshakable kindness, because it is utterly final. A firm kindness, because its resolve is as firm and unbreakable as diamond. A pure kindness, because it is pure by nature. An even kindness, because it is even like space. An arhat’s kindness, because it strikes down the enemy. A bodhisattva’s kindness, because it never tires of bringing beings to maturity. A Tathagata’s kindness, because it wakes up to suchness. A buddha’s kindness, because it wakes sleeping beings. A self-arisen kindness, because it awakens by itself. An awakening kindness, because it is all one taste. A kindness that projects nothing, because it has abandoned liking and aversion. A kindness of great compassion, because it makes the Great Vehicle shine. A tireless kindness, because it regards emptiness and no-self. A kindness that gives the Dharma, because it keeps no teacher’s closed fist. A kindness of morality, because it looks after immoral beings. A kindness of patience, because it harms neither self nor others. A kindness of effort, because it carries the burden of all beings. A kindness of meditation, because it does not savor. A kindness of wisdom, because it knows the right time. A kindness of skill in means, because it shows a door everywhere. A kindness without hypocrisy, because its intent is pure. A kindness without crookedness, because it comes from real intent. A kindness of deep resolve, because it is without blemish. A kindness without deceit, because it is not artificial. A kindness of happiness, because it establishes beings in the happiness of a buddha.

cmp.note: 梵文在玩词源：arhat（阿罗汉）被解释成 ari-han「杀敌者」，所以「阿罗汉的慈，因为杀灭了敌人」。这是古印度常见的通俗词源，白话加注说明敌人指烦恼；英文 strikes down the enemy 只能照译，双关看不出来。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is playing on etymology: arhat is explained as ari-han, “slayer of the enemy,” hence “an arhat’s kindness, because it strikes down the enemy.” This folk etymology was common in ancient India; the plain Chinese adds that the enemy is the afflictions, while the English “strikes down the enemy” can only translate it, and the pun is lost.

cmp.note: 「没有老师的拳头」：指老师把最要紧的教法握在拳头里不肯给人。佛陀说过自己说法「没有师拳」。白话译「没有老师留一手的那种保留」，英文 keeps no teacher’s closed fist 保留了拳头的比喻。
cmp.en: “No teacher’s fist”: a teacher keeping the most important teaching clenched in his fist and not handing it over. The Buddha said that in his teaching there was “no teacher’s fist.” The plain Chinese renders it 没有老师留一手 (“no teacher holding something back”), and the English “keeps no teacher’s closed fist” keeps the image of the fist.

verses.en: That, Manjushri, is a bodhisattva’s great kindness.”
He said: “And what is his great compassion?”
He said: “Every root of goodness he has made, he gives away to all beings.”
He said: “And what is his great sympathetic joy?”
He said: “Having given, he is glad and has no regrets.”
He said: “And what is his great equanimity?”
He said: “That it benefits both sides.”
He said: “What should someone who is afraid of samsara turn to?”
He said: “Manjushri, a bodhisattva who is afraid of samsara should turn to the greatness of the Buddha.”
He said: “Where should someone who wants to stand in the greatness of the Buddha stand?”
He said: “Someone who wants to stand in the greatness of the Buddha should stand in the sameness of all beings.”
He said: “Where should someone who wants to stand in the sameness of all beings stand?”
He said: “Someone who wants to stand in the sameness of all beings should stand for the freeing of all beings.”
He said: “What should someone who wants to free all beings do?”
He said: “Someone who wants to free all beings should free them from the afflictions.”
He said: “How should someone who wants to let go of the afflictions apply himself?”
He said: “Someone who wants to let go of the afflictions should apply himself properly.”
He said: “How does one apply oneself so as to apply oneself properly?”
He said: “One who applies himself to non-arising and non-ceasing applies himself properly.”
He said: “What does he not make arise, and what does he not make cease?”
He said: “He does not make the unwholesome arise, and he does not make the wholesome cease.”
He said: “What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome?”
He said: “The existing self is the root.”
He said: “And what is the root of the existing self?”
He said: “Desire and greed are the root of the existing self.”
He said: “What is the root of desire and greed?”
He said: “Imagining what is unreal is the root of desire and greed.”
He said: “What is the root of imagining what is unreal?”
He said: “Distorted perception is the root of imagining what is unreal.”
He said: “What is the root of distorted perception?”
He said: “Having no ground is the root of distorted perception.”
He said: “What is the root of having no ground?”
He said: “Manjushri, what has no ground, what root could it have? So all things stand on the root of having no ground.”

cmp.note: 「无所立足、没有根基」。鸠摩罗什译「从无住本，立一切法」，「无住」后来成了禅宗的核心词（如《坛经》「无住为本」）。梵文是一连串追问「根本是什么」，最后落在「没有根本」上。英文 having no ground 保留了「地基」的画面。
cmp.en: “Having no footing, no foundation.” Kumarajiva renders the conclusion 从无住本，立一切法 (“from the root of non-abiding, all things are established”), and 无住 (wúzhù, “non-abiding”) later became a core Chan term (the Platform Sutra says “non-abiding is the root”). The Sanskrit is a chain of questions about “what is the root,” ending in “no root at all.” The English “having no ground” keeps the picture of a foundation.

verses.en: Then a goddess who lived in that house, hearing this teaching from those bodhisattvas, great beings, was delighted, thrilled and overjoyed. She showed herself in visible form and scattered heavenly flowers over those great beings and those great disciples. Of the flowers scattered there, those that fell on the bodies of the bodhisattvas dropped to the ground. But those that fell on the bodies of the great disciples stuck right there and did not fall to the ground. Then those great disciples tried to shake the flowers off with their supernormal powers, but they would not fall.
Then the goddess said to the venerable Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, why are you shaking off these flowers?”
He said: “Goddess, these flowers are not proper. So I am removing them.”

The goddess said: “Reverend Shariputra, don’t say that. Why? These flowers are proper. Why so? Because these flowers do not imagine and do not distinguish. It is the elder Shariputra who imagines and distinguishes. Reverend Shariputra, those who have gone forth in the well-taught Dharma and discipline and still imagine and distinguish, they are the ones who are not proper. And the elder imagines and distinguishes. Those who do not imagine and do not distinguish are proper. Look, Reverend Shariputra: flowers do not stick to the bodies of these great beings, because they have abandoned all imagining and distinguishing. It is like a timid man: spirits find their chance to get at him. In the same way, forms, sounds, smells, tastes and things touched find their chance to get at those who are afraid of samsara.

cmp.note: 天女在玩同一个词根 kalp：kalpika 是「合规矩的、可以接受的」（出家人可以用的东西），kalpayati 是「构想、分别」。所以她说「花不构想，所以花是合规矩的；你在构想，所以你不合规矩」。英文 proper / imagine、白话「合宜／构想」都没法保住这个双关，只能把意思说出来。
cmp.en: The goddess is playing on a single root, kalp: kalpika means “allowable, proper” (what a monk may use), and kalpayati means “to imagine, to construct mentally.” So she says: the flowers do not imagine, so they are proper; you imagine, so you are the improper one. Neither the English “proper / imagine” nor the plain Chinese 合宜／构想 (héyí / gòuxiǎng) can keep the pun; they can only spell out the meaning.

verses.en: But those who are free of all fear of samsara and the afflictions, what can forms, sounds, smells, tastes and things touched do to them? Flowers stick to the bodies of those who have not abandoned the habit-traces. So flowers do not stick to the bodies of those who have abandoned all habit-traces.”
Then the venerable Shariputra said to that goddess: “Goddess, how long have you been in this house?”
She said: “As long as the elder’s noble liberation.”
He said: “Then you haven’t been in this house long, goddess.”
She said: “Well, how long has the elder’s noble liberation been?”
At that the elder fell silent.
She said: “Why has the elder, foremost of the greatly wise, fallen silent now? Why doesn’t he answer a question that calls for an answer?”
He said: “Goddess, liberation cannot be put into words. So I don’t know what to say.”

She said: “Every syllable the elder utters, all these syllables have the mark of liberation. Why? Because liberation is not found inside, nor outside, nor in between the two; and the same is true of syllables. So, Reverend Shariputra, don’t teach liberation by doing away with syllables. Why? Because liberation is the sameness of all things.”

cmp.note: 「不要靠去掉文字来说解脱」。舍利弗刚才和维摩诘一样沉默了，但天女不认可：他的沉默是「不知道说什么」，不是不二。这和第八品维摩诘的沉默形成对照。鸠摩罗什译「无离文字说解脱也」。
cmp.en: “Don’t teach liberation by doing away with syllables.” Shariputra has just fallen silent, as Vimalakirti will, but the goddess does not accept it: his silence is “not knowing what to say,” not non-duality. This contrasts with Vimalakirti’s silence in chapter 8. Kumarajiva writes 无离文字说解脱也 (“do not speak of liberation apart from words”).

verses.en: He said: “But goddess, isn’t liberation getting free of passion, hatred and delusion?”

The goddess said: “‘Liberation is getting free of passion, hatred and delusion’: that is a teaching for the conceited. For those without conceit, the very nature of passion, hatred and delusion is liberation.”
Then the venerable Shariputra said to that goddess: “Excellent, excellent, goddess! What have you attained, what have you realized, that you have such eloquence?”

She said: “Reverend Shariputra, I have not attained or realized anything; that is why I have such eloquence. Those who think, ‘We have attained, we have realized,’ are called conceited in the well-taught Dharma and discipline.”
He said: “Goddess, do you belong to the disciples’ vehicle, the solitary buddhas’ vehicle, or the Great Vehicle?”

She said: “I belong to the disciples’ vehicle, because I point out the disciples’ vehicle. I belong to the solitary buddhas’ vehicle, because I lead people into dependent arising. I belong to the Great Vehicle, because I never give up great compassion.

And besides, Reverend Shariputra, people who walk into a grove of champak trees do not smell castor-oil plants; people who walk into a champak grove smell only the scent of champak. In the same way, Reverend Shariputra, those who live in this house, fragrant with the good qualities of a buddha, do not smell the scents of the disciples and solitary buddhas. Reverend Shariputra, even the Shakras, Brahmas and world-guardians, the gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras and mahoragas who come into this house, hearing the Dharma from this good man, leave with the mind set on awakening raised by the scent of a buddha’s good qualities. Reverend Shariputra, in the twelve years I have lived here, I have never once heard a talk about the disciples or solitary buddhas; only talks about great kindness and great compassion, about things beyond thought.

cmp.note: 瞻卜（champak）是一种花香浓郁的黄花树，蓖麻（castor）则气味难闻。中文古译「瞻卜」是音译，现代读者不知道是什么；英文 champak 也需要知道是香花才懂这个比喻。
cmp.en: The champak is a tree with richly scented yellow flowers; the castor-oil plant has an unpleasant smell. The Chinese 瞻卜 (zhānbǔ) is a transliteration that modern readers don’t recognize; the English “champak,” too, only works if the reader knows it is a fragrant flower.

verses.en: Reverend Shariputra, in this house eight amazing, wonderful things are always to be seen. What are the eight?
Here neither night nor day can be told apart: this house is always lit with a golden light. Here the sun and moon cannot be made out and do not shine. That is the first amazing, wonderful thing.
Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, as soon as people come into this house, none of their afflictions trouble them. That is the second amazing, wonderful thing.
Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, this house is never without Shakras, Brahmas, world-guardians and bodhisattvas gathered from other buddha-fields. That is the third amazing, wonderful thing.

Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, this house is never without the hearing of the Dharma, talks connected with the six perfections, and talks on the Dharma of no turning back. That is the fourth amazing, wonderful thing. Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, from the instruments and songs, heavenly and human, played in this house, measureless sounds of the Dharma come forth at all times. That is the fifth amazing, wonderful thing.

Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, in this house there are four great treasuries, full of every kind of jewel and inexhaustible. All the poor and wretched take what flows from them and go away, and they never run out. That is the sixth amazing, wonderful thing.

Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, in this house the Tathagata Shakyamuni, Amitabha, Akshobhya, Ratnashri, Ratnarchis, Ratnachandra, Ratnavyuha, Dushprasaha, Sarvarthasiddha, Prabhutaratna, Simhanadanadin and the Tathagata Simhaghosha, with these at their head, measureless Tathagatas of the ten directions come the moment this good man thinks of them. When they have come, they teach the entry into the Dharma-door called the Secret of the Tathagatas, and then they leave. That is the seventh amazing, wonderful thing.

Moreover, Reverend Shariputra, in this house the splendors of all the palaces of the gods and the splendid arrays of good qualities of all buddha-fields are seen. That is the eighth amazing, wonderful thing.
Reverend Shariputra, these eight amazing, wonderful things are always to be seen in this house. So who, seeing this nature of things beyond thought, would long for the nature of a disciple?”
He said: “Goddess, why don’t you change out of your female state?”

cmp.note: 舍利弗的问题背后是当时一种普遍看法：女身修行有障碍，要先转成男身才能成佛。白话加了「（成男身）」把这层意思补出来；英文 change out of your female state 照字面，读者也能看出它的预设。天女接下来用神通把两人的身体对调，正是在拆这个预设。
cmp.en: Behind Shariputra’s question is a view common at the time: that a woman’s body is an obstacle, and one must first become a man to become a buddha. The plain Chinese adds 成男身 (“into a male body”) to make this explicit; the English “change out of your female state” is literal, and the assumption shows through. The goddess then uses her power to swap their bodies, taking that assumption apart.

verses.en: She said: “For twelve full years I have been looking for the female state, and I can’t find it. Besides, Reverend Shariputra, suppose a magician conjured up a woman, and someone asked her, ‘Why don’t you change out of your female state?’ What would he be saying?”
He said: “She has no real existence at all.”

She said: “In the same way, Reverend Shariputra, since no thing is really established and all things have the nature of a magic illusion, how can it occur to you to ask, ‘Why don’t you change out of your female state?’”

Then the goddess worked such a power that the elder Shariputra appeared just as the goddess looked, and the goddess appeared just as the elder looked. Then the goddess, in the form of Shariputra, asked Shariputra, who now had the form of the goddess: “Reverend Shariputra, why don’t you change out of your female state?”
Shariputra, in the form of the goddess, said: “I don’t know what I would change. My male form has disappeared, and a female form has appeared on me.”

She said: “If the elder can change out of the female state, then all women can change out of the female state too. Just as the elder is not a woman but appears as a woman, so too all women have a woman’s form, yet they are not women, though they appear in a woman’s form. With this in mind the Blessed One said: ‘All things are neither female nor male.’”

Then the goddess released that power, and the venerable Shariputra had his own form again. Then the goddess said to the venerable Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, where has the female form you had gone to now?”
He said: “It was neither made nor changed.”
She said: “In the same way, all things are neither made nor changed. And where there is no making and no changing, that is the word of the Buddha.”
He said: “Goddess, when you pass away from here, where will you be reborn?”
She said: “Wherever someone conjured up by the Tathagata is reborn, there I will be reborn.”
He said: “Someone conjured up by the Tathagata has no passing away and no rebirth.”
She said: “In the same way, no thing has passing away or rebirth.”
He said: “Goddess, how long will it be before you awaken to awakening?”
She said: “When the elder is once more endowed with the qualities of an ordinary person, then I will awaken to awakening.”
He said: “Goddess, it is impossible that I should be endowed with the qualities of an ordinary person.”
She said: “In the same way, Reverend Shariputra, it is impossible that I should awaken to awakening. Why? Because awakening stands on no-place. So, since there is no place, no one will awaken to it.”

cmp.note: 梵文在玩 sthāna 的两个意思：「处所」和「可能」。asthānam etad 是「这是不可能的」，asthānasthitā bodhiḥ 是「菩提立于无处」。天女把舍利弗的「不可能」接过来，变成「菩提没有处所」。英文 impossible / no-place、白话「不可能／无处」都只能分开译，双关保不住。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is playing on two senses of sthāna, “place” and “possibility.” Asthānam etad means “this is impossible,” and asthānasthitā bodhiḥ means “awakening stands on no-place.” The goddess takes Shariputra’s “impossible” and turns it into “awakening has no place.” The English “impossible / no-place” and the plain Chinese 不可能／无处 (bù kěnéng / wú chù) have to translate the two separately, and the pun is lost.

verses.en: The elder said: “Goddess, the Tathagata has said: ‘Tathagatas as many as the sands of the Ganges have awakened, are awakening and will awaken.’”

The goddess said: “Reverend Shariputra, ‘buddhas past, future and present’ is a way of speaking based on letters, counting and convention. But buddhas are not past, future or present, for awakening goes beyond the three times. And has the elder attained arhatship?”
He said: “It is attained by way of not attaining.”
She said: “In the same way, awakening is awakened to by way of not awakening.”
