Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to the venerable Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, this goddess has served ninety-two kotis of buddhas. She plays with the higher knowledges and knowledge; her vows are lofty; she has gained acceptance and reached the state of no turning back. By the power of her vows she lives however she wishes, in order to bring beings to maturity.”
This was chapter six, “The Goddess.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Family of the Tathagatas

verses.en: Then Manjushri, the young prince, said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Son of good family, how does a bodhisattva arrive at the qualities of a buddha?”
He said: “Manjushri, when a bodhisattva goes where one should not go, then the bodhisattva has arrived at the qualities of a buddha.”

cmp.note: gati 有「去处、道路」和「到达、通达」两层意思。gatiṃgata 是「到达了目的地、通达」，agatigamana 是「走不该走的路、走非道」。英文 arrive at / go where one should not go 把两层拆开译；鸠摩罗什译「行于非道，是为通达佛道」，用「道」字把两句连起来，非常巧妙。
cmp.en: Gati means both “a way, a destination” and “arrival, mastery.” Gatiṃgata is “arrived, gone to the goal,” and agatigamana is “going where one should not go, taking the wrong road.” The English “arrive at / go where one should not go” separates the two senses; Kumarajiva’s 行于非道，是为通达佛道 (“walking the non-way is mastering the Buddha’s way”) neatly links the two lines with the single word 道 (dào, “way”).

verses.en: He said: “And what is a bodhisattva’s going where one should not go?”

He said: “When he goes the way of the five worst crimes, yet is not malicious, cruel or hateful. When he goes the way of the hells, yet is free of all the dust of afflictions. When he goes the way of animal birth, yet is free of darkness and blindness. When he goes the way of the asuras (the warring demigods), yet is free of pride, conceit and arrogance. When he goes the way of Yama’s world (the realm of the dead), yet has gathered all the stores of merit and knowledge. When he goes the way of the imperturbable formless states, yet does not land in that destiny. When he goes the way of passion, yet is free of passion for all the pleasures of the senses. When he goes the way of hatred, yet has no aversion to any being. When he goes the way of delusion, yet his mind examines all things with wisdom. When he goes the way of stinginess, yet gives away everything he owns, inside and out, without regard for body or life.

When he goes the way of immorality, yet stands firm in all the morality, training, austere practices and simple living, seeing danger in the slightest fault. When he goes the way of malice, spite and anger, yet dwells in kindness, his mind utterly free of malice. When he goes the way of laziness, yet works hard at seeking every root of goodness, his effort never letting up. When he goes the way of scattered senses, yet his meditation never lapses and he is naturally collected. When he goes the way of poor wisdom, yet is skilled in all worldly and other-worldly sciences and has arrived at the perfection of wisdom. When he goes the way of trickery and flattery, yet has perfected the conduct of skill in means and is skilled at speaking with hidden meaning. When he shows the way of pride, yet becomes a bridge and a causeway for the whole world.

When he goes the way of the afflictions, yet is pure by nature and utterly undefiled. When he goes the way of Mara, yet depends on no one else in any of the qualities of a buddha. When he goes the way of the disciples, yet makes beings hear teachings they have not heard. When he goes the way of the solitary buddhas, yet has perfected great compassion in order to bring beings to maturity. When he goes the way of poverty, yet has gained the jewel-hand and has inexhaustible wealth. When he goes the way of impaired faculties, yet is adorned with the marks and handsome. When he goes the way of birth in a low family, yet is born into the family and clan of the Tathagatas, with stores of merit and knowledge built up. When he goes the way of the weak, the ugly and the despised, yet has gained a body like Narayana (a mighty god of Indian myth) that all beings love to see.

When he shows the conduct of the old and the sick, yet has utterly uprooted illness and passed beyond the fear of death. When he shows the way of wealth, yet often reflects on impermanence and has stilled all seeking. When the bodhisattva shows the splendors of a palace harem and of theater, yet has crossed over the mud of desire and moves about without a home. When he goes the way of dullness, yet is adorned with varied eloquence and has gained the dharanis. When he goes the way of other teachers, yet becomes a true ford. When he goes the way of the whole world, yet has turned away from every destiny. When he goes the way of nirvana, yet does not let go of the continuity of samsara. That, Manjushri, is how a bodhisattva goes where one should not go and has arrived at all the qualities of a buddha.”

cmp.note: tīrthika（外道）字面是「造渡口的人」，tīrtha 是渡口、圣地。所以「走外道的路，却成为真正的渡口」是同词根的双关。英文 other teachers / a true ford 只能把意思分开说，看不出两词同源。
cmp.en: Tīrthika, “a teacher of another school,” literally means “a ford-maker,” since tīrtha is a river ford or holy crossing. So “he goes the way of other teachers, yet becomes a true ford” is a pun on one root. The English “other teachers / a true ford” can only give the two meanings separately, without showing they share a root.

verses.en: Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, what is the family of the Tathagatas?”

He said: “Son of good family, the existing self is the family of the Tathagatas. Ignorance and the thirst for existence are the family. Passion, hatred and delusion are the family. The four distortions are the family. The five hindrances are the family. The six sense fields are the family. The seven stations of consciousness are the family. The eight wrong ways are the family. The nine grounds of resentment are the family. The ten paths of unwholesome action are the family. Son of good family, this is the family of the Tathagatas. In short, son of good family, the sixty-two views are the family of the Tathagatas.”

cmp.note: gotra 原义是「牛栏」，引申为「家族、血统、种姓」。中文译「种」（如来种），带着「种子」的意思，所以鸠摩罗什的「一切烦恼为如来种」常被读成「烦恼是成佛的种子」。梵文更接近「家族、出身」：如来出身于烦恼之中。英文 family 取的是后者。
cmp.en: Gotra originally means “cow-pen,” and by extension “family, lineage, clan.” The Chinese renders it 种 (zhǒng), which also means “seed,” so Kumarajiva’s 一切烦恼为如来种 (“all afflictions are the 种 of the Tathagata”) is often read as “afflictions are the seed of buddhahood.” The Sanskrit is closer to “family, origin”: the Tathagatas come from among the afflictions. The English “family” follows that sense.

verses.en: He said: “Manjushri, what do you have in mind when you say this?”

He said: “Son of good family, someone who sees the unconditioned and stands in certainty cannot raise his mind toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Someone who lives in the house of afflictions, in the conditioned, who has not seen the truth, can raise his mind toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Son of good family, it is like this: blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses and fragrant lotuses do not grow on dry high ground. Thrown into mud and sandbanks, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses and fragrant lotuses grow. In the same way, son of good family, the qualities of a buddha do not grow in beings who have reached the certainty of the unconditioned. The qualities of a buddha grow in beings who are in the mud and sandbanks of the afflictions. It is like seeds that do not grow in the sky but grow when planted in the ground. In the same way, the qualities of a buddha do not grow in those who have reached the certainty of the unconditioned.

The mind set on awakening arises when a view of an existing self as big as Mount Sumeru has arisen, and from that the qualities of a buddha grow. So in this way too, son of good family, you should understand: as all afflictions are, so is the family of the Tathagatas. Son of good family, it is like this: without going down into the great ocean, one cannot bring up a priceless jewel. In the same way, without going down into the ocean of afflictions, one cannot produce the jewel of a mind set on all-knowing.”

Then the elder Mahakashyapa gave his approval to Manjushri, the young prince: “Excellent, excellent, Manjushri! What you have said is well said and true. The afflictions are the family of the Tathagatas. How could people like us raise the mind set on awakening now? Someone who has committed the five worst crimes can raise the mind set on awakening and can awaken to the qualities of a buddha; but not I.

Just as the five pleasures of the senses are useless and powerless for a man whose faculties are impaired, in the same way all the qualities of a buddha are useless and powerless for a disciple who has abandoned all the fetters; he no longer has the strength to take them up. So, Manjushri, it is ordinary people who are grateful to the Tathagata, not the disciples. Why? Because ordinary people, hearing of a buddha’s good qualities, raise their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening so that the line of the Three Jewels is not cut off. But the disciples, even if they hear for their whole lives of a buddha’s qualities, powers and kinds of confidence, cannot raise their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.”

Then a bodhisattva named Sarvarupasamdarshana (“Showing Every Form”), who had gathered in that same assembly, was seated there. He said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Householder, where are your mother and father, your servants, workers and hired men? Where are your friends, relatives and kin? Where are your followers, your horses, elephants, chariots, foot soldiers and vehicles?” When this was said, Vimalakirti the Licchavi answered the bodhisattva Sarvarupasamdarshana in verses:
“Good sir, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of bodhisattvas, and skill in means is their father; from these the guides of the world are born. (1)”

cmp.note: 「智慧为母，方便为父」。这首偈把前一品「智慧与方便要互相摄持」的道理，化成一个家庭的比喻。鸠摩罗什译「智度菩萨母，方便以为父，一切众导师，无不由是生」，是中文佛教极常引的一偈。
cmp.en: “Wisdom is the mother, skill in means the father.” This verse turns the earlier teaching that wisdom and skill in means must hold each other into the image of a family. Kumarajiva’s version, 智度菩萨母，方便以为父，一切众导师，无不由是生 (“the perfection of wisdom is the bodhisattva’s mother, skill in means the father; all the guides are born from these”), is one of the most quoted verses in Chinese Buddhism.

verses.en: “Their wife is delight in the Dharma; kindness and compassion are their two daughters; truth and Dharma are their two sons; their house is thinking on the meaning of emptiness. (2)”
“All the afflictions are their pupils, doing their bidding as they please; the factors of awakening are their friends, with whom they wake up to the highest awakening. (3)”
“These six perfections are the companions who always follow them; the ways of gathering people are their women’s quarters; the teachings are their songs and music. (4)”
“Their garden is the dharanis, bright with the flowers of the factors of awakening; its fruit is the knowledge of liberation, and its trees are the great wealth of the Dharma. (5)”
“The liberations are their lotus ponds, filled with the waters of samadhi and covered with lotuses of purity, where the stainless ones bathe. (6)”
“The higher knowledges are their mounts; the unsurpassed Great Vehicle is their carriage; the mind set on awakening is the charioteer, and the road is the auspicious eightfold path. (7)”
“Their ornaments are the marks and the eighty minor signs; conscience and shame are their clothes; their good and lovely intentions make them beautiful. (8)”
“They are rich in the wealth of the true Dharma; their business is teaching the Dharma; their great profit is practice, and they dedicate it to awakening. (9)”
“Their bed is the four meditations, spread with a pure livelihood; their wake-up call is wisdom, always joined with learning. (10)”
“Their food is the deathless; their drink is the taste of liberation; their bath is pure intent; morality is their perfumed ointment. (11)”
“Having struck down the enemy, the afflictions, they are heroes, never defeated; relying on the banner of the seat of awakening, they overpower the four Maras. (12)”
“Unborn and never coming into being, they deliberately show a birth; they are seen in every field, risen like the king of rays, the sun. (13)”
“They worship kotis of buddhas, the guides, with every kind of offering, yet they never lean on themselves or on the Buddha. (14)”
“They purify buddha-fields to suit the conduct of beings; they have reached a field like space, and they have no notion of ‘being’ about any being. (15)”
“The forms of all beings, the sounds and voices they utter, the fearless bodhisattvas show them all in a single instant. (16)”
“They understand the work of Mara, and they go along with the Maras; having reached the perfection of skill in means, they show every kind of action. (17)”
“They become old and sick, and show themselves dead, to bring beings to maturity, living in the Dharma that is like illusion. (18)”
“They show the burning at the end of the eon, burning up the whole earth, to show beings who think things are permanent that all is impermanent. (19)”
“Invited by thousands of kotis of beings in a single kingdom, they eat in all their houses, and they turn them all toward awakening. (20)”
“Whatever spells or sciences there are, the many kinds of crafts, they have mastered them all, bringing happiness to every being. (21)”
“However many sects there are in the world, they go forth in all of them, to set free beings who have fallen into all kinds of views. (22)”
“They become moons or suns, Shakras, Brahmas, lords of creatures; they become water and fire, earth and wind as well. (23)”
“In ages of plague they become the finest medicine, by which beings are freed and become happy and well. (24)”
“In ages of famine they become food and drink; having taken away hunger and thirst, they teach the Dharma to living beings. (25)”
“In ages of the sword they meditate on kindness, and they set many hundreds of kotis of beings in freedom from malice. (26)”
“In the middle of a great battle the bodhisattvas, of great strength, take neither side, and they bring people round to peace and harmony. (27)”
“Whatever hells there are in buddha-fields beyond thought, they go there on purpose, for the good of beings. (28)”
“In whatever destinies are known among animals, they teach the Dharma everywhere; that is why they are called guides. (29)”
“They show sensual pleasures, and they show meditation to meditators; they leave Mara helpless and give him no opening. (30)”
“As one might show the wonder of a lotus in the middle of a fire, so they show the wonder of pleasures and meditation together. (31)”

cmp.note: 「火中生莲」：鸠摩罗什译「火中生莲华，是可谓希有；在欲而行禅，希有亦如是」，后来「火中莲」成了中文里很常见的比喻。梵文的意思一致。
cmp.en: “A lotus in the middle of fire”: Kumarajiva’s 火中生莲华，是可谓希有；在欲而行禅，希有亦如是 (“a lotus growing in fire is rare indeed; practicing meditation amid desire is just as rare”) made 火中莲 (huǒ zhōng lián, “a lotus in the fire”) a common image in Chinese. The Sanskrit means the same.

verses.en: “On purpose they become courtesans to draw men in; having lured them with the hook of desire, they establish them in the knowledge of a buddha. (32)”
“They are always village headmen, caravan leaders, royal priests, chief ministers and ministers, for the good of beings. (33)”
“For poor beings they become an inexhaustible treasure; giving them gifts, they make them raise the mind set on awakening. (34)”
“Among beings stiff with pride they become great champions, and make them seek the highest awakening, which uproots all pride. (35)”

cmp.note: 字面是「大裸者」，指赤身角力的大力士。白话加注说明了；英文直接译 great champions。鸠摩罗什译「大力士」，同样取意。
cmp.en: Literally “great naked one,” meaning a strongman who wrestles stripped. The plain Chinese explains this in a note; the English simply says “great champions,” and Kumarajiva likewise translates the sense as 大力士 (dàlìshì, “strongman”).

verses.en: “For beings tormented by fear they always stand in front; giving them fearlessness, they bring them to maturity for awakening. (36)”
“Becoming sages with the five higher knowledges, living the holy life, they set beings in morality, in patience, gentleness and self-control. (37)”
“Seeing beings here who prize being served, the guides become their servants or slaves, or take up being their pupils. (38)”
“By whatever means beings may come to delight in the Dharma, they show every kind of action, well trained in great skill in means. (39)”
“Their training is endless, and endless their sphere; they have endless knowledge and set free endless beings. (40)”
“Even if all the buddhas spoke for kotis of eons, for hundreds of kotis of eons, the end of their good qualities would not be easy to tell. (41)”
“What wise person, hearing these teachings, would not seek the highest awakening, except for lowly beings who have no wisdom at all? (42)”
(End of the verses.)
This was chapter seven, “The Family of the Tathagatas.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Entering the Dharma-Door of Non-Duality

verses.en: Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to those bodhisattvas: “Good sirs, speak as it comes to you: what is the bodhisattvas’ way of entering the Dharma-door of non-duality?”

cmp.note: 梵文是一个长复合词：advaya（不二）+ dharma-mukha（法的门、入口）+ praveśa（进入）。英文拆成 entering the Dharma-door of non-duality，中文古译「入不二法门」几乎逐字对应。英文 non-duality 是哲学书面语，梵文 advaya 只是「没有两个」，口气比英文朴素得多。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is one long compound: advaya (“not two”) + dharma-mukha (“door, entrance of the Dharma”) + praveśa (“entering”). The English unpacks it as “entering the Dharma-door of non-duality”; Kumarajiva’s 入不二法门 (rù bù’èr fǎmén, “enter the not-two Dharma-gate”) matches it almost word for word. English “non-duality” sounds like a philosophy-book term, while Sanskrit advaya simply means “not two,” a much plainer word.

cmp.note: 字面是「让它在你心里亮起来」，意思是「想到什么就说什么」。英文 speak as it comes to you、鸠摩罗什「各随所乐说之」都抓住了「随兴而说」的意思。
cmp.en: Literally “let it shine forth (in your mind),” meaning “say whatever occurs to you.” The English “speak as it comes to you” and Kumarajiva’s 各随所乐说之 (gè suí suǒ lè shuō zhī, “each speak as you please”) both keep this sense of speaking freely.

verses.en: A bodhisattva named Dharmavikurvana (“Wonders of the Dharma”) was present there, and he said: “Son of good family, arising and perishing are two. What has not been born and has not arisen has no perishing at all. Gaining the acceptance that things are unborn: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: kṣānti 本义是「忍耐、接受」。中文「无生法忍」的「忍」保留了这个字，但现代读者会以为是「忍受」；英文 acceptance 更接近「安然接受『法本无生』这件事」的意思。
cmp.en: Kṣānti originally means “patience, acceptance.” The Chinese 无生法忍 (wúshēng fǎ rěn, “the forbearance of the unborn Dharma”) keeps the character 忍 (rěn), which modern readers take as “putting up with something”; the English “acceptance” is closer to the idea of calmly accepting that things are, at root, unborn.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Shrigupta (“Guarded by Glory”) said: “‘I’ and ‘mine’ are two. When no self is projected onto things, there is no ‘mine.’ And this not-projecting is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: samāropa 是「强加、虚构」：把本来没有的「我」加到事物上。英文 projected、白话「虚构」都译出了这个动作；鸠摩罗什改成「若无有我，则无我所」，说成「没有我」，少了「是我们自己加上去的」这一层。
cmp.en: Samāropa means “superimposing, projecting”: laying a “self” onto things where there is none. The English “projected” and the plain Chinese 虚构 (xūgòu, “fabricate”) both keep this action; Kumarajiva rewrites it as 若无有我，则无我所 (“if there is no self, there is no ‘mine’”), which states that there is no self but loses the point that we are the ones adding it.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Shrikuta (“Peak of Glory”) said: “Defilement and purification are two. When defilement is fully understood, there is no thinking about purification. The path that uproots every kind of thinking and leads to sameness: that is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Sunakshatra (“Lucky Star”) said: “Stirring and thinking are two. What does not stir and does not attend has nothing to take up; to be free of anything to take up is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 「没有可着手处、没有要处理的事」。白话译「无所造作」，英文 nothing to take up；鸠摩罗什改成「无念则无分别」，把它换成了中国读者熟悉的「无分别」。
cmp.en: “Having nothing to take up, nothing to work on.” The plain Chinese says 无所造作 (wú suǒ zàozuò, “nothing contrived”), the English “nothing to take up”; Kumarajiva substitutes 无念则无分别 (“no thought, hence no discrimination”), swapping in the idea of “non-discrimination” that Chinese readers already knew.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Subahu (“Strong Arm”) said: “The mind set on awakening and the mind of a disciple are two. But when one sees that minds are all alike, like a magic show, there is neither a mind set on awakening nor a disciple’s mind. That sameness in the character of minds is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Animisha (“Unblinking”) said: “Grasping and not grasping are two. What one does not grasp, one does not find; and there one does not add or take away. Not acting on any thing and not busying oneself with any thing: that is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Sunetra (“Fine Eyes”) said: “Having one mark and having no mark are two. But one who does not mark things out and does not draw distinctions makes neither one mark nor no mark. Entering the sameness of having marks and lacking them: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 复合词可以读成「相、离相、与二者平等的相」。白话把它拆成三样（相、非相、平等相），英文读成「有相与无相的平等」。原文结构有两种读法，这里拿不准。
cmp.en: The compound can be read as “mark, absence of mark, and the mark of their sameness.” The plain Chinese splits it into three items, 相、非相、平等相 (“mark, non-mark, sameness-mark”); the English reads it as “the sameness of having marks and lacking them.” The compound allows both readings, and it is hard to be sure.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Pushya said: “Wholesome and unwholesome are two. When neither the wholesome nor the unwholesome is set up, that is the signless; and at the very limit of the signless there is non-duality. Crossing through there is entering non-duality.”
The bodhisattva Simha (“Lion”) said: “Being at fault and being blameless are two. But one who, with knowledge bound fast like a diamond, is neither bound nor freed: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 梵文是「有过失」与「无过失」，指行为该不该受指责。白话译「有罪、无罪」贴近；鸠摩罗什改成「罪、福为二」，变成了「罪」与「福报」这对中国人熟悉的概念。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit pair is “being at fault” and “being blameless,” about whether an action deserves blame. The plain Chinese 有罪、无罪 (“guilty, not guilty”) is close; Kumarajiva turns it into 罪、福 (zuì, fú, “sin and merit”), a pair more familiar to Chinese readers.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Simhamati (“Lion Mind”) said: “‘This has outflows, this has no outflows’: that is two. But one who has reached the Dharma of sameness does not form the notions ‘with outflows’ and ‘without outflows.’ Nor has he arrived at a state with no notions; nor has he reached sameness within some sameness of no-notions; nor is he tangled in notions. Entering in this way is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: āsrava 字面是「漏出、流出」，指心往外漏向外物的烦恼。中文「有漏、无漏」保留了这个画面；英文 outflows 也照字面译，但英文读者需要说明才懂。
cmp.en: Āsrava literally means “leaking, flowing out”: the afflictions by which the mind leaks out toward things. The Chinese 有漏、无漏 (yǒulòu, wúlòu, “leaking, not leaking”) keeps the picture; the English “outflows” is also literal, but an English reader needs this explanation to follow it.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Sukhadhimukta (“Intent on Happiness”) said: “‘This is happiness, this is not happiness’: that is two. But one who has left all pleasures behind, whose understanding is like open space, and who, through perfectly pure knowledge, clings to nothing: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 梵本这一对是「乐与非乐」；鸠摩罗什本这位菩萨讲的却是「有为、无为为二」，后面的「离一切数」也和梵本不同。可能是鸠摩罗什所据的本子不一样。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit this pair is “happiness and non-happiness”; in Kumarajiva’s version this bodhisattva speaks instead of 有为、无为 (yǒuwéi, wúwéi, “conditioned and unconditioned”), and the following words 离一切数 (“free of all numbering”) also differ. Kumarajiva may have been working from a different manuscript.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Narayana said: “‘This is worldly, this is beyond the world’: that is two. Whatever is worldly is empty by its very nature; there, nothing goes out beyond and nothing goes down into, nothing flows on and nothing scatters. Where there is no going out and no going in, no flowing and no scattering: that is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Dantamati (“Tamed Mind”) said: “Samsara and nirvana are two. By seeing the nature of samsara one neither wanders on in samsara nor passes into nirvana. Waking up to it like this is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Pratyakshadarshin (“Seeing Directly”) said: “Ending and not ending are two. Ending is what has ended completely; and what has ended completely does not need to be brought to an end, so it is called ‘unending.’ And what is unending is momentary; and what is momentary has no ending. One who enters like this should be called one who has entered the Dharma-door of non-duality.”

cmp.note: 梵文在玩谐音：kṣaya（尽）、akṣaya（不尽）、kṣaṇika（刹那的）。英文 ending / unending / momentary、中文「尽、不尽、刹那」都保不住这层音韵，只能保住道理。鸠摩罗什干脆改写成「无尽相即是空」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is playing on sound: kṣaya (“ending”), akṣaya (“unending”), kṣaṇika (“momentary”). Neither the English nor the plain Chinese can keep the wordplay, only the argument. Kumarajiva simply rewrites it as 无尽相即是空 (“the mark of the unending is emptiness”).

verses.en: The bodhisattva Samantagupta (“Guarded All Around”) said: “Self and no-self are two. One who cannot find even a self, what will he make into a ‘no-self’? One who sees the nature of the self does not make two: that is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Vidyuddeva (“God of Lightning”) said: “Knowledge and ignorance are two. Knowledge has ignorance as its very nature; and ignorance has no nature of its own, cannot be counted, and has passed beyond every way of counting. Realizing this is realizing non-duality, and that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 梵文说「明以无明为本性」。白话照梵文译；鸠摩罗什却译成「无明实性即是明」，方向正好反过来：不是明里有无明，而是无明的实性就是明。中国佛教后来常引的是鸠摩罗什这句。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “knowledge has ignorance as its nature.” The plain Chinese follows it; Kumarajiva instead writes 无明实性即是明 (“the true nature of ignorance is knowledge”), turning the direction around. Later Chinese Buddhism usually quotes Kumarajiva’s version.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Priyadarshana (“Lovely to See”) said: “Physical form and ‘empty’ are two. But physical form itself is emptiness. Emptiness does not come from form being destroyed; the very nature of form is emptiness. In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness and ‘empty’ are two. But consciousness itself is emptiness. Emptiness does not come from consciousness being destroyed; the very nature of consciousness is emptiness. Knowing and waking up to the five heaps of grasping in this way is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 「空不是因为色毁灭了才有」。这句针对的是一个常见误会：以为「空」是把东西拿掉之后剩下的状态。英文、白话、鸠摩罗什「非色灭空」都照译了，和《心经》「色即是空」是同一个思路。
cmp.en: “Emptiness does not come from form being destroyed.” This line answers a common misunderstanding: that “empty” is what is left after something has been removed. The English, the plain Chinese and Kumarajiva’s 非色灭空 (fēi sè miè kōng, “not: form destroyed, then empty”) all keep it; it is the same thought as the Heart Sutra’s “form is emptiness.”

verses.en: The bodhisattva Prabhaketu (“Banner of Light”) said: “The four elements are one thing and the space element is another: that is two. But the four elements have the very nature of space. In the past they have the nature of space, in the future they have the nature of space, and in the present, too, they have the nature of space. Knowing how to enter the elements in this way is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 四大（地、水、火、风）加上虚空，梵文都叫 dhātu（界、元素）。英文 elements、白话「元素」都贴切；鸠摩罗什用「种」（四种、空种），现代读者较难看出是指元素。
cmp.en: The four great elements (earth, water, fire, wind) and space are all called dhātu (“element”) in Sanskrit. The English and plain Chinese “elements” both fit; Kumarajiva uses 种 (zhǒng, “kind, seed”), as in 四种 and 空种, which a modern reader may not recognize as “elements.”

verses.en: The bodhisattva Sumati (“Good Mind”) said: “The eye and visible forms are two. But one who fully understands the eye is not drawn to forms, not repelled by them, and not confused by them; such a one is called ‘at peace.’ The ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and things touched, the mind and mental objects are two. But one who fully understands the mind is not drawn to mental objects, not repelled by them, and not confused by them; such a one is called ‘at peace.’ For one who stands in peace like this, there is entry into non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Akshayamati (“Endless Mind”) said: “Giving, and dedicating it to all-knowing, are two. But all-knowing has the very nature of giving, and dedication has the very nature of all-knowing. In the same way, morality, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom, and dedicating them to all-knowing, are two. But all-knowing has the very nature of wisdom, and dedication has the very nature of all-knowing. Entering the single way here is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 「转向、转化」，佛教里指把修行的功德转向某个目标，中文叫「回向」。英文 dedicate 只表达了「献给」，少了「转个方向」的意思。
cmp.en: “To turn, to transform”: in Buddhism, to turn the merit of one’s practice toward a goal, in Chinese 回向 (huíxiàng, “turn toward”). The English “dedicate” conveys “offering it to,” but loses the sense of turning it in a new direction.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Gambhirabuddhi (“Deep Understanding”) said: “Emptiness is one thing, the signless another, and the wishless another: that is two. For what is empty has no sign at all; what is signless is wishless; and where there is no wishing, neither mind nor thought nor mental consciousness is at work. Where there is one door to liberation, all the doors to liberation are to be seen: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 「没有立下目标、无所希求」。英文 wishless、白话「无愿」都照字面；鸠摩罗什译「无作」，侧重「不造作」，意思偏了一点。三者合称「三解脱门」。
cmp.en: “Without any aim set up, wanting nothing.” The English “wishless” and the plain Chinese 无愿 (wúyuàn, “no wish”) are literal; Kumarajiva’s 无作 (wúzuò, “not acting”) leans toward “not contriving,” a slight shift. Together with emptiness and the signless, these are called “the three doors of liberation.”

verses.en: The bodhisattva Shantendriya (“Calm Senses”) said: “Buddha, Dharma and Sangha are two. For the Dharma belongs to the Buddha, and the Sangha has the Dharma as its nature. All these jewels are unconditioned; the unconditioned is space; and the way of all things is like space. Following it through in this way is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 梵文说「法属于佛」「僧以法为本性」，是三者互相依属；鸠摩罗什改成「佛即是法，法即是众」，直接说三者是同一个，说得更彻底。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “the Dharma belongs to the Buddha” and “the Sangha has the Dharma as its nature”: the three depend on one another. Kumarajiva writes 佛即是法，法即是众 (“the Buddha is the Dharma, the Dharma is the Sangha”), declaring them simply identical, a stronger claim.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Apratihatachakshus (“Unobstructed Eye”) said: “The existing body and the ending of the existing body are two. But the existing body itself is its ending. Why? Because he does not set up the view ‘this is an existing body,’ the very view by which one imagines either ‘existing body’ or ‘the ending of the existing body.’ Without imagining, without distinguishing, utterly without distinguishing, he has reached the nature of ending; nothing comes into being and nothing passes away. That is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 字面是「现存的身体、实有的身」，专指把五蕴当成一个真实的「我」的那个身。英文 the existing body、白话「有身」都照字面；鸠摩罗什只写「身」，结尾还加了梵本没有的「不惊、不惧」。
cmp.en: Literally “the existing body, the body taken as real”: specifically the body one takes as a real “self” made of the five heaps. The English “existing body” and the plain Chinese 有身 (yǒushēn, “existing body”) are literal; Kumarajiva writes just 身 (shēn, “body”), and adds at the end 不惊、不惧 (“not startled, not afraid”), which the Sanskrit lacks.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Suvinita (“Well Trained”) said: “Restraint of body, speech and mind: that is two. Why? Because these things have the mark of not being put together. Not putting together the body has the same mark as not putting together speech, and that has the same mark as not putting together the mind. And the not-putting-together of all things is to be known and followed. Knowing this not-putting-together is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 「不加以造作、不组合」：abhisaṃskāra 是把东西拼凑、造作出来。英文 not being put together 照字面；白话「无造作」、鸠摩罗什「无作」意思相同。鸠摩罗什还把「约束」改成了「身口意业」。
cmp.en: “Not fashioning, not putting together”: abhisaṃskāra is to assemble or fabricate something. The English “not being put together” is literal; the plain Chinese 无造作 and Kumarajiva’s 无作 (“no making”) mean the same. Kumarajiva also changes “restraint” into 身口意业 (“the karma of body, speech and mind”).

verses.en: The bodhisattva Punyakshetra (“Field of Merit”) said: “Producing formations that are meritorious, unmeritorious or imperturbable: that is two. But not producing meritorious, unmeritorious or imperturbable formations: that is non-dual. The formations that are meritorious, unmeritorious and imperturbable are empty of any mark of their own; in that emptiness there are no meritorious, unmeritorious or imperturbable formations. To trace it through in this way is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Padmavyuha (“Array of Lotuses”) said: “What rises up from the rising of a self is two. One who fully understands the self does not raise up two. For one who stands in non-duality there is no making-known; and having no making-known is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 「使之被知、表示、表象」。白话译「了别」，鸠摩罗什译「识」。英文 making-known 照字面，读起来生硬，但避免了把它当成「意识」本身。这里原意不完全确定。
cmp.en: “Making known, representation.” The plain Chinese renders it 了别 (liǎobié, “discerning”) and Kumarajiva 识 (shí, “consciousness”). The English “making-known” is literal and stiff, but avoids treating it as consciousness itself. The exact sense here is not fully certain.

verses.en: The bodhisattva Shrigarbha (“Womb of Glory”) said: “What is brought about by taking things as found is two. What one does not get, one does not find; one neither takes it up nor throws it out. There, where there is no taking up and no throwing out: that is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Chandrottara (“Above the Moon”) said: “Darkness and light are two. Neither darkness nor light: that is non-dual. Why? Because for someone who has entered the attainment of cessation there is neither darkness nor light. All things have that mark. Entering sameness here is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Ratnamudrahasta (“Jewel-Seal Hand”) said: “Delighting in nirvana and not delighting in samsara are two. One who neither delights in nirvana nor dislikes samsara: that is non-dual. Why? Because freedom only makes sense for someone who is bound. One who was never bound at all, why would he look for freedom? A monk neither bound nor freed feels neither delight nor dislike: that is entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Manikutaraja (“King of the Jewel Peak”) said: “The path and the wrong path are two. For one who has set out on the path, the wrong path does not arise. For one who stands where nothing arises, there is no notion ‘path’ and no notion ‘wrong path.’ For one who fully understands notions, the mind does not step into two: that is his entering non-duality.”

The bodhisattva Satyanandin (“Delighting in Truth”) said: “True and false are two. One who sees the truth does not even see truth; how could he see falsehood? Why? Because he does not see with the eye of flesh, he sees with the eye of wisdom. And he sees in such a way that he does not see apart. Where there is neither seeing nor seeing apart: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: paśyati 是「看」，vi-paśyati 是「分开来看、细看」。英文 does not see apart 照字面；白话「没有另作分辨地看」意思对；鸠摩罗什改成「无见无不见」，变成了「看与不看」的对仗。
cmp.en: Paśyati is “to see”; vi-paśyati is “to see apart, to see in detail.” The English “does not see apart” is literal and the plain Chinese has the same sense; Kumarajiva writes 无见无不见 (wú jiàn wú bú jiàn, “no seeing and no not-seeing”), turning it into a balanced pair of seeing and not-seeing.

verses.en: When those bodhisattvas had each given their own explanation in this way, they said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, what is a bodhisattva’s entering of non-duality?”

Manjushri said: “Good sirs, all of you have spoken well. And yet everything you have explained, all of it, is two. Leaving aside even a single explanation: not uttering anything about any thing, not declaring, not voicing, not proclaiming, not speaking, not making known: that is entering non-duality.”

cmp.note: 梵文里文殊先说「你们说的一切，其实都还是二」，再说「不说」才是不二。鸠摩罗什删掉了这句批评，只留下「如我意者，于一切法无言无说」，语气客气得多，读者也就看不出前面三十一位菩萨的说法统统被否定了。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit, Manjushri first says “everything you have explained is still two,” and only then says that not speaking is non-duality. Kumarajiva drops this criticism and keeps only 如我意者，于一切法无言无说 (“as I see it, in all things there is no word and no speech”). His Manjushri is far more polite, and readers no longer see that all thirty-one bodhisattvas before him have just been set aside.

cmp.note: sthāpayitvā 可以是「放下」，也可以是佛教梵文常见的「除了……之外」。白话、英文都取「连一种说法也放下」；若取后一种，就是「除了这一句说明之外」。拿不准。
cmp.en: Sthāpayitvā can mean “setting aside” or, as often in Buddhist Sanskrit, “except for.” The plain Chinese and the English both take it as “leaving aside even a single explanation”; on the other reading it would be “apart from this one statement.” This is uncertain.

verses.en: Then Manjushri, the young prince, said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Son of good family, we have each given our own explanation. Now you too, speak as it comes to you: explain entering the Dharma of non-duality.”
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said nothing at all.

cmp.note: 梵文只有三个词：「离车人维摩诘，成了沉默的」。没有形容、没有动作。英文 said nothing at all、白话「沉默不语」、鸠摩罗什「默然无言」都和原文一样短。后来中国禅宗称之为「维摩一默」「一默如雷」，那是后人的评语，经文本身一个字也没加。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is just a few words: “Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi became silent.” No description, no gesture. The English “said nothing at all,” the plain Chinese 沉默不语 (chénmò bù yǔ, “silent, not speaking”) and Kumarajiva’s 默然无言 (mòrán wú yán, “silent, without words”) are all as short as the original. Later Chinese Chan called it 维摩一默 (Wéimó yí mò, “Vimalakirti’s one silence”) and 一默如雷 (yí mò rú léi, “a silence like thunder”), but those are later readers’ words; the sutra itself adds nothing.

verses.en: Then Manjushri, the young prince, gave his approval to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is the bodhisattvas’ entering of the Dharma-door of non-duality: here there is no activity of letters, sounds, utterances or making-known.”

cmp.note: 梵文列了四样：字母、声音、发声、表示。白话译成「文字、声音、言语、表达」；鸠摩罗什压成「乃至无有文字、语言」，又加了一个「真」字：「是真入不二法门」，暗示前面各位的说法不算「真」入。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit lists four things: letters, sounds, utterances, signals. The plain Chinese gives all four; Kumarajiva compresses them into 乃至无有文字、语言 (“even to having no written words or speech”) and adds the word 真 (zhēn, “truly”): 是真入不二法门 (“this is truly entering the not-two Dharma-gate”), hinting that the earlier answers were not true entry.

verses.en: While this teaching was being given, five thousand bodhisattvas entered the Dharma-door of non-duality and gained the acceptance that things are unborn.
This was chapter eight, “Entering the Dharma-Door of Non-Duality.”

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Food Brought by an Emanated Bodhisattva

verses.en: Then this thought came to the venerable Shariputra: “It is almost time, and these great beings are not getting up. Where are they going to eat?”

cmp.note: 「时间快到尽头了」：指出家人只能在中午以前进食，过了正午就不能吃。白话「时间快到了」没有把这层说出来；英文 It is almost time 也一样，读者需要知道这个戒律背景。
cmp.en: “The time is nearly at its end”: monks may eat only before noon, and after midday they may not eat. The plain Chinese 时间快到了 (“it’s almost time”) does not spell this out, nor does the English “It is almost time”; the reader needs this monastic rule as background.

verses.en: Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi, knowing with his mind the thought in the venerable Shariputra’s mind, said to the venerable Shariputra: “Reverend Shariputra, the eight liberations that the Tathagata has taught: dwell in those liberations. Don’t listen to the Dharma with a mind smeared with thoughts of food. But wait a moment, Reverend Shariputra, and you will eat food such as you have never tasted.”

Then, at that moment, Vimalakirti the Licchavi entered a samadhi of such a kind and performed such a feat of supernormal power that he showed those bodhisattvas and those great disciples a world called Sarvagandhasugandha (“Sweetest of All Scents”), above this buddha-field, past buddha-fields as many as the sands of forty-two Ganges rivers. There a Tathagata named Gandhottamakuta (“Highest Peak of Scent”) now lives, dwells and carries on. In that world, whatever heavenly and human scents waft in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions, scents even finer than those waft from the trees. In that world not even the names of disciples and solitary buddhas exist; there is only a gathering of pure bodhisattvas.

cmp.note: 这位如来的梵文名是「香中最高的峰」，鸠摩罗什译「香积」，世界名「众香」。中文名字简洁好记，英文保留梵文音译并在括号里给意思。
cmp.en: This Tathagata’s Sanskrit name means “Highest Peak of Scent”; Kumarajiva calls him 香积 (Xiāngjī, “Heaped Fragrance”) and his world 众香 (Zhòngxiāng, “All Fragrances”). The Chinese names are short and memorable; the English keeps the Sanskrit names and gives their meaning in brackets.

verses.en: The Tathagata Gandhottamakuta teaches them the Dharma. In that world the pavilions are made entirely of scents, and the walkways, gardens and palaces are made entirely of scents. The scent of the food those bodhisattvas eat spreads through measureless worlds.

At that time the Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, had sat down to his meal with those bodhisattvas. There, young gods called Gandhavyuhahara (“Feeding on Arrays of Scent”), who had set out in the Great Vehicle, were busy attending on and serving that Blessed One and those bodhisattvas. And the whole assembly here saw that world, that Blessed One and those bodhisattvas seated at their meal.
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to all those bodhisattvas: “Good sirs, which of you is willing to bring food from that buddha-field?” But because of Manjushri’s power, no one was willing.
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, aren’t you embarrassed by an assembly like this?”
He said: “Son of good family, hasn’t the Tathagata said that those still in training should not be looked down on?”

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi, without getting up from his bed, conjured up an emanated bodhisattva in front of those bodhisattvas. His body was golden in color and adorned with the marks and minor signs, and his form shone so brightly that it outshone the whole assembly.

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to that emanated bodhisattva: “Go, son of good family. Above, past buddha-fields as many as the sands of forty-two Ganges rivers, there is a world called Sarvagandhasugandha. A Tathagata named Gandhottamakuta is there, who has just sat down to his meal. Go there, bow your head to that Tathagata’s feet on my behalf, and say: ‘Vimalakirti the Licchavi bows his head to the Blessed One’s feet and asks whether the Blessed One has little pain and little trouble; whether he gets up easily; whether his daily life, strength, ease, freedom from fault and comfort are good.’ And say this: ‘Blessed One, give me what is left over from your meal. It will do the work of a buddha in the Saha world, and it will make beings of lowly inclination delight in a noble outlook,

cmp.note: 「娑婆世界」：就是我们这个世界。sahā 一般解作「堪忍」，众生在这里要忍受种种苦。中文音译「娑婆」，英文保留 Saha；第一次出现时，读者需要知道它指的就是我们这个世界。
cmp.en: “The Saha world”: our own world. Sahā is usually explained as “endurance,” since beings here must endure many sufferings. Chinese transliterates it 娑婆 (Suōpó), and the English keeps “Saha”; on first meeting it the reader needs to know it simply means our world.

verses.en: and the Tathagata’s name will be spread far and wide.’”

Then that emanated bodhisattva said “Very well” to Vimalakirti the Licchavi, agreeing, and he was seen in front of those bodhisattvas with his face turned upward; but those bodhisattvas did not see him go.

Then that emanated bodhisattva arrived at the world Sarvagandhasugandha. There he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, and said: “Blessed One, the bodhisattva Vimalakirti bows his head to the Blessed One’s feet and asks whether you have little pain and little trouble; whether you get up easily; whether your daily life, strength, ease, freedom from fault and comfort are good.”

And bowing his head to the Blessed One’s feet, he said: “Blessed One, give me the food left over from your meal. It will do the work of a buddha in the Saha world; it will make those beings of lowly inclination delight in the noble qualities of a buddha; and the Blessed One’s name will be spread far and wide.”

Then the bodhisattvas in the buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, were astonished and said to that Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta: “Blessed One, where does such a great being come from? Where is that Saha world? And what is this thing called ‘lowly inclination’?” So those bodhisattvas questioned that Tathagata.

Then that Blessed One said to those bodhisattvas: “Sons of good family, below this buddha-field, past buddha-fields as many as the sands of forty-two Ganges rivers, there is the Saha world. There a Tathagata named Shakyamuni teaches the Dharma to beings of lowly inclination, in a buddha-field of the five corruptions. There a bodhisattva named Vimalakirti, who stands in the liberation beyond thought, teaches the Dharma to bodhisattvas. He has sent this emanated bodhisattva to proclaim my name, to make known the praise of this world, and to bring out the roots of goodness of those bodhisattvas.”
Then those bodhisattvas said: “Blessed One, how great must that bodhisattva be, if even his emanation has such supernormal power, strength and confidence?”
That Blessed One said: “That bodhisattva is so great that he sends emanations to all buddha-fields, and those emanations attend to beings by doing the work of a buddha.”

Then that Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, gave that bodhisattva the food, steeped in every scent, in a bowl filled with every scent. Then ninety thousand bodhisattvas set out, saying: “Blessed One, we will go to that Saha world, to bow to that Blessed One Shakyamuni, and to see this Vimalakirti and those bodhisattvas.”

That Blessed One said: “Go, sons of good family, if you think it is time. But, sons of good family, withdraw your scents before you enter that world, so that its beings do not become intoxicated and careless. And withdraw your own forms, so that the beings of the Saha world do not feel ashamed. And do not form a notion that the world is inferior and then a feeling of aversion. Why? Because buddha-fields are fields of space; but to bring beings to maturity, the buddhas, the blessed ones, do not show the whole domain of a buddha.”

Then the emanated bodhisattva took that food, and with those ninety thousand bodhisattvas, by the power of the Buddha and the power of Vimalakirti, in an instant, a moment, a flash, he vanished from the world Sarvagandhasugandha and appeared in the house of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.

There Vimalakirti conjured up ninety thousand lion thrones just like the earlier lion thrones, and those bodhisattvas sat on them. The emanated bodhisattva offered the bowl full of food to Vimalakirti the Licchavi. The scent of that food perfumed the whole great city of Vaishali, so that the entire thousandfold world was filled with fragrance. Then the brahmins and householders of Vaishali, and the lord of the Licchavis, named Somacchatra, smelled that scent; amazed and astonished, delighted in body and mind, he came together with a full eighty-four thousand Licchavis. And the very scent of that food stirred the earth-dwelling young gods, and the gods of the realm of desire and the realm of form, and they came to the house of Vimalakirti the Licchavi.

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to the elder Shariputra and those great disciples: “Reverends, eat this deathless food of the Tathagata, which has been infused with great compassion. But don’t tie your minds to narrow practice, or you won’t be able to make this offering pure.”
Then this thought came to some of the disciples: “How can such a huge assembly eat from such a small amount of food?”

The emanated bodhisattva said to those disciples: “Venerable ones, don’t measure the wisdom and merit of the Tathagata by your own wisdom and merit. The four great oceans might run dry, but this food will never run out. Even if all beings ate it for an eon, in mouthfuls the size of Mount Sumeru, it would not run out. Why? This food left over in the Tathagata’s bowl is born of inexhaustible morality, concentration and wisdom; it cannot be used up.”

Then the whole assembly was satisfied by that food, and still the food did not diminish. And the bodhisattvas, disciples, Shakras, Brahmas, world-guardians and other beings who ate that food felt in their bodies the same happiness the bodhisattvas feel in the world called Adorned with All Happiness. And from all the pores of their skin came a scent just like the scent of the trees in that world Sarvagandhasugandha.

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi, knowing full well, said to the bodhisattvas who had come from the buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta: “Sons of good family, how does the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta teach the Dharma?”

They said: “That Tathagata does not teach the Dharma with words and letters. Those bodhisattvas are trained by scent alone. Under whatever scent tree those bodhisattvas sit, such a scent comes from it that, the moment they smell it, they gain the samadhi called Mine of All Bodhisattva Qualities; and the moment they gain that samadhi, all the qualities of a bodhisattva arise in them.”

cmp.note: 「不用文字言语说法」，只用香气教化。这和上一品维摩诘的沉默、本品后面讲的「以种种方式做佛事」连成一线：说法不一定靠语言。鸠摩罗什译「彼土如来无文字说，但以众香令诸天人得入律行」。
cmp.en: “He does not teach the Dharma with words and letters,” only with scent. This links with Vimalakirti’s silence in the previous chapter and with the later teaching that the work of a buddha is done in many ways: the Dharma does not depend on words. Kumarajiva writes 彼土如来无文字说，但以众香令诸天人得入律行 (“the Tathagata of that land teaches without words, only through fragrances leading gods and humans into disciplined practice”).

verses.en: Then those bodhisattvas said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “And how does the Blessed One Shakyamuni teach the Dharma here?”

He said: “Good sirs, these beings are hard to tame. For these beings who are hard to tame, he gives only talks that tame those who are as stubborn and hard to tame as wild horses. And what is the taming of the stubborn and hard to tame, and what are talks that tame them? Like this: ‘These are the hells. This is animal birth. This is Yama’s world. These are the unfree states. This is birth with poor faculties. This is misconduct of body; this is the result of misconduct of body. This is misconduct of speech; this is the result of misconduct of speech. This is misconduct of mind; this is the result of misconduct of mind. This is killing. This is stealing. This is sexual misconduct. This is lying. This is divisive speech.

cmp.note: 「倔强难驯的（马）」。鸠摩罗什译「刚强难化」，后来成了中文里形容娑婆众生的常用语。白话译「像劣马一样难调伏」，英文 as stubborn … as wild horses 保留了马的比喻。
cmp.en: “Stubborn, unbroken (of a horse).” Kumarajiva’s 刚强难化 (gāngqiáng nán huà, “hard and stubborn, difficult to transform”) became the usual Chinese description of the beings of our world. The plain Chinese says “hard to tame like a bad horse,” and the English “as stubborn … as wild horses” keeps the horse image.

verses.en: This is harsh speech. This is idle chatter. This is covetousness. This is malice. This is wrong view. This is the result of these. This is stinginess. This is immorality. This is anger. This is laziness. This is distraction. This is poor wisdom. This is the fruit of poor wisdom. This is breaking the training rules of the monastic code. This is the monastic code. This should be done. This should not be done. This is practice. This is striving. This is an obstruction. This is no obstruction. This is an offense. This is no offense. This is being cleared of an offense. This is the path. This is the wrong path. This is wholesome. This is unwholesome. This is blameworthy. This is blameless. This has outflows. This has no outflows. This is worldly. This is beyond the world. This is conditioned. This is unconditioned. This is defilement. This is purification. This is samsara. This is nirvana.’

By explaining many things like this, he settles beings whose minds are like wild horses. Just as a wild horse or elephant is tamed only when it is pricked to the quick, in the same way these beings here, hard to tame and stubborn, are tamed by talks that explain every kind of suffering.”

Those bodhisattvas said: “How amazing the Blessed One Shakyamuni is! He hides the greatness of a buddha and tames stubborn beings in a poor, rough way. And the bodhisattvas who live in a buddha-field as hard as this have great compassion beyond thought.”

Vimalakirti said: “Good sirs, it is just as you say. The bodhisattvas who are born here have firm great compassion. In this world they will do more for the good of beings in a single lifetime than is done for the good of beings in that world Sarvagandhasugandha in a thousand eons.

Why? Because, good sirs, here in the Saha world there are ten ways of heaping up the good that do not exist in other buddha-fields, and they take them up. What are the ten? Gathering in the poor through giving; gathering in the immoral through morality; gathering in the hostile through patience; gathering in the lazy through effort; gathering in the scattered through meditation; gathering in those of poor wisdom through wisdom; teaching how to pass beyond the eight unfree states to those caught in them; teaching the Great Vehicle to those whose practice is narrow; gathering in, through roots of goodness, those who have not planted roots of goodness; and constantly bringing beings to maturity through the four ways of gathering people. They take up these ten ways of heaping up the good, which do not exist in other buddha-fields.”
Those bodhisattvas said: “Having what qualities does a bodhisattva, when he passes away from the Saha world, go to a pure buddha-field unharmed and unhurt?”

Vimalakirti said: “Sons of good family, a bodhisattva who has eight qualities, when he passes away from the Saha world, goes to a pure buddha-field unharmed and unhurt. What are the eight? Thinking, ‘I must do good to all beings, and seek no good at all from them’; bearing the suffering of all beings and giving away all his roots of goodness to all beings; having no hostility toward any being; loving all bodhisattvas as he loves the Teacher; not rejecting teachings he has not heard, nor those he has heard, when he hears them; not envying the gains of others and not being proud of his own gains, and so taming his mind; examining his own faults and not accusing others of their offenses; and, delighting in care, taking up every good quality.
A bodhisattva who has these eight qualities, when he passes away from the Saha world, goes to a pure buddha-field unharmed and unhurt.”

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi and Manjushri, the young prince, taught the Dharma in that gathered assembly in such a way that a full thousand living beings raised their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and ten thousand bodhisattvas gained the acceptance that things are unborn.
This was chapter nine, called “Bringing the Food Made by an Emanation.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Perishable and the Imperishable

verses.en: Now at that time, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma in the Amrapali grove, the circle of the gathering became wide and spacious, and the assembly appeared golden. Then the venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is this a sign of, that the Amrapali grove has become so spacious and the whole assembly appears golden?”
The Blessed One said: “Ananda, it is Vimalakirti the Licchavi and Manjushri, the young prince, who are about to come to the Tathagata surrounded by a great assembly.”
Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to Manjushri, the young prince: “Manjushri, let us go to the Blessed One. These great beings will see the Tathagata and bow to him.”
He said: “Let’s go, son of good family, whenever you think it is time.”

Then Vimalakirti the Licchavi performed such a feat of supernormal power that he set that whole assembly, along with the lion thrones, on his right hand and went to where the Blessed One was. When he arrived, he set the assembly down on the ground, bowed his head to the Blessed One’s feet, walked around the Blessed One seven times keeping him on his right, and stood to one side.

Then the bodhisattvas who had come from the buddha-field of the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, and the others, got down from those lion thrones, bowed their heads to the Blessed One’s feet and stood to one side. In the same way the Shakras, Brahmas, world-guardians and young gods bowed their heads to the Blessed One’s feet and stood to one side.
Then the Blessed One greeted those bodhisattvas with a talk on the Dharma and said: “Sons of good family, sit down, each on your own lion throne.”
With the Blessed One’s permission, they sat down.
Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Shariputra: “Shariputra, have you seen the play of these bodhisattvas, these foremost of beings?”
He said: “I have seen it, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said: “And what notion arose in you about it?”
He said: “Blessed One, a notion beyond thought arose in me: I see such actions of theirs, beyond thought, that I can neither think about them, weigh them nor count them.”
Then the venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I am smelling a scent I have never smelled before. Whose scent is this, so unusual?”
He said: “Ananda, the scent is coming from the bodies of these bodhisattvas, from all the pores of their skin.”
Shariputra said too: “Venerable Ananda, the same scent is coming from all the pores of our skin as well.”
He said: “Where does this scent come from?”
He said: “Vimalakirti the Licchavi brought food from the buddha-field of the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, from the world Sarvagandhasugandha. All who ate it have this scent coming from their bodies.”
Then the venerable Ananda said to the bodhisattva Vimalakirti: “Son of good family, how long will this scent last?”
He said: “Until this food has been digested.”
Ananda said: “And how long will it take for this food to be digested?”
He said: “It will be digested in seven times seven days, and after that its strength will spread for another seven days. And it will cause no indigestion.

Reverend Ananda, monks who have not entered certainty and eat this food will digest it when they have entered certainty. Those who have entered certainty and eat it will not digest it until their minds are freed. Beings who have not raised the mind set on awakening and eat it will digest it when they have raised the mind set on awakening. Those who have raised the mind set on awakening and eat it will not digest it until they have gained acceptance. And those who have gained acceptance and eat it will digest it when they are only one birth away from awakening.

Reverend Ananda, it is like a medicine called Sweetness: once it is in the stomach it is not digested until all the poison throughout the body has gone, and only after that is the medicine digested. In the same way, Reverend Ananda, that food is not digested until all the poison of the afflictions has been neutralized, and only after that is the food digested.”
Then the venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, this food is doing the work of a buddha.”
He said: “So it is, Ananda, so it is, just as you say.

Ananda, there are buddha-fields in which bodhisattvas do the work of a buddha. There are buddha-fields in which the tree of awakening does the work of a buddha. There are buddha-fields in which seeing the marks and form of a Tathagata does the work of a buddha. In the same way, the sky, open space, does the work of a buddha. That is how those beings are trained.

In the same way, explanations by the comparisons of a dream, a reflection, the moon in water, an echo, a magic show and a mirage, and by analysis of words, do the work of a buddha for beings. There are buddha-fields in which making things known in words does the work of a buddha. Ananda, there are buddha-fields so pure that not uttering, not speaking, not pointing out, being inexpressible does the work of a buddha for those beings.

cmp.note: 「不说、不讲、不可言说」也在做佛事。这一句把第八品维摩诘的沉默、本品的香饭，都归入同一个道理：佛事不限于说话。英文、白话、鸠摩罗什「无言无说、无示无识」意思一致。
cmp.en: “Not uttering, not speaking, being inexpressible” also does the work of a buddha. This line brings Vimalakirti’s silence in chapter 8 and the fragrant food of this chapter under one principle: the work of a buddha is not limited to speech. The English, the plain Chinese and Kumarajiva’s 无言无说、无示无识 (“no word, no speech, no showing, no knowing”) agree.

verses.en: Ananda, there is no posture and no use of things by the buddhas, the blessed ones, that does not do the work of a buddha for the training of beings. Ananda, even these four Maras and the eighty-four thousand doors of the afflictions by which beings are defiled, the buddhas, the blessed ones, do the work of a buddha with all of them.

Ananda, this is the Dharma-door called Entering All the Qualities of a Buddha. A bodhisattva who has entered this Dharma-door is not cast down or humbled by buddha-fields that have all the noble splendors and good qualities, and is not elated or puffed up by them either. Instead he feels the greatest reverence for the Tathagatas: ‘How amazing it is that the buddhas, the blessed ones, who are convinced of the sameness of all things, show buddha-fields of so many kinds in order to bring beings to maturity!’

Ananda, it is like this: buddha-fields differ in their various good qualities, but the space over a buddha-field, the sky, has no differences. In the same way, Ananda, the Tathagatas differ in their form bodies, but the unobstructed knowledge of the Tathagatas has no differences.

For, Ananda, all buddhas are the same in form, color, radiance, body, marks, nobility of family, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the powers, the kinds of confidence, the qualities of a buddha, great kindness, great compassion, the wish to help, bearing, conduct, practice, length of life, teaching the Dharma, bringing beings to maturity, freeing beings, purifying fields and fulfilling all the qualities of a buddha. That is why they are called ‘perfectly awakened one,’ ‘Tathagata’ and ‘Buddha.’

Ananda, even if you lived for an eon, you could not easily master the full meaning and analysis of these three words. Ananda, even if all the beings in the great galaxy of a billion worlds were like you, foremost among the learned, having gained the dharani of memory, all those beings like Ananda could not master in an eon the settled meaning and explanation of these three words, ‘perfectly awakened one,’ ‘Tathagata’ and ‘Buddha.’ That is how measureless a buddha’s awakening is, Ananda; that is how far beyond thought the wisdom and eloquence of the Tathagatas are.”
Then the venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, from today on I will no longer claim to be foremost among the learned.”

The Blessed One said: “Ananda, don’t lose heart. Why? Ananda, I declared you foremost among the learned with the disciples in mind, not the bodhisattvas. Leave the bodhisattvas aside, Ananda; a wise person should not try to fathom them. Ananda, one could measure the depth of all the oceans, but one cannot measure the depth of the bodhisattvas’ wisdom, knowledge, memory, dharanis and eloquence. Ananda, you disciples should leave the bodhisattvas’ practice alone. Why? Ananda, the splendors that Vimalakirti the Licchavi showed in the space of a single morning meal could not be shown by all the disciples and solitary buddhas who have supernormal powers, with all their magical transformations and miracles, in hundreds of thousands of kotis of eons.”

Then all the bodhisattvas who had come from the buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathagata Gandhottamakuta, from the world Sarvagandhasugandha, joined their palms and bowed to the Tathagata, and said: “Blessed One, we give up the thoughts with which we formed a notion that this buddha-field was inferior. Why? Because, Blessed One, the domain of the buddhas, the blessed ones, is beyond thought. Through skill in means, to bring beings to maturity, they show the splendors of a field in whatever way they wish. Blessed One, give us a gift of the Dharma, so that when we have gone back to that world Sarvagandhasugandha we may remember the Blessed One.”

The Blessed One said: “Sons of good family, there is a liberation of the bodhisattvas called the Perishable and the Imperishable. You should train in it. What is it? The perishable is what is conditioned; the imperishable is what is unconditioned. A bodhisattva should neither exhaust the conditioned nor settle in the unconditioned.

cmp.note: kṣaya 是「尽、耗尽、会坏灭的」，akṣaya 是「无尽、不坏」。这里分别指有为法和无为法。鸠摩罗什译「有尽无尽」，名句是「不尽有为，不住无为」。英文 the Perishable and the Imperishable 照字面；下文 exhaust（耗尽）与 perishable 同源于 kṣaya，英文没法用同一个词。
cmp.en: Kṣaya means “exhaustion, perishing, what wears out,” and akṣaya “inexhaustible, imperishable”; here they stand for the conditioned and the unconditioned. Kumarajiva renders the title 有尽无尽 (“the exhaustible and the inexhaustible”), and his famous line is 不尽有为，不住无为 (“do not exhaust the conditioned, do not dwell in the unconditioned”). The English “the Perishable and the Imperishable” is literal; “exhaust” in the next line comes from the same Sanskrit kṣaya, which English cannot show with one word.

verses.en: Not exhausting the conditioned means this: not falling away from great kindness; not abandoning great compassion; not forgetting the mind set on all-knowing that one set out with in deep resolve; not tiring of bringing beings to maturity; not giving up the ways of gathering people; giving up body and life to uphold the true Dharma; never being satisfied with roots of goodness; standing firm in skill at dedication; not being lazy in seeking the Dharma; keeping no teacher’s closed fist in teaching the Dharma; being eager to see and worship the Tathagatas; not fearing deliberate rebirths; being neither elated by success nor cast down by failure; not looking down on those still in training; loving those who are trained as one loves the Teacher; properly drawing in those overwhelmed by afflictions; not losing oneself in the pleasures of solitude; not clinging to one’s own happiness, but being absorbed in the happiness of others; regarding the meditations, samadhis and attainments as the Avici hell; regarding samsara as a garden and a palace; regarding beggars as good friends; regarding giving away everything one owns as fulfilling all-knowing; regarding the immoral as people to protect; regarding the perfections as mother and father; regarding the things that belong to awakening as one’s own household; never thinking one has gathered enough roots of goodness; building one’s own field out of the good qualities of all buddha-fields; offering an open sacrifice to fulfill the marks and minor signs; adorning body, speech and mind by doing no evil; wandering through samsara for countless eons with pure body, speech and mind; not losing heart, through courage of mind, on hearing of the measureless qualities of a buddha; taking up the sword of wisdom to subdue the enemy, the afflictions; fully understanding the heaps, elements and sense fields so as to carry the burden of all beings; burning with effort to crush Mara’s army; being free of pride in order to seek the Dharma; having few wants and being content in order to take hold of the Dharma of seeking knowledge; not mixing with any worldly things, so as to be loved by all the world; not disturbing any posture, so as to go along with the world; producing the higher knowledges, so as to show every kind of action; having dharani, memory and knowledge, so as to hold all that has been heard; knowing which faculties are higher and which lower, so as to cut off the doubts of all beings; having unobstructed power in order to teach the Dharma; having unobstructed eloquence through gaining eloquence; enjoying the good fortune of gods and humans through purity in the ten wholesome actions; standing on the path of Brahma in order to produce the four immeasurables; gaining a buddha’s voice by requesting teachings, rejoicing in them and applauding them; gaining a buddha’s bearing by excelling in restraint of body, speech and mind and losing oneself in nothing; urging people toward the Great Vehicle, so as to draw together the community of bodhisattvas; and being careful, so as not to lose any good quality.

cmp.note: 「把禅定当作无间地狱，把生死当作花园宫殿」：对菩萨来说，沉入禅定享受寂静反而是陷阱，生死轮回却是可以救人的地方。这是全经最大胆的颠倒之一。鸠摩罗什译「于诸禅定如地狱想，于生死中如园观想」，意思相同。
cmp.en: “Regarding the meditations as the Avici hell, and samsara as a garden and a palace”: for a bodhisattva, sinking into the peace of meditation is a trap, while samsara is where beings can be helped. This is one of the boldest reversals in the sutra. Kumarajiva’s 于诸禅定如地狱想，于生死中如园观想 says the same.

verses.en: That, sons of good family, is how a bodhisattva who is convinced of these teachings does not exhaust the conditioned.

And how does he not settle in the unconditioned? When he masters emptiness but does not realize emptiness; masters signlessness but does not realize signlessness; masters wishlessness but does not realize wishlessness; masters not-putting-together but does not realize not-putting-together. He considers ‘impermanent,’ yet is never satisfied with roots of goodness. He considers ‘suffering,’ yet is reborn deliberately. He considers ‘no-self,’ yet does not give up the self. He considers ‘peaceful,’ yet does not produce final peace. He considers ‘solitary,’ yet exerts himself with body and mind. He considers ‘homeless,’ yet does not leave the home of bright qualities.

He considers ‘without grasping,’ yet carries the burden of beings he has taken up. He considers ‘without outflows,’ yet goes along with the course of samsara. He considers ‘without activity,’ yet acts to bring beings to maturity. He considers ‘selflessness,’ yet does not give up great compassion for beings. He considers ‘the unborn,’ yet does not fall into the certainty of the disciples. He considers things as hollow, worthless, without core, without owner and without abode, yet his merit is not hollow, his knowledge is not worthless, his intentions are fulfilled, he has been consecrated with self-arisen knowledge, he is devoted to self-arisen knowledge, he has grasped the definitive meaning, and he stands in the family of the buddhas. That, sons of good family, is how a bodhisattva convinced of these teachings does not settle in the unconditioned and does not exhaust the conditioned.

Because he is devoted to the store of merit, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he is devoted to the store of knowledge, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he has great kindness, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he has great compassion, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he brings beings to maturity, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he longs for the qualities of a buddha, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he is perfecting the marks of a buddha, he does not settle in the unconditioned; in order to perfect all-knowing knowledge, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he is skilled in means, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he has examined things well with wisdom, he does not exhaust the conditioned. In order to purify a buddha-field, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he is upheld by the Buddha, he does not exhaust the conditioned.

Because he feels for the good of beings, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he shows the meaning of the Dharma, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he has a store of roots of goodness, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because roots of goodness have left their imprint on him, he does not exhaust the conditioned. In order to fulfill his vows, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he is wishless, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because his intent is pure, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because his deep resolve is pure, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he plays with the five higher knowledges, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he has the six higher knowledges of a buddha’s knowledge, he does not exhaust the conditioned. In order to complete the store of the perfections, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because the time is not yet complete, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he gathers the wealth of the Dharma, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he has no use for a narrow Dharma, he does not exhaust the conditioned.

Because he gathers every medicine, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he gives medicine as each one needs, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because of his firm promise, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he carries out his promise, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he gathers the medicine of the Dharma, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he gives the medicine of the Dharma as suits each case, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Because he fully understands the disease of the afflictions of all beings, he does not settle in the unconditioned; because he calms every disease, he does not exhaust the conditioned. That, sons of good family, is how a bodhisattva does not exhaust the conditioned and does not settle in the unconditioned. This is called the bodhisattvas’ liberation of the Perishable and the Imperishable. Good sirs, you should practice it.”

Then those bodhisattvas, hearing this teaching, were delighted, thrilled, overjoyed, glad, full of joy and happiness. To honor the Blessed One, those bodhisattvas and this teaching of the Dharma, they covered this whole great galaxy of a billion worlds knee-deep with arrays of every kind of powdered perfume, incense and flowers, and strewed flowers over the Blessed One’s assembly. They bowed their heads to the Blessed One’s feet, walked around the Blessed One three times keeping him on their right, and uttered words of joy. Then they vanished from this buddha-field, and in an instant, a moment, a flash, they were back in that world Sarvagandhasugandha.
This was chapter ten, called “The Perishable and the Imperishable: A Gift of the Dharma.”

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Bringing Over the World Abhirati and Seeing Akshobhya

verses.en: Then the Blessed One said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Son of good family, when you want to see the Tathagata, how do you see the Tathagata?”

When this was said, Vimalakirti the Licchavi said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, when I want to see the Tathagata, I see the Tathagata by not seeing. I see him as unborn at the beginning, not passing on at the end, and not standing anywhere in the present. Why?

cmp.note: 「以不看的方式看」。鸠摩罗什改写为「如自观身实相，观佛亦然」，把重点放在「像观察自己身体的真实相那样观佛」，梵文没有这层比较。英文照梵文译。
cmp.en: “I see by not seeing.” Kumarajiva rewrites it as 如自观身实相，观佛亦然 (“as one contemplates the true mark of one’s own body, so one contemplates the Buddha”), shifting the emphasis to a comparison with seeing one’s own body, which the Sanskrit does not have. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: His nature is the suchness of form, yet he is not form. His nature is the suchness of feeling, yet he is not feeling. His nature is the suchness of perception, yet he is not perception. His nature is the suchness of mental formations, yet he is not mental formations. His nature is the suchness of consciousness, yet he is not consciousness. He is not made of the four elements; he is like the element of space. He is not born of the six sense fields; he has gone beyond the range of the eye, beyond the range of the ear, of the nose, of the tongue, of the body and of the mind. He is not mixed with the three realms; he is free of the three stains; he follows the three doors of liberation; he has reached the three knowledges; he has reached without reaching. He has gone to the limit of non-attachment to all things; he is the limit of reality, yet without limit. He stands in suchness, yet is unconnected with it. He is not produced by causes and does not depend on conditions. He is neither without marks nor with marks; neither of one mark nor of many marks.

He is not marked, not discerned, not distinguished. He is not on this shore, nor on the far shore, nor in the middle. He is not here, not there; not from here, not from elsewhere. He is not to be known by knowledge, nor based on consciousness. He is neither dark nor light. He is without name or sign. He is neither weak nor strong. He is not in any place or region. He is neither lovely nor unlovely. He is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.

He cannot be described in any terms: not by giving, not by stinginess; not by morality, not by immorality; not by patience, not by malice; not by effort, not by laziness; not by meditation, not by distraction; not by wisdom, not by stupidity. He is neither describable nor indescribable. He is not described by truth, nor by falsehood; not by leading out of the world, nor by not leading out.

He cannot be gone to, nor not gone to. Every sound and expression is cut off in him. He is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit. He is neither worthy of offerings nor one who purifies offerings. He cannot be grasped or touched. He has no home. He is unconditioned. He is beyond reckoning. He is the same through sameness, equal to the nature of things. His effort is beyond compare, beyond all weighing. He has not gone, nor not gone, nor gone beyond. He is not seen, heard or known. He is free of all knots. He has reached sameness with all-knowing knowledge. He is the same as all beings. He has reached the non-difference of all things. He is blameless in every way. He has nothing, no impurity, no parts, no imagining. He is not made, not born, not arisen, not come into being, not produced, and will not come to be. He is without fear, without affliction, without sorrow, without elation, without agitation. He cannot be described by any conventional expression.
Blessed One, such is the body of the Tathagata, and that is how it should be seen. Those who see it like this see rightly; those who see it otherwise see wrongly.”
Then the venerable Shariputra said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, from which buddha-field did Vimalakirti, this son of good family, pass away before coming to this buddha-field?”
The Blessed One said: “Shariputra, ask this good man himself: ‘Where did you pass away from to be born here?’”
So the venerable Shariputra said to Vimalakirti the Licchavi: “Son of good family, where did you pass away from to be born here?”
